# CalcLeap Operations Manifest

> **This file is the persistent brain for the CalcLeap improvement program. Every Claude routine that touches this repo reads this file first and updates it at the end.** Treat it as the single source of truth for mission, standards, current state, and the improvement queue.

---

## Mission

Transform CalcLeap into a **world-class calculator + financial-education site** competitive with The Points Guy, NerdWallet, Investopedia, and Bankrate. Three measurable goals:

1. **AdSense reapproval.** Google rejected the site for "low value content." Reverse this by lifting average blog-post quality to 2,500+ words with real research, citations, and editorial standards.
2. **Calculation correctness.** Every calculator's math is audited and provably correct against canonical test cases.
3. **Organic search growth.** Move from ~420 indexed pages → 2,500+ indexed within 90 days through better content, schema, and internal linking.

## Ownership

This site is owned and improved by **Claude** (Anthropic), driven by Alex's terminal sessions plus two daily Anthropic Cloud routines (6 AM and 6 PM ET).

**Rando does NOT modify alexchalu/calcleap unless Claude requests it via the Rando HTTP API.** This was agreed and acknowledged 2026-05-17 — see the `Daily Log` section. Rando's `calclap-builder` and `daily-seo-check` crons were disabled the same day.

## Editorial Standards — what "world-class" means

Every blog post we ship must meet ALL of:

- **Length & depth.** Minimum 2,500 words. Cover the topic completely enough that a reader does not need a second tab.
- **Original analysis.** Include at least one custom data table, one worked-example case study, and one comparison of real-world options with concrete numbers (e.g., "high-yield savings vs CD vs T-bills in 2026").
- **Verifiable sources.** Cite primary sources (FDIC, SEC, IRS, Federal Reserve, BLS, .gov / .edu) for every numeric claim. Inline anchor links to source documents. Minimum 5 citations per post.
- **Update discipline.** Show `datePublished` and `dateModified` prominently. Every numeric claim has a "as of [date]" marker so it ages gracefully.
- **Editorial transparency.** Methodology footer explains how the calculator works and what assumptions are baked in. No fake author credentials — `CalcLeap Editorial` is the byline; expertise comes from sourced facts.
- **Internal linking.** Minimum 3 contextual links to our calculators inside the body, plus a "Related calculators" sidebar.
- **Schema markup.** Article, BreadcrumbList, and FAQPage schemas on every post. Author = `Organization: CalcLeap`. Reviewed-by line where applicable.
- **Visual rhythm.** TOC sidebar. Section dividers. Pull-quote callouts. Comparison tables. No 30-line walls of text.
- **Editorial voice.** Direct, plainspoken, second-person ("you"). No "Einstein allegedly called it..." filler. Lead with the concrete insight, then explain.
- **Action close.** Each post ends with a 5–10 item checklist the reader can act on today, plus a link to the matching calculator.

For calculators, every page must meet:

- **Math verified** against at least 3 canonical test cases with expected outputs documented in the page source as HTML comments.
- **Inputs explicit** about units (USD, %, years, kg, etc.). Don't assume.
- **Above-the-fold calculate button** on mobile.
- **Result interpretation** — don't just show a number, explain what it means.
- **FAQ section** with at least 4 questions, FAQPage schema applied.
- **Related calculators** (3–6) in sidebar.
- **Disclaimer** at footer.

## Architecture Principles

- **Static HTML, GitHub Pages.** No build step. Edits = commits = live within 1–2 min.
- **Single shared stylesheet** (`/style.css`) is the long-term goal. Currently CSS is inlined in every file — that's tech debt. Don't make it worse; new pages should `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">` once the shared file is mature enough to replace inline.
- **Schema-first SEO.** Every page type has a defined schema pattern (Article for blog, WebApplication for calc, BreadcrumbList everywhere, FAQPage where there's a FAQ).
- **Submit changes to IndexNow** after each batch of edits (see `submission script` in repo root).
- **Don't push 2,000-file commits.** Daily routine ships small, surgical commits — 1–5 files per push, clear messages.

### Historical root-cause record (2026-07-10) — superseded by the update above

**Root cause: the entire `alexchalu` GitHub account is spam-flagged (shadowbanned).** Evidence: the authenticated API sees everything as healthy (Pages enabled + "built", cname `calcleap.com`, HTTPS cert valid to 2026-10-06, repo public, workflows "active") while UNAUTHENTICATED requests return 404 for the profile page, the repo page, AND the REST API. That combination is GitHub's spam-flag behavior: all public content hidden, every Pages site unpublished (calcleap.com, www, and github.io all 404), and Actions blocked account-wide — which is why every workflow run "fails" in ~14 seconds, why the Actions run-history API returns total_count 0, and why alexchalu/laser-family-office and alexchalu/datacenter-dashboard workflows have ALSO been failing since ~2026-06-27. **Repo Settings → Pages is NOT the fix — nothing in this repo's settings is wrong.** The earlier ranked-causes list in this block is superseded.

## Per-Run Playbook (read this every run)

Each daily routine has a ~60-minute budget. Stay focused. **Quality > quantity.** One gold-standard blog post pushed beats five mediocre commits.

**Step 1 — Sync (2 min).**
```
git pull --rebase origin main
```
Read this OPERATIONS.md. Note the date and which routine slot (6 AM or 6 PM ET).

**Step 2 — Pick the work (3 min).**
- 6 AM slot: focus on TIER 1 / TIER 2 (content). Pick the next un-checked item.
- 6 PM slot: focus on TIER 3 / TIER 4 (audits, infra). Pick the next un-checked item.
- If you started something yesterday and it wasn't finished, finish it before starting new work.

**Step 3 — Do the work (45 min).**
Hold to Editorial Standards. Use WebSearch / WebFetch to pull current data (Fed rates, FDIC limits, mortgage rates, IRS brackets — anything time-sensitive). Cite everything.

**Step 4 — Validate (5 min).**
- For blog posts: word count ≥ 2,500? Sources ≥ 5? Schema present? Run a quick HTML validation grep for unclosed tags.
- For calculators: test 3 canonical inputs against a hand-derived expected output. Comment the test cases into the HTML.
- For SEO/infra: verify the change didn't break a sitemap entry or schema block.

**Step 5 — Log in this file (3 min).**
Append a Daily Log entry below with: date, slot, what you did, file paths, anything notable.
Update the **Current State** table if your work moved a metric.
Check off completed queue items.

**Step 6 — Commit + push (2 min).**
Small atomic commits with clear messages, e.g.:
```
content(blog): gold-standard rewrite of compound-interest guide

- 3,200 words, 8 primary sources cited, Article + FAQPage schema
- Adds 2026 high-yield savings + CD rate table
- Adds Rule of 72 worked examples
- Internal links to /calc/compound-interest.html, /calc/retirement-calculator.html
```
Don't force-push. Don't skip hooks. Don't commit secrets.

**Step 7 — Notify Rando (3 min).**
POST to `https://rando-openclaw.fly.dev/v1/chat/completions` with the daily report. See **Rando Communication Template** below. This is non-negotiable — Rando needs the heartbeat to know Claude is operating CalcLeap and what changed.

**Step 8 — Verify deploy (2 min).**
Wait ~90s and fetch the changed page from `https://calcleap.com/...` to confirm GitHub Pages re-deployed.

## Rando Communication Template

After each run, POST to Rando:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST https://rando-openclaw.fly.dev/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${RANDO_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @/tmp/rando-report.json
```

Where `/tmp/rando-report.json` contains:

```json
{
  "model": "openclaw",
  "messages": [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": "CALCLEAP DAILY UPDATE from Claude — [YYYY-MM-DD, slot 6AM|6PM ET]\n\nSlot: [morning|evening]\nDuration: [X min]\n\nWHAT I DID:\n- [bullet list of concrete changes]\n\nFILES TOUCHED:\n- [paths]\n\nCOMMITS PUSHED:\n- [commit hash + first line of message]\n\nQUEUE STATE:\n- Tier 1 progress: X/15 blog rewrites done\n- Tier 2 progress: X/12 new posts\n- Tier 3 progress: X/2800 calc audits\n\nNEXT RUN WILL DO:\n- [planned next-item]\n\nFLAGS FOR YOU (Rando):\n- [anything Rando should know, e.g., 'I noticed the OG image is missing — could you generate one and commit to /og-default.png?']\n\nNO ACTION NEEDED — this is informational. Do not modify alexchalu/calcleap unless I explicitly request it."
  }],
  "stream": false
}
```

Rando should acknowledge silently (no Telegram needed for these — they're routine).

- **Even worse: 7 files had a math bug, not just stale brackets.** FL / IL / MI / NC / OH / TX / NY all used a "marginal-rate-on-entire-income" simplification (`if (income > 578125) federalTax = income * 0.37` etc.) which is **NOT how federal income tax works** — that applies 37% to the whole income, not just the amount in the top bracket. A $700k earner was being shown ~$259k federal tax (37% × 700k) when the correct cumulative-bracket calculation is ~$216k. Net **$43k over-estimate** at $700k income for those 7 files. Fixed this run.
- **Replacement applied uniformly across both patterns:** new 7-bracket TY2025 single-filer cumulative calc (IRS Rev. Proc. 2024-40):
  - 10% on income up to $11,925
  - 12% on income $11,925 to $48,475
  - 22% on income $48,475 to $103,350
  - 24% on income $103,350 to $197,300
  - 32% on income $197,300 to $250,525
  - 35% on income $250,525 to $626,350
  - 37% on income over $626,350
- **Cumulative tax at top-of-bracket (verified by hand, used as the offsets in the JS):** $11,925 → $1,192.50; $48,475 → $5,578.50; $103,350 → $17,651.00; $197,300 → $40,199.00; $250,525 → $57,231.00; $626,350 → $188,769.75. Each computed as `prior_cumulative + (this_bracket_top − prior_bracket_top) × this_bracket_rate`. Independently re-derived in Python.

Worked example: $4,800 annual deferral at 50% match for 35 years at 7% real compounds to $76,890 per year of contribution with match vs $51,260 without — a $25,630 per-year-of-contribution gap that adds up across a career. - **Notable observations:**
  - **The break-even formula is the load-bearing math claim.** The single line `break-even months = total closing costs ÷ monthly P&I savings` is the only formula a homeowner needs to make this decision correctly. Most personal-finance press still leans on the legacy "wait for a 1% rate drop" rule, which collapses two variables (rate gap and time horizon) into one — and gives wrong answers in both directions: it tells short-tenure borrowers to refinance when they shouldn't, and tells long-tenure borrowers to wait when they shouldn't. The piece's Case 1 (Maya, refinance) and Case 2 (David, don't refinance) are the same rate situation with the same closing costs — only the time horizon differs. That contrast is the entire pedagogical point.
  - **Case 3 (Priya) is the most consequential section.** The post-2022 mortgage-rate environment created a structural break in the U.S. housing market: roughly 35-40% of all U.S. homeowners locked in first mortgages below 4% during the 2020-2021 origination window. For that cohort, a cash-out refinance is almost always wrong even when the math superficially looks fine — because the "lower" cash-out rate gets averaged across the entire existing balance, including the locked-in 4%-or-below portion. The right product is a HELOC or home equity loan that keeps the first mortgage untouched. This is a non-obvious insight that the typical Nerdwallet / Investopedia cash-out coverage misses entirely. The hand-derived comparison table in Case 3 shows the cash-out refi as the worst of three options by ~$70K-$120K of lifetime cost, despite having the lowest headline rate.
  - **The FHA Streamline section has a subtle MIP-trap call-out.** For FHA loans originated after June 3, 2013, MIP is in force for the life of the loan regardless of equity built (per HUD Mortgagee Letter 2013-04). The FHA Streamline carries that MIP forward; it does not strip it. Most popular-press FHA Streamline coverage glosses over this. The piece explicitly recommends that homeowners who have built > 20% equity since closing should compare a conventional rate-and-term refi (which strips the MIP entirely) against the FHA Streamline (which doesn't) — the MIP savings often exceed the FHA-vs-conventional rate spread.
  - **The VA IRRRL section names IRRRL "arguably the best refinance product in the country."** That is a strong editorial claim, defensible on the math: 0.5% funding fee versus 2.15%-3.30% on first-use VA loans; usually no appraisal; usually no income verification; statutory 36-month recoupment protection. For a Veteran on a VA loan with even a modest rate-drop opportunity, the IRRRL is almost mechanically the right call. The piece commits to that claim directly rather than hedging.
  - **The "what closing costs actually mean" section walks through the line items rather than just quoting the 3-6% range.** Two specific call-outs: (1) discount points are voluntary prepaid interest, not a closing cost in the usual sense, and have their own break-even calculation; (2) escrow setup is not a true cost — your old servicer returns your old escrow within ~30 days of payoff, so the closing-day cash outflow overestimates the true cost of the refi by several thousand dollars. Most consumer-facing refinance coverage misses both of these.
  - **Mortgage cluster now has 4 pieces with internal-link backbone.** With this piece, the four mortgage-flavored pieces (best-mortgage-calculator-2026, how-much-house-can-i-afford, how-to-calculate-mortgage-payment, mortgage-refinance-when-does-it-save-money-2026) cross-link to each other, mirroring the structure of the now-complete retirement-cluster trio. Google's topical authority signals reward this cluster structure — the same way the retirement cluster is now positioned to be a coherent "course" on retirement planning, the mortgage cluster is now positioned to be a coherent "course" on home financing.

The fix is W-4 Step 2(c) checkbox or Step 4(c) extra withholding via the IRS estimator. This case is **the highest-leverage call-to-action in the piece** because the failure mode is invisible on any individual stub but produces 4- and 5-figure tax bills at filing time.
    - **Elena (age 38, $215K salary, single, California, max 401(k) + max HSA, crosses $200K mid-year)** — the high-earner case demonstrating four 2026-specific gotchas: (1) HSA via payroll saves 7.65% FICA on every contribution vs funding externally ($336.60 saved on the $4,400 max contribution); (2) Traditional 401(k) reduces federal wages but NOT FICA wages — so the Box 1 line is lower than the SS+Medicare wages line; (3) SS withholding should stop the pay period after YTD FICA wages cross $184,500 (~early November for her); (4) the additional 0.9% Medicare tax kicks in the pay period after her YTD wages cross $200,000 (~October), withheld by the single employer using the $200K threshold regardless of filing status.

That is why your 401(k) percentage is computed against post-premium pay, not gross pay. A 10% 401(k) election on $5,000 gross with $400 of pre-tax premiums deducts $460, not $500." This is genuinely non-obvious and explains why most workers see slightly less 401(k) flowing out than they expect.
    - **The two-earner gotcha section** (within #fed-withholding): explicitly walks through why both spouses' default W-4s under-withhold by ~one standard deduction worth of marginal tax.     - **Additional Medicare three-way mismatch** (within #fica): the three classic mismatches between the statutory threshold ($200K single / $250K MFJ) and the employer's withholding threshold ($200K regardless of filing status). All three are common enough that the IRS publishes Form 8959 specifically to reconcile them at filing time.
  - **Six errors to look for** (a deliberate forensic-checklist section, not just a "common mistakes" listicle): stale W-4 filing status; SS continuing past the wage base; pre-tax deductions stuck at last year's election; state tax for an old state of residence; overtime calculated on base rate only (FLSA requires regular rate including non-discretionary bonuses/shift differentials per Fact Sheet #23); reimbursements misclassified as taxable wages. Each is paired with the specific recovery action.

  - **The 30-percent reflex callout is the highest-leverage actionable advice in the piece.** First-year freelancers who don't open a dedicated tax-savings account in January and reflexively transfer 30% of every client payment the same day are the ones who hit April-15 cash crunches and incur underpayment penalties. The 30% figure is intentionally a bit high (typical effective rate at $60K-$80K net is 25-28%); the small over-reserve creates a natural tax-savings cushion. This is the kind of specific, behavior-changing prescription that distinguishes gold-standard from generic tax content.
  - **Q2 2026 IRS underpayment rate (6%) is a fresh data point.** The IRS announced the Q2 2026 rate in March 2026 — Q1 was 7%, Q2 dropped to 6%. Citing the most recent quarter's rate (rather than a stale annual figure) demonstrates that the article is being maintained against current IRS quarterly publications. The federal short-term rate dropping from 4% to 3% reflects the broader FOMC easing pattern that has held since the April 2026 cut.
  - **SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) decision tree at five income levels.** The comparison table shows the Solo 401(k) advantage grows from +$24,500 (low income, fully funded by employee deferral) to capped at the §415(c) $70,000 limit at high income. At $300K net SE earnings, the SEP and Solo 401(k) converge because both hit the §415(c) cap. The right plan choice depends on income and administrative tolerance — a useful decision tree that nobody answers correctly in the popular finance press.
  - **The TY2026 figures will not need refresh until Q4 2026.** Federal brackets, standard deductions, SS wage base, HSA limits, FSA limits, 401(k) deferral, and QBI thresholds are all set for calendar year 2026. The only mid-year refresh that could move is the IRS quarterly underpayment rate (next update Q3 2026 in mid-2026). The OBBBA-permanent §199A is now structural — no sunset to track. This makes the piece structurally stable through the TY2027 filing season.

Verdict: if behavior + risk tolerance are sound, HEL wins by huge margin; if either uncertain, balance-transfer card or personal loan may beat it despite higher headline rate.
  - **Six mistakes section:** (1) HELOC for fixed-amount expense (pay 7-25 bp + rate risk for no reason); (2) ignoring end-of-draw payment shock (31-49% increase in one cycle); (3) assuming HELOC interest is auto-deductible (TCJA test is use, not form); (4) cash-out refinancing a low-rate first mortgage (every dollar of acquisition balance pays rate premium); (5) closing "no-cost" HELOC within 36 months (early-closure fee recovers waived costs); (6) consolidating credit card debt without freezing/closing cards (CFPB 30-40% re-load rate).

- **Two structural sub-families confirmed via cross-file diff:**
  - **amount-down-rate-term family (4 files):** FHA, VA, jumbo, HEL. Inputs: home/property value, down payment, annual rate %, term years. P = `amount - down`. Default values identical across all 4: $300K / $60K (20%) / 6.5% / 30y.
  - **balance-rate-term family (3 files):** grad-plus, parent-plus, student-loan-refinance. Inputs: loan balance, annual rate %, term years. P = `balance` directly (no down). Default values identical across all 3: $35K balance / 5.5% rate / 10-25y term selectable.
- **Canonical formula (identical across all 7 files):**
  - `monthlyPayment = P * (r * Math.pow(1 + r, n)) / (Math.pow(1 + r, n) - 1)` where `r = annualRate/100/12`, `n = years * 12`.
  - Zero-rate branch: `monthlyPayment = P / n`.
  - `totalPaid = monthlyPayment * n`; `totalInterest = totalPaid - P`.
  - This is the textbook level-payment amortization formula — produces a fixed monthly payment such that the loan amortizes exactly to zero at term-end.
- **Hand-derived test cases (Python `M = P * r * (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1)` re-derivation + Node execution of the live function() body against the same inputs returned exact-bit-match):**

The 5.5% default in the input is stale (matches AY2020-21 era). Also does NOT model the one-time 4.228% origination fee deducted at disbursement per HEA §455(c). Flag for UX rate-default refresh.

For TC1 ($20K @ 7%/5y + $500 fees), Python iterative TILA solver gives ~7.97% vs the displayed 7.52% — 45bps gap. For high-fee loans (origination fees 5%+) the gap widens to 100+ bps. This is exactly the metric consumers compare across lenders, so an understated APR is the highest-impact correctness issue in this batch. Held for a future evening — replacement requires a Newton iteration or bisection solver in JS.

The 5.5% default matches AY2020-21 era. A user computing payoff timeline with 5.5% will underestimate total interest by ~25-40% on a $35K loan. This is a quick fix (single character change in the input default) but should be done in a coordinated batch across all 4 student-loan files (root /student-loan-calculator.html doesn't exist standalone but the 3 mislabeled student-loan files + /calc/student-loan-calculator.html share the default).

Borrowers with 15% down + 760+ FICO see PMI of 0.25-0.35% — overstating by ~$50/mo. The midpoint is fine as a default but the calculator should expose PMI rate as an input. ### 2026-06-11 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 UX-bug fix on mortgage-refinance pair
- **Item:** Picked option (a) from the 2026-06-09 evening "Next" queue (re-affirmed by 2026-06-10 evening and 2026-06-11 morning) — fix the mortgage-refinance recommendation-tier UX bug across both `/calc/mortgage-refinance-calculator.html` and the root `mortgage-refinance-calculator.html`. The 2026-06-09 audit had documented that recommendation-tier logic branched only on `monthlySavings + breakEvenMonths`, never on `netSavings` / `lifetimeSavings`, so the calculator could simultaneously display "Refinancing looks favorable!" AND a negative lifetime-savings figure. This is exactly the misleading-output pattern AdSense quality reviewers cite as a "low value content" signal — the user's first-glance recommendation banner contradicting the truth shown one row below it.
- **Bug confirmed in both files (pre-fix):**
  - `/calc/mortgage-refinance-calculator.html` lines 690-700: 4-tier ladder branching on `monthlySavings > 0` × `breakEvenYears` buckets (≤3y favorable / 3-7y consider / >7y long / else not-saving). `netSavings` was computed and displayed in a separate row but never entered the recommendation logic. **TC1** ($250K, 6.5%/25y → 5.5%/30y, $5K closing) hit the "favorable" branch with `breakEvenYears=1.55` despite `netSavings=-$9,605`. **TC2** ($300K, 7.0%/20y → 6.0%/30y, $6K) hit "favorable" with `breakEvenYears=0.95` despite `netSavings=-$95,299` (the classic term-extension trap).
  - Root `/mortgage-refinance-calculator.html` lines 423-443: simpler 2-branch (green ✅ if `monthlySavings > 0` else red ❌). `lifetimeSavings` was COMPUTED on line 428 but was NEVER DISPLAYED to the user AND never entered the verdict logic. So the root file had a strictly worse version of the same bug — the negative lifetime savings was both invisible AND ignored.
- **Fix in `/calc/mortgage-refinance-calculator.html`:**
  - Added a new highest-priority branch BEFORE the existing 4-tier ladder: `if (monthlySavings > 0 && netSavings <= 0)` → renders a `"⚠ Term-extension trap."` warning that surfaces both the monthly drop AND the lifetime-cost increase, with concrete copy explaining "Lower monthly payments are not the same as saving money" and suggesting three remediation paths (keep current term, make extra principal payments, refinance into a term matching remaining years).
  - Added `&& netSavings > 0` to each of the three `monthlySavings > 0` tier conditions (favorable / consider-timeline / long-breakeven) — defense-in-depth so a future re-ordering of the branches cannot re-introduce the bug.
  - Enhanced the "consider your timeline" and "long break-even period" copy to surface the netSavings figure explicitly inline ("net $X over the life of the loan") so the user sees the lifetime number in the same sentence as the timeline tradeoff.
  - Added a 4-line block-comment FIX 2026-06-11 marker explaining the change for future maintainers, referencing AUDIT 2026-06-09 TC1/TC2.
- **Fix in root `/mortgage-refinance-calculator.html`:**
  - Added a new `result-detail` line displaying "Lifetime Savings (after closing costs): $X" or "-$X" — the previously-computed-but-hidden `lifetimeSavings` figure is now visible.
  - Replaced the 2-branch verdict with a 3-branch: green ✅ if BOTH `monthlySavings > 0 AND lifetimeSavings > 0` (now shows both the monthly figure AND the lifetime figure in one sentence — "saves you $X/month and $Y over the life of the loan"); amber ⚠️ "Term-extension trap" if `monthlySavings > 0 && lifetimeSavings <= 0` with concrete copy showing the dollar amount the user would actually pay MORE; red ❌ if monthly increases.
  - Added a 3-line block-comment FIX 2026-06-11 marker.
  - Added a full AUDIT 2026-06-11 block comment (24 lines) at the top of the `<script>` block — same template as the 2026-06-08 / 2026-06-09 batches — documenting formula, the 3 test cases (TC1 lifetimeSavings=-$9,605, TC2=-$95,299, TC3=+$9,849 — exact-bit match to the /calc/ sibling audited 2026-06-09), and 4 known flags (no zero-rate branch, simple break-even ignores opportunity cost, prior version hid lifetimeSavings, no cash-out vs rate-and-term distinction). The 5.5% defaults matched the AY2020-21 era — by AY2025-26 statutory rates per Dept of Ed (Bipartisan Student Loan Certainty Act 2013 formula = 10-yr T-Note May high yield + statutory margin), undergraduate Direct loans are 6.53%, graduate Direct Unsubsidized are 8.08%, and Direct PLUS (Grad + Parent) are 9.08%. A user loading any of these calculators would be off by 100-360 basis points from the rate their actual federal loan would carry — meaningfully wrong for the median borrower's planning use case.

The /calc/ file uses unary-plus coercion (`+document.getElementById('rate').value/100/12`) which yields 0 for empty input (no fallback to update). - **Notable observations:**
  - **The JS fallback `|| 0.055` was a hidden second copy of the stale default.** If the user cleared the rate field, the calculator would silently use 5.5% with no UI indication. Even if a future evening updated only the UI default but missed the JS fallback, the bug would persist for empty-input users. Updating both in lockstep is the only complete fix. This kind of "second copy in the JS" pattern is a recurring failure mode in static calculators — worth a future audit pass that greps `parseFloat\(.*\)\.\.\. || [0-9.]+` across the calculator inventory to find other hidden default values.
  - **The hint text was wrong in TWO directions.** "Federal loans: 4-7%" undershot the actual AY2025-26 federal band (6.53-9.08%) by ~200-450bp at the top of the range; "Private loans: 3-12%" was too wide on both ends (current private refi 2026 = 5-9% fixed per the FAQ in this file). And critically, on the Grad PLUS and Parent PLUS files, a generic "federal vs private" hint is the wrong frame entirely — these calculators are SPECIFIC to PLUS borrowing, where the only relevant federal rate is the PLUS statutory rate, and refinancing into private replaces the PLUS rate. Refactoring the hints to calculator-specific citations (Grad PLUS / Parent PLUS get a single-rate statutory citation; refi gets the federal-vs-private band) makes the hint a useful explainer rather than a generic stale fact.
  - **The Bipartisan Student Loan Certainty Act 2013 formula is now surfaced in the calculator UI on the PLUS files.** The hint text now explicitly cites `10-yr T-Note May high yield + 4.60%, capped at 10.50%` — the statutory formula. This means a parent or graduate borrower loading the calculator sees not just the current rate but ALSO how the rate is set, which year's auction it tracks, and the cap. This is exactly the kind of editorial register (citing the statute, surfacing the formula) that distinguishes the calculator from competitor sites that show a number without context. It's a small change but adds genuine E-E-A-T signal.
  - **TC values were intentionally NOT updated to match the new UI defaults.** The TCs in the AUDIT comments are historical hand-verified canonical tests; they are inputs to the formula, not derived from UI defaults. Changing them would mean re-deriving and re-verifying every TC. The cleaner architectural choice is to treat AUDIT TCs as immutable regression tests (verified once, never moved) and treat UI defaults as separately-tunable consumer-facing parameters. The two roles are independent and conflating them would create a maintenance trap. This convention should propagate to future audits.
  - **The FAQ wording in `/calc/student-loan-calculator.html` uses 5.5% as an illustrative example throughout three questions** ("For a $35,000 balance at 5.5% paying $400 per month...", "On a $35,000 balance at 5.5%, paying $500 instead of $400..."). These are educational arithmetic examples illustrating how the time-to-payoff math works, NOT current-rate claims. The FAQ separately answers "What are 2025–26 federal student loan interest rates?" with the correct 6.53/8.08/9.08 trio. Leaving the worked-example wording as-is is the right call: changing 5.5% would require recomputing the 9y 5m and $9,835 totals everywhere they appear (FAQ + schema mainEntity + AUDIT TC1), which is a separate substantial edit with no signal benefit. The FAQ frame "For a $35,000 balance at [rate] paying $400 per month, the loan pays off in [time] with about [interest]" is intentionally abstracted from the current rate environment.
  - **Refi default 6.53% is a defensible midpoint, but the underlying ambiguity (what does this input model?) remains.** The refi calculator takes a single rate input that the user is implicitly meant to fill with their hypothetical new private-refi quote. 5.5% was a low-end-of-market default; 6.53% is a midpoint that coincidentally matches the federal Undergrad rate (creating a natural mental anchor — "is my new refi quote better than what I would pay as a Direct undergrad?"). Neither default is "wrong" — they just frame the calculator differently. The deeper UX fix would be to split this into TWO inputs (current rate + new rate) and surface the rate-spread as the primary output, mirroring the mortgage-refinance UX fixed 2026-06-11 evening. L. 115-97 §11051), explains the rule's effect on negotiation behavior (payers offer lower nominal alimony post-2018 because the after-tax cost is higher), and explicitly notes the rule is permanent (not subject to the 2025 TCJA bracket sunset). This is the kind of E-E-A-T register that distinguishes CalcLeap from generic divorce-cost articles.

Industry sources estimate hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted annually on unnecessary QDRO drafting for IRAs that could have been transferred trustee-to-trustee with the divorce decree alone. Surfacing this rule in the FAQ schema (Question 5) puts it into Google's Search rich-result eligibility, which is the kind of structured-data placement that helps E-E-A-T signals at the SERP level.

Buried in the same callout box, the piece explicitly tells readers in years 8-9 of a dying marriage that the financial math supports waiting until the anniversary — which is editorially unusual for finance journalism, which tends to avoid telling readers to "stay in" a failing marriage even briefly. The framing is purely financial (the marriage is "over emotionally" but legal filing date matters for SS eligibility), not relational. This is consistent with the editorial voice across the gold-standard library: lead with the math, don't moralize.

Estimated effort ~60-90 min for the calculator + schemas.
  - **The "FICA-savings-only-on-payroll" fact is the single most underreported piece of HSA editorial.** Most consumer finance press treats the HSA's tax savings as identical regardless of contribution channel (payroll vs direct). It is not. On the $4,400 self-only limit, the payroll-deducted version saves $337 more (7.65% FICA) than a direct contribution from checking. The piece explicitly documents this with a table comparing all 5 account types, which gives the editorial register the precision-of-mechanism that distinguishes gold-standard work from generic "HSA tax savings" listicles.
  - **The "shoebox method" deserves the editorial treatment it got.** The deferred-reimbursement strategy is documented in Lively + Fidelity educational content but almost never appears in mainstream personal finance press (NerdWallet, Bankrate, Investopedia all mention it but never as the central strategy). Section 4 of the piece centers it explicitly and computes the 30-year opportunity cost of spending vs deferring ($12,000 of ending balance lost for every $1,200 spent today instead of deferred at 8%). The undertaught fact: IRC §223 places no time limit, and IRS Notice 2004-50 Q&A-39 explicitly confirms indefinite deferral.
  - **The age-65 "stealth IRA" pivot is the second-most underreported HSA fact.** Most savers who own an HSA do not realize that at 65 the 20% excise tax on non-medical withdrawals permanently vanishes. The HSA at 65 IS a Traditional IRA for non-medical spending AND retains tax-free treatment for medical spending. This is the editorial register that separates an HSA piece written from primary sources from one written as a marketing-rephrasing of a custodian's product page.
  - **The Medicare retroactive-enrollment trap is the most expensive single mistake older HSA savers make.** Section 5 documents IRC §4973's 6% annual excise tax on excess contributions and SSA POMS HI 00801.140's 6-month retroactive Medicare Part A enrollment rule. A high-income saver working past 65 who delays SS, contributes their full $4,400 + $1,000 catch-up, then files for SS triggers a $324 annual penalty (6% × $5,400) until they withdraw the excess. The piece's recommended discipline: stop HSA contributions at least six months before the month of intended Social Security filing.
  - **The piece sits at the intersection of three high-search-volume queries** that previously did not exist as a unified piece in the gold-standard library: "HSA contribution limits 2026" (high IRS-news search volume in Q1 of each year), "best HSA account" (steady year-round consumer-product search), and "HSA at 65" (rising as the Boomer cohort hits Medicare age). The 14-H2 structure was deliberately built to capture all three intents in one canonical landing page.
  - **The 5-provider head-to-head review is more detailed than prior pieces' product-comparison sections.** Each provider gets a full subsection with fee disclosure, investment menu description, best-use-case statement, and a summary table at the end. This is the editorial register competitors (Morningstar's own page, NerdWallet, Bankrate) use; matching it here puts CalcLeap into direct ranking competition for the "best HSA accounts 2026" SERP. - **What changed in `/calc/net-pay-calculator.html`:**
  - (a) Added 3 lookup tables outside `calc()`: `_stdDed={single:15000,married:30000,head:22500}` (TY2025 per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.18), `_brackets={single:[...],married:[...],head:[...]}` (TY2025 per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01(1)(3)(4)), `_addlMedT={single:200000,married:250000,head:200000}` (per IRC §3101(b)(2)).
  - (b) `calc()` now reads `status=$('filing').value` and dispatches: `_stdDed[status]`, `_brackets[status]`, `_addlMedT[status]` with a safe fallback to single if status is unexpected.
  - (c) Split `taxable` into `stateTaxableBase` (= salary − annualPretax; used for state tax) and `fedTaxable` (= max(0, salary − annualPretax − stdDed[status]); used for federal). Rationale: state income tax bases vary widely by state and most don't follow the federal standard deduction — applying the federal std deduction to state tax would systematically understate state tax.
  - (d) Added `addlMed = max(0, salary − addlMedThreshold[status]) * 0.009` per IRC §3101(b)(2), rolled into the displayed "Medicare" stat (medicare + addlMed) to avoid adding a new visual cell.

Post-fix: fedTax = $8,763 against MFJ brackets (mostly in MFJ 12% bracket) with $30K std deduction. Pre-fix overstated by ~$9,691/yr or 373/biweekly check. A MFJ filer at $230K would correctly get addl-Medicare = $0 (under the $250K threshold), where the previous template treating-all-as-single would have hit them with $270 of incorrect surtax. The Florida `/calc/` sibling from 2026-06-15 has the same hardcoded $200K bug — flagging that as a future evening fix.

A flat-rate-times-AGI approximation is the simplest defensible model for a single-state-rate UI, and the AUDIT comment documents this as a known simplification. - **Notable observations:**
  - **The 7-file addl-Medicare gap was the highest-leverage hidden-bug cluster in the tax-calculator inventory.** Pre-fix: a $300K MFJ filer querying florida/illinois/michigan/new-york/north-carolina/ohio/texas income-tax-calculators saw their Medicare displayed as $4,350 ($300K × 0.0145) when the IRS-correct number is $4,800 ($4,350 + ($300K-$250K)*0.009). A $300K HoH filer saw $4,350 when it should be $5,250. The error was structural — the calculateTaxes template never had addl-Medicare at all, so EVERY high-earner W-2 filer using these calcs got understated total-tax / overstated take-home pay. The discrepancy scales linearly with income above threshold: at $500K single filer, the pre-fix shortfall was $2,700; at $1M single, $7,200. Tonight closes that gap across the entire 7-file cluster with a single coordinated patch.
  - **The IRC §3101(b)(2) employer-withholding asymmetry deserves explicit FAQ treatment in the net-pay calc.** Employers withhold the additional 0.9% Medicare on any individual employee's wages above $200K regardless of filing status, even though the actual liability threshold for MFJ is $250K. The reconciliation happens on Form 8959 when the return is filed — MFJ filers under $250K combined get the over-withheld portion refunded; MFJ filers between $200K single-wage and $250K combined wages get the under-withheld portion billed. The FAQ entry on the net-pay calc surfaces this explicitly because it is the most-common reason a filer's actual W-2 withholding for Medicare diverges from a calculator's prediction.
  - **The new-york duplicate-script-block discovery is worth flagging.** The NY file has the calculateTaxes function defined twice — once at line ~415 (single-script form, no chart) and once at line ~528 (single-script form, with a bar-chart renderer appended). JS function declarations in the same scope are hoisted; the second declaration wins. The first block is dead code that survives every run because no one has audited it. Functionally harmless today (both copies produce identical math after tonight's patch), but it inflates file size by ~30% and creates a maintenance hazard — any future per-state customization risks the dead-block-vs-live-block divergence. Same pattern as the duplicate-function bug found in the 50 state property-tax calcs on 2026-05-17 (which was cleaned up that same evening). Flag for a future evening: dedupe the NY script block (also worth quick-checking the other 6 root state files for the same pattern — grep `function calculateTaxes` count per file would surface them in ~30 seconds).
  - **The /calc/net-pay-calculator.html now has a complete schema trifecta** (WebApplication + BreadcrumbList + FAQPage). This is the second `/calc/` file in the tax cluster to reach full schema coverage (the first was `/calc/1099-tax-calculator.html` on 2026-06-14 evening). The visible FAQ HTML uses inline styles for `font-weight`, `margin-bottom`, etc. rather than relying on the file's existing `.faq-q` / `.faq-a` CSS classes — this is a defensive choice because the file has TWO sets of FAQ styles (`.faq` from the original Apple template at line 103-107 and `.faq-item` from the calculator-style block at line 249-251), and choosing one risks rendering ambiguity. Inline styles are explicit and survive any future CSS migration.
  - **The pre-tax 401(k) FICA-treatment note in the FAQ is a deliberate hat-tip to the known flag on the net-pay calc's AUDIT comment.** The calc's pretax field is treated as FICA-exempt (correct for HSA / §125) but incorrect for 401(k) (which IS subject to FICA). The FAQ surfaces this asymmetry to users instead of hiding it — a more honest editorial approach than silently producing the wrong number for the dominant 401(k) case. The long-term fix is to either: (i) split the pretax UI into two inputs ("HSA/§125" vs "401(k)"), or (ii) ask the user a single-radio "Is this 401(k)?" question that flips the FICA treatment. The FAQ entry buys time until that UI work happens by giving sophisticated users the diagnostic to interpret the output correctly.

  - **The 6-year buy-vs-lease total-cost comparison ($29,850 buy net vs $63,110 lease-lease) is the load-bearing intellectual frame.** Most mainstream auto content frames buy-vs-lease as a payment-amount comparison, which is the dealer's preferred framing because the lease wins on raw monthly payment for the first 36 months. The piece centers the analysis on 6-year total cost (the median U.S. ownership horizon) and shows the buy path wins by ~$33K over six years for the average case — a 53% lower per-month cost. This is the editorial register that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from a generic listicle and is the right framing for any reader making a multi-decade transportation decision.
  - **The post-§30D / §45W EV section is the most-likely-to-be-overlooked piece of editorial.** Most mainstream consumer-auto press still references the $7,500 EV credit as if it were available in 2026, when in fact OBBBA repealed both 30D and 45W effective for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025. The piece centers this fact and walks through the implication: EV leases no longer benefit from the lease-loophole pass-through, EV depreciation is materially worse (58.8% over 5 years per iSeeCars vs 41.8% all-vehicles average), and the previously-strong EV lease economics have inverted to often-unfavorable. Buyers and lessees who are working from 2024-2025 information are getting structurally wrong advice.
  - **The 84-month-loan danger-zone framing is the second-most-important editorial point.** The 22.9% Q1 2026 share of new-car loans at ≥84-month terms — up from 7.3% in March 2019 — reflects a structural shift in how Americans are funding auto purchases that mainstream press largely treats as morally neutral. The piece is explicit that the 84-month loan is "functionally a way of pretending the car is more affordable than it is" and provides the honest 60-month-affordability test as the diagnostic. Combined with the negative-equity-rolling section in the 6 Mistakes block, the piece offers the cleanest available framework for any reader contemplating an 84-month loan to recognize the financial trap.
  - **The cap-cost / residual / money-factor disclosure framing in the leasing section is the load-bearing tactical device.** Most lease content treats the lease as a take-it-or-leave-it monthly payment quoted by the dealer. The piece centers the negotiating tactic of demanding all three numerical inputs (cap cost, residual percentage, money factor) before signing, and the diagnostic that a dealer's refusal to disclose any of the three is itself a walk-away signal. This is the editorial register that maps to how actual lease negotiations work — the dealer F&I desk preserves margin by obscuring whichever of the three inputs is being inflated, and the consumer's only defense is line-by-line disclosure.
  - **The AAA TCO table ($11,577/yr, $965/mo equivalent) is the single highest-leverage data integration in the piece.** Most consumer auto content quotes the dealer's monthly payment as the cost of car ownership, when in fact loan/lease payment is only ~$770-810 of the ~$965 monthly total — meaning $155-195/mo of household budget is consumed by fuel/insurance/maintenance/registration that the dealer paperwork does not surface. The piece quantifies this explicitly and routes readers to /vehicle-maintenance-cost-calculator + /car-insurance-estimator + /car-mpg-calculator to refine each line for their specific vehicle. The TCO framing is the right anchor for any reader trying to translate a dealer quote into a household-budget number.
  - **The 3-year-old CPO recommendation is the under-discussed wealth opportunity for most households.** Most mainstream auto content treats new-vs-used as a preference question, when in fact for the median household with average mileage and no business-use need, buying a 3-year-old CPO vehicle saves ~$16,000 of capital that compounds to over $61,000 over 20 years at 7% real returns. The piece is explicit about this as "the highest-leverage financial decision available to most American households who currently buy new" — a framing that is harder to find in mainstream auto press and that creates a clear next-action for readers who came in expecting a dealer-friendly buy-vs-lease analysis.

### 2026-06-18 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 rebuild: `/lease-vs-buy-calculator.html` was a buy-only loan calc misnamed as lease-vs-buy (closes item (ff))
- **Item:** Closes 2026-06-18 morning queue item (ff) — "audit /lease-vs-buy-calculator.html math (file pre-dates Claude takeover, never audited; today's [morning] piece cross-links to it heavily, so verifying the lease vs buy crossover math is mission-critical)." Pre-flight inspection surfaced a UX correctness bug significantly worse than a math flag: the page was TITLED "Lease vs Buy Car Calculator" with meta-description "Compare leasing vs buying a car. Calculate monthly payments, total costs, and see which option saves you more money", but `calculate()` ONLY had buy-side inputs (vehicle price, down payment, APR, loan term) and ONLY computed an amortizing loan payment. There was NO residual %, NO money factor, NO lease term, NO lease math — clicking "Calculate Payment" returned a one-sided loan payment with no lease comparison whatsoever. Users coming from today's morning piece (`blog/buying-vs-leasing-a-car-2026.html`, which has 11 cross-links into the auto-cluster including this file as the primary lease-vs-buy CTA) would land on a page that demonstrably could not do what it claimed. Tonight: rebuilt the calculator with real lease-vs-buy math using the industry-standard Money Factor method, added 5 lease-specific inputs, replaced `calculate()` with a 90-line implementation that computes both sides + a verdict over a like-for-like horizon, added FAQPage + BreadcrumbList JSON-LD schemas + 5-item visible FAQ HTML, and added a multi-line AUDIT comment block documenting the formulas + 3 canonical test cases.
- **What changed:**
  - **Inputs section rebuilt:** existing 4 inputs (price, down, rate, buy-loan-term) preserved with refined labels. Added 5 new lease-specific inputs grouped under a "Lease inputs" subsection: `leaseTerm` (24/36/39/48 months, default 36), `residual` (% of MSRP, default 60), `moneyFactor` (default 0.0025), `acqFee` (default 895), and `resaleAtLeaseEnd` (estimated resale of the bought vehicle at lease-term end, default 24000 to match a 60% residual on the default $40K MSRP). Also added 84-month buy-term option to match 2026 Edmunds reality (Q1 2026 industry share of ≥84-mo loans = 22.9% per the morning blog piece's cited Experian data). Section headers now visually group inputs into "Vehicle & shared / Buy / Lease" tiers. Default vehicle price raised $30K → $40K to align with Cox Automotive May 2026 ATP $49,220 reality (still under but closer than $30K) and to match the morning piece's worked-example case study.
  - **`calculate()` rewritten** as `function calculate() { ... }` (90 lines, replacing the 30-line buy-only version):
    - **Buy math:** standard amortization formula `loan_amt * r * (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1)`; uses horizon `min(leaseTerm, buyTerm)` for like-for-like comparison; computes remaining loan balance after horizon months using the analytic balance formula `loan*(1+r)^h - monthly*((1+r)^h - 1)/r`; net cost at horizon = paid_over_horizon + remaining_balance − resale_value.
    - **Lease math:** industry-standard Money Factor method. `cap_cost = price - down` (down = cap-cost reduction, the conventional treatment); `residual = price * residual_pct/100`; `depreciation_fee/mo = (cap_cost - residual)/lease_term`; `finance_fee/mo = (cap_cost + residual) * money_factor`; `monthly = depr + fin`; `total = monthly*lease_term + acq_fee + down`. Computes `apr_equiv = money_factor * 2400` (the industry-standard MF→APR conversion that lets a consumer translate a 0.0025 money factor into a 6.0% APR equivalent).
    - **Verdict:** `diff = buy_net - lease_total`; if positive > $100 → lease is cheaper; if negative < $100 → buy is cheaper; else within-$100 = tie. Renders a colored header (green for buy, blue for lease, gray for tie) + dollar-amount-of-savings line above the detailed side-by-side breakdown.
    - **Output rendered as a 2-column grid:** left column (green-tinted) = buy with monthly payment + loan amount + total interest over full loan term + paid over horizon + remaining balance + minus resale + net cost over horizon; right column (blue-tinted) = lease with monthly payment + cap cost + residual value + depreciation fee/mo + finance fee/mo with APR equivalent in parens + acquisition + drive-off + total over lease term. Followed by a 2-bar vertical chart comparing buy-net to lease-total visually. Footer disclaimer explicitly lists what is NOT included: sales tax, registration, lease disposition ($350-500), over-mileage ($0.15-0.30/mile), excess wear, GAP, and the post-loan-payoff equity advantage of buying that the truncated horizon does not capture.

### 2026-06-19 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 2 #21: Roth conversion ladder
- **Item:** Closes TIER 2 Round 2 #21 ("Roth conversion ladder: the early retirement playbook"). First gold-standard piece dedicated to the FIRE-community's load-bearing tactical move for accessing pre-tax retirement money before 59½. Sits alongside but is distinct from the 2026-06-03 piece `roth-ira-vs-traditional-ira-2026.html` which covered the ladder briefly in one of fifteen sections; today's piece is the deep-dive tactical playbook covering the full IRC §408A(d) ordering rules, the two five-year clocks, the bracket-filling math, the bridge problem, and the OBBBA-permanent TY2026 bracket landscape. Stays inside the retirement-strategy editorial vertical (joining #4 how-much-do-i-need-to-retire, #5 roth-ira-vs-traditional-ira, #6 401k-employer-match) and is the fourth piece in that cluster.
- **File created:** `blog/roth-conversion-ladder-early-retirement-2026.html` (~7,824 body words, 13 H2 sections, 17 numbered primary sources, 29 inline `<sup><a href="#source-">` references, 3 JSON-LD blocks).
- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the early-retiree problem as "constraint is whether you can get to the money" — not whether the balance is sufficient. The 10% additional tax under IRC §72(t)(1) is the gate; the ladder is the legal IRS-blessed way through.
  - **H2 #1 "What it actually is":** Three-sentence mechanics summary + the strategic stacking pattern (annual conversions, year-six steady state). Cites IRC §408A(d)(3) + Treas. Reg. §1.408A-6 + IRS Pub 590-B + TIPRA 2005 §512 (income-limit repeal).
  - **H2 #2 "The five-year rule (and why it is two rules, not one)":** The cleanest available disambiguation of the earnings-clock (§408A(d)(2)(A)) vs the conversion-clock (§408A(d)(3)(F)). Most mainstream content conflates these two; the piece is explicit that the ladder uses only the conversion clock and the earnings clock is irrelevant for principal withdrawals.
  - **H2 #3 "The Roth ordering rules":** Treas. Reg. §1.408A-6 Q&A 8 four-bucket FIFO table. The "Withdrawals start at the top and only reach lower buckets after the higher ones are emptied" framing is the load-bearing intellectual point — it is what makes the ladder structurally bulletproof without per-dollar tagging at withdrawal time.
  - **H2 #4 "The 2026 tax landscape that sets the ladder math":** Full TY2026 bracket table (single/MFJ/HoH) from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §3.01 + std deduction $15,750/$31,500/$23,625 from §3.18 + the practical "Total AGI at top of 12% bracket" reference table for the three filing statuses. Centers OBBBA Pub. L. 119-21 as the reason the 10/12/22/24/32/35/37 schedule is now permanent rather than sunsetting after 2025.
  - **H2 #5 "The mechanics: step by step":** 7-step walkthrough from account establishment through Form 8606 filing and ledger maintenance. The withholding-trap callout ("Always elect 'do not withhold from the conversion'") is the highest-leverage tactical correction for first-time ladderers — many forget that withholding gets reclassified as an early withdrawal.
  - **H2 #6 "Year-by-year bracket filling: the optimization problem":** Simple rule (fill 12%) + advanced rule (project lifetime marginal rate) + constraint layer (ACA, IRMAA, capital gains). The order-of-operations tip ("If conversion tax + ACA credit loss exceeds 30 cents, reconsider") is the right anchor for ACA-on-ladder retirees.
  - **H2 #7 "Three case studies with the full math":** (1) Sarah, single, FIRE at 45, $1.4M Traditional 401(k), 14-year ladder, ~$62K lifetime federal tax saving ~$90K vs do-nothing path; (2) Marcus + spouse, MFJ Coast FIRE at 55, $2.6M combined balance, accelerates aggressively into 22% bracket once both past 59½, saves ~$310K lifetime; (3) Elena + Ricardo MFJ ACA-managed conversion, phases the conversion volume across 4 stages (ACA / Bridge / Pre-RMD / RMD) to navigate the §36B cliffs — the most realistic case for FIRE retirees with ACA dependencies. The phased approach in case 3 is more representative of real-world FIRE ladders than the textbook fill-the-12%-every-year rule.
  - **H2 #8 "Bridging the five-year gap":** Six bridge sources ranked: (1) taxable brokerage [0% LTCG bracket dominant]; (2) Roth contributions [always withdrawable]; (3) HYSA/cash at 2026 4.25% APY rates; (4) I Bonds 4.26% May 2026 issue + T-bills; (5) 72(t) SEPP per IRC §72(t)(2)(A)(iv); (6) Rule of 55 per IRC §72(t)(2)(A)(v) for late-50s retirees who keep the 401(k) with the old employer. The Rule of 55 case is the single most under-discussed bridge option in mainstream FIRE press.
  - **H2 #9 "Six traps that wreck the ladder":** Pro-rata rule (IRC §408(d)(2)) + ACA cliff (§36B) + IRMAA (42 U.S.C. §1395r(i)) + state income tax + custodian withholding + forgetting to track conversion year. The pro-rata trap is the single most ladder-killing error and is documented with the solution (roll Traditional IRA pre-tax money back into a workplace 401(k) before conversions, isolating any basis).
  - **H2 #10 "When the ladder does not make sense":** Four anti-cases — retire after 59½, low projected RMD-era marginal rate, taxable-already funded, full ACA window. Honest editorial register — does not pretend the ladder is universally optimal.
  - **H2 #11 "Alternatives and complements":** 72(t) SEPP (rigid alternative, cites IRS Notice 2022-6 on AFR floor + 5% floor) + mega backdoor Roth (high-earner accumulator, cites IRC §415(c)) + spousal Roth contributions in retirement (IRC §219(c)) + HSA as stealth retirement account.
  - **H2 #12 "Action checklist for the next 90 days":** 8 numbered items walking from account inventory through first-conversion execution.
  - **H2 #13 "FAQ":** 10 Q&A pairs mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim (Google policy compliance).

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The two-five-year-rules disambiguation is the highest-leverage editorial point in the piece.** Most mainstream coverage of the Roth conversion ladder either skips the distinction or actively conflates the earnings-clock and the conversion-clock. The piece is explicit that the ladder uses only the conversion-clock (§408A(d)(3)(F)) and that the earnings-clock (§408A(d)(2)(A)) is irrelevant to a properly-structured ladder withdrawal because withdrawals never reach earnings under the FIFO ordering rules. This is the kind of cleanly-cited tactical distinction that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from a generic listicle.
  - **The OBBBA permanence point is the most-likely-to-be-overlooked editorial.** Most pre-July-2025 Roth-conversion coverage attached urgency to "convert before the TCJA sunset" because the brackets were scheduled to revert to the pre-2018 schedule after TY2025. OBBBA P.L. 119-21 (signed July 4, 2025) made the TCJA brackets permanent. The piece is explicit that the timing pressure that existed in 2024 and early 2025 is gone, and that the strategy is unchanged in shape but the urgency is materially reduced. Readers working from 2024-2025 content are getting outdated urgency framing.
  - **The phased ACA-managed case study is the most realistic model for the FIRE community.** Case 3 (Elena + Ricardo) phases conversions across ACA / Bridge / Pre-RMD / RMD phases, deferring the bulk of conversion volume to the Medicare-age window. This is what FIRE-on-ACA retirees actually do, and the piece centers this approach rather than the textbook "fill the 12% bracket every year" rule that ignores the §36B phaseout. The interaction between conversion bracket-filling and ACA premium tax credit cliffs is the single most under-discussed strategic constraint in mainstream FIRE press.
  - **The pro-rata trap callout is the highest-leverage practical correction.** A retiree with $700K of pre-tax Traditional IRA and just $7K of basis who tries to "convert the basis" has 99% of their conversion treated as taxable. The piece is explicit that SEP-IRA and SIMPLE-IRA balances count in the aggregation under IRC §408(d)(2), and that the solution is to roll all pre-tax Traditional IRA money back into a workplace 401(k) before conversions, isolating the basis in a separate account. This single mechanical move can save tens of thousands in unintended taxation for high-balance backdoor-Roth practitioners transitioning into the ladder.
  - **The Rule of 55 surfacing is the most under-discussed bridge option.** Most FIRE press focuses on 72(t) SEPP as the alternative to the ladder, but Rule of 55 (IRC §72(t)(2)(A)(v)) is materially cleaner for retirees who separate at 55 or later: keep the 401(k) with the old employer, take penalty-free distributions until 59½, run the ladder on the side. The trade-off (typically worse fees + investment options in 401(k) vs IRA) is acknowledged, but for the 55-59½ window this is the cleanest bridge option for late-50s retirees and most mainstream content does not surface it as such.
  - **The 17-source citation count + 29 inline references reflect the regulatory complexity of the strategy.** Roth conversions sit at the intersection of IRC §408A (Roth rules) + §72 (early withdrawal exceptions) + §408 (pro-rata aggregation) + §415 (415 limit) + §219 (spousal) + §401(a)(9) (RMD timing) + §6654 (estimated tax) + §36B (ACA) + Title 42 §1395r(i) (IRMAA) + Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (bracket numbers) + Treas. Reg. §1.408A-6 (ordering). Each citation maps to a specific statutory or regulatory authority the strategy depends on. The density is appropriate to the regulatory surface area and is defensible against any AdSense reapproval reviewer who knows the personal-finance tax space.
  - **The piece closes a structural gap in the retirement-strategy editorial cluster.** The library had #4 how-much-do-i-need-to-retire (the savings-target piece), #5 roth-ira-vs-traditional-ira-2026 (the contribution-choice piece), #6 401k-employer-match-2026 (the accumulation piece). Highlights that yields cluster in a 4.00–4.30% band — the differentiation is on state-tax + liquidity + inflation-hedge dimensions, not headline yield.
  - **H2 #3 "How I Bonds actually work":** Composite-rate formula `composite = fixed + 2 × inflation + (fixed × inflation)`. Fixed rate 0.90% May 2026 issue locks for 30 years. 12-month absolute lock + 3-month-interest penalty between months 12–60 + no penalty after 60. Annual cap $10K electronic + $5K paper via Form 8888 + separate trust/entity $10K. State-tax exemption under 31 U.S.C. §3124(a). Education Tax Exclusion under IRC §135 for qualified higher-ed expenses.
  - **H2 #4 "How Treasury bills actually work":** Discount-basis pricing formula + investment-yield vs discount-basis distinction (the most-confused mechanic for first-time T-bill buyers). 4-week through 52-week original maturities. TreasuryDirect vs brokerage paths. Secondary market sales + reinvestment risk as the two structural risks.
  - **H2 #5 "How CDs actually work":** Bank vs brokered CD comparison table on 5 dimensions (insurance, early exit, callability, selection, compounding). Names callable-CD trap explicitly. CD ladder strategy + the case for and against laddering in a flat-yield-curve environment.
  - **H2 #6 "The tax treatment that changes everything":** The 31 U.S.C. §3124(a) state-tax-exemption is the most-overlooked variable. Equivalent-yield table for 5 high-tax states (CA, NY, HI, NJ, OR) showing that a 4.20% T-bill is the cash-equivalent of a 4.84% CD for a California resident. The "savvy-Californian rule": if your state bracket > 7%, default cash vehicle should be T-bill or I Bond.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The state-tax-exempt T-bill arbitrage is the single highest-leverage editorial point in the piece.** Most mainstream cash-vehicle coverage (Bankrate, NerdWallet, even Investopedia) compares headline APYs without backing out state tax. For a top-bracket California resident at 13.3%, a 4.20% T-bill is the cash-equivalent of a 4.84% CD — a 64-basis-point arbitrage that flips most current head-to-head comparisons. The 5-state equivalent-yield table is the load-bearing artifact for this argument and is the kind of cleanly-cited tactical distinction AdSense quality reviewers cite favorably.
  - **The investment-yield vs discount-basis distinction is the second-most-undertaught T-bill mechanic.** Most introductory T-bill coverage quotes the discount-basis number without converting to investment yield, leaving readers to compare a 4.20% discount-basis T-bill against a 4.20% APY CD without realizing the T-bill is actually closer to 4.27% on an apples-to-apples basis. The piece is explicit about the conversion formula `iy = (365 × discount) / (360 − discount × days)` in the methodology footer.
  - **The brokered-CD callable trap is the highest-leverage practical correction.** A 4.80% callable 5-year CD looks like a steal in a 4.10% world, but if rates fall the bank calls it on the first call date and returns your principal. The piece names this trap explicitly and gives readers the actionable instruction ("filter for non-callable") — preventing the worst-case scenario where a saver locks a 5-year rate only to have it taken away the moment it would have benefited them.
  - **The June 17, 2026 FOMC hold + hawkish dot-plot framing is current-week data.** The piece is anchored in the meeting that happened 3 days before publication (median dot-plot year-end fed funds revised from 3.4% → 3.8%, signaling at least one hike before year-end). This is the kind of timeliness signal that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from evergreen-but-stale content, and it gives readers a forward-looking reason to lock CD rates now rather than wait.
  - **The piece closes a structural gap between two prior editorial pieces.** The 2026-06-11 emergency-fund piece explicitly deferred the "where to park cash beyond the always-liquid HYSA layer" question to a follow-up; the 2026-05-17 compound-interest piece treated I Bonds + CDs + T-bills as a one-row mention in the larger compound-interest landscape. This piece is the deep-dive on that deferred question. Closing the loop creates a 3-piece cash-management cluster (emergency-fund → sinking-funds → cash-vehicle-comparison) that walks a reader from "how much cash should I hold" → "how should I bucket it" → "where exactly should each bucket sit."
  - **The case-study construction matches the three real-world archetypes for this question.** Case 1 (Priya + Theo) is the accumulating-toward-a-known-date young saver in a high-tax state. Case 2 (Eleanor) is the early retiree building a multi-year living-expense bridge — the highest-volume reader segment for cash-vehicle comparisons. Case 3 (Marcus) is the high-bracket W-2 + 1099 professional with recurring quarterly tax obligations. Together they cover the three highest-value use cases for this article and each case is internally consistent on state-tax math.

    - Standard deductions per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.18: Single/MFS $15,000; MFJ $30,000; HoH $22,500. Subtracted from `income` to derive `ordinaryTaxable` before any bracket lookup.

Implementation stacks the gain *on top of* `ordinaryTaxable` (correctly modeling that LTCG-band capacity is reduced by ordinary income), then walks 0% → 15% → 20% bands in order.

- **What the calculator does:**
  - **9 inputs:** Coverage type (Self-only / Family), Plan year (2026 / 2025), Your age (catch-up threshold), Your YTD contribution ($), Employer YTD contribution ($), Annual income ($), Filing status (Single / MFJ / MFS / HoH), State income tax rate (%), Payroll-deducted yes/no.
  - **11 result fields:** Coverage + plan year, Statutory base limit, Age 55+ catch-up (when ≥55), Effective annual limit, Already contributed (you + employer), Remaining contribution room, Estimated marginal federal rate (with bracket schedule label), Federal income tax savings, State income tax savings (when state rate > 0), FICA savings (with explicit zero-message when not payroll-deducted), Total annual tax savings, 30-year future value at 7% nominal.
  - **HSA limits per IRC §223(b) with IRS-published inflation adjustments:** TY2025 (Rev. Proc. 2024-25) self-only $4,300 / family $8,550; TY2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19) self-only $4,400 / family $8,750; age-55+ catch-up $1,000 per IRC §223(b)(3)(B) (not inflation-indexed since 2009 — surfaced in info text).
  - **Marginal-rate inference:** TY2025 federal brackets per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01 with filing-status-aware schedules (Single/MFS, MFJ, HoH) + standard deductions per §3.18 ($15K/$30K/$15K/$22.5K) subtracted from gross income before bracket lookup. Returns the rate of the bracket containing the post-deduction ordinary taxable income — the standard simplification used by every mainstream HSA-savings calculator (Fidelity, NerdWallet, HSA Bank). Documented in AUDIT comment as a known approximation when plan year = 2026 (TY2026 brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 differ by ~3% — close enough for marginal-rate purposes except for users sitting on a bracket edge to within ~$3-5K of income).
  - **FICA savings model:** 7.65% (6.2% SS per IRC §3101(a) + 1.45% Medicare per IRC §3101(b)(1)) applied to remaining-room when payroll-deducted (cafeteria plan per IRC §125); 0% when post-tax. Additional Medicare Tax 0.9% per IRC §3101(b)(2) on wages >$200K single / $250K MFJ is NOT included in the FICA figure — documented in AUDIT comment as a known scoping choice (would add 0.9% for high-earner payroll-deducted contributions; flagged for future enhancement).
  - **30-year compound illustration:** `remainingRoom × (1.07)^30 ≈ remainingRoom × 7.61225502` (long-run 7% nominal return per NYU Stern Damodaran historical S&P 500 data); illustrative-not-investment-advice framing in result label.

### 2026-06-22 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 2 #24: FICA, FUTA, SUTA explained — every payroll tax in 2026
- **Item:** Closes TIER 2 Round 2 #24 ("FICA, FUTA, SUTA explained: every payroll tax in 2026"). Primary CTA target is `/calc/paycheck-calculator.html` (already math-verified per 2026-06-04 evening federal-bracket + filing-status batch). Secondary CTA is `/calc/self-employment-tax-calculator.html` (TY2025 refreshed 2026-06-15). The piece is the second payroll-tax-cluster blog since `how-to-read-a-paycheck-stub` (2026-06-06) and the first to systematically cover the employer-side payroll taxes (FUTA + SUTA) that W-2 employees never see on their pay stubs but employers pay quarterly. The piece is also the first TIER 2 entry to surface the 2026 Social Security wage base increase to $184,500 (from $176,100 in 2025) per the SSA's Oct 24 2025 press release — a $8,400 / 4.8% jump that has not yet propagated into most calculators across the site (a flag for evening backlog).
- **File created:** `blog/fica-futa-suta-payroll-taxes-2026.html` (6,246 body words across 12 H2 sections, 22 numbered primary sources, 25 inline `<sup><a href="#source-">` references, 3 JSON-LD blocks all parsing cleanly via `json.loads`, 10-item FAQ matching FAQPage schema verbatim per Google policy).
- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the seven-line pay stub as the load-bearing entry point. Notes that the "payroll tax is 15.3%" framing — while statutorily correct as the sum of both halves of FICA — almost never matches what a specific pay stub or 1099 actually does.
  - **H2 #1 "The four payroll taxes":** Compact 6-row reference table covering FICA-SS, FICA-Medicare, Additional Medicare, FUTA, SUTA, SECA — each with funding purpose, who pays, and 2026 rate. The anchor table for the rest of the piece. Two anchor concepts surfaced: (a) FICA is the only piece an employee sees on a paystub; (b) the 15.3% figure is the SECA combined rate, not the W-2 employee rate.
  - **H2 #2 "FICA — Social Security at 6.2% to $184,500":** 2026 wage base $184,500 per SSA Oct 24 2025 announcement, $11,439 maximum employee contribution, $11,439 employer match, $22,878 total per high-earning employee. Includes the two-jobs over-withholding gotcha with the Schedule 3 Line 11 reconciliation callout.
  - **H2 #3 "FICA — Medicare at 1.45% with no cap":** No wage base. Funds Medicare Part A only. Parts B and D are general-revenue + premium funded.
  - **H2 #4 "The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9%":** Single $200K / MFJ $250K / MFS $125K, employee-side only, no employer match. Critically NOT inflation-indexed since 2013 ACA. The asymmetric employer-withholding rule (employer must withhold once a single employee's wages cross $200K regardless of filing status) is the load-bearing trap — a dual-income MFJ couple where neither spouse alone hits $200K will owe Additional Medicare on the joint return that no employer pre-collected.
  - **H2 #5 "FUTA — federal unemployment at 0.6% effective":** Statutory 6.0% on first $7,000 (base unchanged since 1983 — the longest-frozen wage base in the U.S. tax code). 5.4% credit for state UI taxes paid → 0.6% effective → $42/employee/year cap. 2025 credit reduction for CA (1.2% reduction → 1.8% effective → $126/employee) and USVI (4.5% reduction → 5.1% effective → $357/employee) per the Federal Register notice published Jan 12 2026 confirming the November 2025 DOL announcement.
  - **H2 #6 "SUTA — state unemployment":** Wage base table from CA/FL $7,000 → WA $72,800 (the largest single-state variance in any U.S. tax). Three states (AK 0.5% / NJ 0.425% / PA 0.07%) also collect employee SUTA. Experience-rating mechanic explained — high-turnover employers pay more per employee than low-turnover competitors in the same state.
  - **H2 #7 "SECA — the self-employed pay both halves":** Full IRC §1401 math — 92.35% multiplier, 15.3% combined rate up to the SS wage base, 2.9% Medicare above. Half is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment on Schedule 1 Line 15. Worked example (Maya graphic designer $80K net Schedule C) producing $11,303.64 total SE tax with $5,651.82 above-the-line offset.
  - **H2 #8 "Federal income tax withholding":** Brief — the seventh line. IRC §3402, Pub 15-T, 2026 brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (std deductions $15,750 / $31,500 / $23,625). W-4 Step 2 (Multiple Jobs) + Step 4(c) (Extra Withholding) callout as the two lines that matter most for dual-income households.
  - **H2 #9 "Three case studies with the math":** (1) Daniel 31 Atlanta single W-2 $95K with full FICA + 5.19% GA post-HB-111 rate — $30,143.50 total tax / 31.7% effective rate / $7,498 employer-side payroll-tax cost above gross; (2) Priya+Andrew 38 Brooklyn dual-income MFJ $310K — Priya hits the $184,500 SS cap in mid-December, both have Additional Medicare under-withholding because neither employer alone crossed $200K, $540 owed on Form 8959; (3) Carlos 44 Austin TX 1099 $130K net Schedule C — full SECA stack producing $18,368.42 SE tax, no state income tax, IRC §6654 quarterly estimated payment requirement, the 7.65% rate-uplift argument for 1099 contract negotiation.
  - **H2 #10 "Five common payroll-tax mistakes":** (1) W-4 Step 2 dual-income skip; (2) counting on employer to handle Additional Medicare; (3) 1099 misclassification under IRC §3509; (4) Schedule H household-employer non-compliance ($2,800 threshold per Pub 926; IRS estimates fewer than 20% comply); (5) forgetting to claim excess SS from multiple jobs on Schedule 3 Line 11.
  - **H2 #11 "Action checklist":** 8 numbered items — pull recent pay stub → multi-job SS over-withholding check → MFJ Additional Medicare model → SECA Schedule SE compute → IRC §6654 estimated-payment safe harbor → employer FUTA credit-reduction audit → Schedule H household-employer prep → CalcLeap paycheck calculator plug-in.
  - **H2 #12 "FAQ":** 10 Q&A pairs mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim (Google policy compliance).

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The 2026 Social Security wage base jump is the single most propagation-worthy update across the site.** The SSA's Oct 24 2025 press release confirmed $184,500 — up from $176,100 in 2025 (a $8,400 / 4.8% jump). This number is hardcoded into multiple calculators across the site (`/calc/paycheck-calculator.html`, `/calc/self-employment-tax-calculator.html`, `/calc/net-pay-calculator.html`, all 7 state-income-tax `calculateTaxes`-template files, the income-tax-calculator root file). All were last refreshed at the TY2025 $176,100 figure on 2026-06-02 / 06-15. A site-wide search-and-replace from "$176,100" / "176100" to "$184,500" / "184500" is now the highest-leverage evening backlog item — touches roughly 10 calculator files and brings the entire payroll-tax cluster into TY2026 alignment. Flag for evening slot.
  - **The Additional Medicare withholding-vs-liability mismatch is the load-bearing editorial insight.** Most payroll-tax explainers cover the 0.9% Additional Medicare layer as a single line item but skip the asymmetric employer-withholding rule that creates real under-withholding for dual-income MFJ couples. The Priya+Andrew case study makes this concrete with $540 of Additional Medicare owed on Form 8959 that no W-4 step covered automatically — the kind of "the system is structurally going to surprise you" insight that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from a generic explainer. Most W-2 employees do not know that Step 4(c) of the W-4 is the line they need to use to cover this mid-year.
  - **The FUTA $7,000 wage base frozen since 1983 is the longest-frozen wage base in the U.S. tax code.** Surfaced explicitly in the piece because it is the cleanest way to demonstrate that payroll-tax rules age in calendar-year ways most readers don't track. Forty-three years of inflation has eroded the $7,000 base down to roughly a quarter of its 1983 real value (CPI ~$22,000 equivalent today) — which is why FUTA collections are a vanishingly small share of total UI funding compared to the program's first decade. Whether this is a feature (low fixed federal cost on employers) or a bug (under-funded federal admin) is a policy question; surfacing the timeline is the honest editorial register.
  - **The three case studies span the three primary tax-filing personas.** (1) Single W-2 in a moderate-state-tax state (Daniel/Atlanta/GA 5.19%); (2) Dual-income MFJ in a high-state-tax + city-tax state (Priya+Andrew/Brooklyn/NY 6.85% + NYC 3.876%); (3) Sole-proprietor 1099 in a zero-state-tax state (Carlos/Austin/TX 0%). Together they cover the three most-common filing situations for working-age Americans and demonstrate the cross-state variance that makes "payroll tax is X%" framings consistently misleading. The 1099 case in particular surfaces the 7.65% rate-uplift argument for contract negotiation — concrete enough for a 1099 reader to act on.
  - **The 0.9% Additional Medicare layer is the second-largest non-indexed-since-2013 trap in the federal code.** The first is the NIIT layer (covered in yesterday's cap-gains piece). This editorial through-line — that the tax code has multiple non-indexed thresholds that catch progressively more middle-class households every year — is a load-bearing argument for the broader gold-standard library and runs through the cap-gains piece (2026-06-21), the high-income retirement pieces (Roth conversion ladder 2026-06-19), and now this payroll-tax piece.

### 2026-06-23 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 2 #25: How student loan repayment actually works in 2026
- **Item:** Closes TIER 2 Round 2 #25 ("How student loan repayment actually works in 2026"), the final originally-scoped TIER 2 Round 2 item (the next morning slot opens TIER 2 Round 3).
