The piece is the first dedicated student-loan-cluster blog in the gold-standard library and lands at the exact moment the federal landscape is the most changed it has been since 2010 — SAVE struck down by 8th Circuit Feb 2025, OBBBA Pub. L. 119-21 signed Jul 4 2025 §82001 creating the new Repayment Assistance Plan effective for first-time federal borrowers on or after Jul 1 2026.
- **File created:** `blog/how-student-loan-repayment-works-2026.html` (7,969 body words across 14 H2 sections, 24 numbered primary sources, 36 inline `<sup><a href="#source-">` references, 3 JSON-LD blocks all parsing cleanly via `json.loads`, 10-item FAQ matching FAQPage schema verbatim per Google policy).
- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the 43 million federal borrowers / $1.78T outstanding scale, anchors the SAVE-to-RAP transition, and previews the 14-section scope. The deck explicitly calls out the legal-and-statutory reset as the load-bearing reason the article exists in June 2026.
  - **H2 #1 "The 2026 landscape in numbers":** 10-row reference table — outstanding debt $1.78T, 43M borrowers, $38,400 average / $20,000 median (the long-tail observation), 2025-26 Direct rates (6.39%/7.94%/8.94%), annual undergrad limit $7,500 third-year-and-above, $31K dependent / $57.5K independent aggregate cap, 7.5M defaulted borrowers pre-pause. The numerical anchor for the rest of the piece.
  - **H2 #2 "Federal vs. private — the loan-type taxonomy":** 9-row feature-by-feature comparison table covering interest rate / cosigner / IDR access / PSLF / death-disability discharge / deferment / origination fee / bankruptcy / Treasury Offset access. Surfaces the FFEL wrinkle — pre-July-2010 federal loans originated by private lenders, federal for some purposes (deferment, IBR) but not others (PSLF requires consolidation to Direct).
  - **H2 #3 "2025-26 Direct Loan interest rates and how they're set":** Full rate-setting walkthrough — May 2025 10-year T-Note auction 4.342% + statutory add-ons 2.05%/3.60%/4.60% per HEA §455(b)(8) = 6.39%/7.94%/8.94%; the 8.25%/9.50%/10.50% statutory caps act as ceilings but are not binding; 1.057%/4.228% origination fees netted from disbursement but interest accrues on gross; effective APR ~9.78% on PLUS over 10 years with origination drag. AY 2026-27 forecast based on 10-year T trading 4.20-4.45% Q1-Q2 2026.
  - **H2 #4 "The standard 10-year repayment plan":** Fixed-rate amortization formula with worked $35K-at-6.39%/10y = $394.44/mo / $12,332 interest example. Explicitly notes this is the default — borrowers who do nothing land here.
  - **H2 #5 "Income-driven repayment in 2026 — the post-SAVE landscape":** 6-row IDR-plan comparison table including the repealed SAVE row for reference. Walks the discretionary-income formula at 150% FPL = $23,475 single for 2026 and computes the $55K-AGI single example: $31,525 discretionary income × 10% / 12 = $262.71/mo IBR. Surfaces the marriage-tax-filing trap as a callout — MFJ pulls spouse income into IDR; MFS bars §221 deduction; the right answer depends on PSLF eligibility.
  - **H2 #6 "The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) — the OBBBA replacement for SAVE":** Full 10-tier AGI bracket table (1% under $10K through 10% above $150K) + the four core mechanics: (a) payment is % of AGI not "discretionary income"; (b) no negative amortization — ED covers any interest exceeding payment; (c) 30-year forgiveness clock (360 qualifying payments); (d) forgiveness becomes taxable beginning 2026 because OBBBA did not extend ARPA's §108(f)(5) exclusion. The $50/dep reduction floor + the $10/mo minimum are documented.
  - **H2 #7 "Public Service Loan Forgiveness in 2026":** 5-requirement rubric (eligible loans / employer / full-time work / 120 qualifying payments / annual Form PSLF). $76B cumulative discharge to 1.06M borrowers per ED Dec 2025. The new §82008 "substantial illegal purpose" employer restriction currently in negotiated rulemaking — flagged for borrowers at organizations touching contested federal-state legal issues (immigration, certain reproductive health, gender-affirming care). The PSLF+RAP interaction callout — RAP lowers the 10-year payment total, which means more is forgiven at year 10 tax-free.
  - **H2 #8 "Refinancing federal loans into private loans — almost never the right move":** The standard pitch ($80K-grad-balance refi from 7.94% to 5.99% saves $9,400) vs. the three things it ignores (IDR loss, PSLF loss, statutory discharge loss). The 3 narrow scenarios where refi makes sense — high-income medical/dental specialists with no PSLF plan, stable high-income professionals with 3-5-year payoff and 200+ bps spread, Parent PLUS holders with no income-recapture risk. Calls out that the standard scenario where this is marketed is precisely the scenario where it destroys the federal-borrower protection stack.
  - **H2 #9 "The §221 student loan interest deduction in 2026":** Full TY2026 phase-out table per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §3.21 ($85K-$100K single / $170K-$200K MFJ / MFS-disallowed). $30K-at-6.39%-undergrad-year-1 = $1,800 interest × 22% bracket = $396 federal savings worked example. The MFS-disallowed gotcha plus the gift-to-borrower workaround when a parent pays the student-borrower's loans.
  - **H2 #10 "What happens if you default":** 270-day timeline + Treasury Offset Program enforcement stack (federal tax refunds, 15% SS offset with $750/mo floor, 15% wage garnishment via HEA §488A administrative — no court order, state tax refund interception, 7-year credit reporting, ineligibility for forbearance/IDR/PSLF). Fresh Start program closed Oct 2 2024; recovery now requires either 9-payment rehabilitation or Direct Consolidation + immediate IDR enrollment.

  - **H2 #12 "Five common student loan mistakes":** (1) refinancing federal before checking PSLF eligibility; (2) not certifying PSLF employment annually; (3) missing §221 because lender didn't issue 1098-E ($600 threshold); (4) MFJ filing while one spouse is on IDR pulls spouse income in; (5) letting loans default rather than calling servicer for forbearance — federal forbearance was a phone call away.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The SAVE-to-RAP transition is the single most-changed piece of federal benefits policy of the 2025-26 cycle.** SAVE was the most generous IDR plan in U.S. history when finalized in 2023 — 5% of discretionary income above 225% FPL, full interest subsidy, 10-year forgiveness for borrowers with under $12,000 in original principal. Striking it down via 8th Circuit injunction in Feb 2025 and replacing it with RAP via OBBBA §82001 created the post-2010 federal landscape's most consequential policy reset. The 8M SAVE-enrolled borrowers placed in interest-free administrative forbearance during 2024-2025 are an entire population of borrowers whose repayment timing was reset twice within 18 months — first by the litigation pause, then by the OBBBA transition. The piece anchors the editorial register here because most borrowers I checked in research forums still believe SAVE is "paused" — they don't know it was repealed.
  - **The 8.94% Direct PLUS rate is the highest fixed federal student loan rate since the variable-rate program ended in 2006.** Combined with the 4.228% origination fee that PLUS borrowers also carry, the effective APR over a 10-year term is approximately 9.78% — higher than most 2026 private student loan refinance offers for excellent-credit borrowers. This creates a structural arbitrage opportunity for high-credit graduate borrowers and parents that did not exist before 2024, when federal rates were below 7%. The piece surfaces this as the strongest argument for the 3 narrow private-refi scenarios but is careful to frame it as the exception not the rule for everyone else.
  - **The forgiveness-becomes-taxable shift on Jan 1 2026 is the single most-undermarketed editorial insight.** OBBBA did NOT extend ARPA's §108(f)(5) gross-income exclusion for student loan forgiveness. Beginning TY2026, any IDR forgiveness (RAP at year 30, IBR at year 20-25, ICR at year 25) is taxable as ordinary income in the year forgiven — the "tax bomb" that financial planners have warned about since IBR was created in 2007 is now structurally back. The only forgiveness that remains permanently tax-free is PSLF under IRC §108(f)(1) and the Total and Permanent Disability discharge. The 30-year RAP borrower with $40K forgiven at year 30 could face a $9K-$15K federal tax bill depending on their other income — a meaningful net-cost adjustment to the RAP-is-generous narrative.
  - **The three case studies span the three most common borrower archetypes in 2026.** Undergrad with modest balance (Maya, $28K), graduate with stacked PLUS in non-profit work (Diego, $135K), Parent PLUS holder with restricted IDR access (Susan, $100K). Each case study yields a DIFFERENT optimal plan — Maya goes accelerated-standard, Diego goes RAP+PSLF, Susan goes accelerated-standard despite PSLF eligibility because her remaining work-years don't cover the 120-payment threshold. The plan-is-borrower-dependent register is the load-bearing argument against the generic "everyone should be on IDR" framing that dominates much of the public discussion.
  - **The OBBBA §82008 "substantial illegal purpose" PSLF employer restriction is the most-watched regulatory development in the cluster.** Negotiated rulemaking began Oct 2025 to draft implementing regulations. As of the publication date no employers have been disqualified. But borrowers at organizations whose work touches contested federal-state legal issues (immigration, certain reproductive-health services, gender-affirming care) should monitor the Federal Register docket. The piece surfaces this without political editorializing — describes the statutory text, the regulatory process, and the monitoring action, leaves the reader to draw their own conclusions about their own organization.
  - **The piece opens a new editorial cluster (the student-loan cluster).** Pre-piece the gold-standard library had zero student-loan pieces. The piece can anchor future cluster expansions: a future "How PSLF actually works in 2026" deep-dive (single-topic expansion of H2 #7), a "Parent PLUS guide for parents" (single-topic expansion of Case 3), a "Refinancing student loans: when it actually saves you money" (single-topic expansion of H2 #8 with calculator integration), a "RAP vs IBR vs PAYE — which legacy IDR plan to switch to" (decision-tree expansion). - **Notable observations:**
  - **The fresh policy stack of 2025-2026 made W-2 vs 1099 the most consequential it has been since TCJA.** Three independent threads converged in the last 18 months: (1) DOL's Jan 2024 final rule restored the 6-factor economic-reality test that broadens FLSA contractor reclassification exposure; (2) OBBBA Jul 2025 made TCJA's MID suspension AND QBI 199A permanent — formalizing the W-2 deduction-disadvantage that was scheduled to snap back in 2026; (3) SSA's Oct 2025 announcement of the $184,500 wage base + IRS's Oct 2025 Notice 2025-67 with $24,500 401(k) limit lifted the 1099-side retirement-plan headroom meaningfully. The piece is the first in the library to synthesize all three threads in one place.
  - **The 1099 rate multiplier formula is the single most-asked question in the cluster.** Most career-advice blogs use a single number ("multiply by 1.3x"). The piece breaks the multiplier into seven components and shows it ranges from 1.20x (married-with-spouse-coverage in low-tax state) to 1.55x (SSTB worker in high-tax state, family ACA, no spouse coverage). The multiplier-by-profile table is the most directly-actionable single thing in the article — most readers can identify themselves in one of the 5 profile rows.
  - **The QBI § 199A 20% deduction is structurally unavailable to W-2 employees and is the largest single tax advantage of the 1099 path.** At incomes between roughly $80K and the SSTB threshold ($250.5K single / $501K MFJ in 2026), QBI eliminates roughly half the SECA premium, making the comparison far closer than the simple "you owe both halves of FICA" framing suggests. The OBBBA permanence framing is critical — pre-OBBBA, QBI was scheduled to expire end of 2025, which would have flipped the W-2 vs 1099 math meaningfully starting TY2026; with permanence, the 1099 deduction-stack advantage is structural.
  - **The Maya/Diego/Susan triplet spans the three most economically distinct 1099 archetypes.** Each case study yields a DIFFERENT answer relative to the 1.5x multiplier rule of thumb. Maya gets 2.42x effective rate, way above multiplier → clearly 1099. Diego gets 2.29x in absolute terms but his family-health + NY/NYC tax compress the take-home advantage to 1.5x (right at the multiplier line). Susan gets 1.67x absolute → close to the multiplier but the SSTB QBI bite + 6% match value collapse the advantage to barely 1.27x = a tie. The narrative reads as "1099 wins all three" but the magnitude of victory varies 5x across the three archetypes.
  - **The misclassification penalty stack is materially larger than most companies realize.** IRC §3509 is the IRS's reduced-rate provision that companies use to argue down their exposure — but in practice the §3509 rate is one of FOUR penalty layers (IRC §3509 + §6651 + §6656 + 29 U.S.C. §216(b) FLSA + interest), all of which stack. The piece anchors the editorial register at "intentional vs unintentional matters but both are expensive" rather than the typical career-blog framing of "you might face penalties" — the worker's leverage in negotiating W-2 treatment IS this stack.
  - **The S-Corp election callout in the action checklist is the load-bearing tax-planning lever above ~$100K Schedule C income.** The piece intentionally caveats but doesn't deep-dive S-Corp because doing it right requires a full follow-on article (the reasonable-salary rule per Rev. Rul. 74-44, the basis-tracking rule under IRC §1366, the state-entity tax wrinkles in CA/NY/IL, the QBI interaction). Flagged as the natural follow-on TIER 2 piece — recommendation #31 below if Round 3 continues.
  - **The piece opens a new sub-cluster within the payroll/tax cluster (the "career economics" sub-cluster).** Prior payroll/tax cluster pieces (FICA/FUTA/SUTA + self-employed-1099 + how-to-read-paycheck-stub + how-to-file-taxes + capital-gains + student-loan + negotiate-salary-raise) all approached payroll/tax from the "how to file" or "how to optimize" angle. - **Notable observations:**
  - **The piece is the first to fully synthesize the PSLF policy stack post-OBBBA + post-Missouri-v.-Biden + post-final-rule.** Most existing PSLF coverage online is fragmented across (a) pre-OBBBA blog posts that assume SAVE is still operative, (b) post-OBBBA-but-pre-Nov-2025-final-rule posts that don't model the substantial-illegal-purpose narrowing, and (c) tax-treatment explainers that conflate §108(f)(1) with §108(f)(5) and miss the structural difference. The article's load-bearing original analysis is the §108(f)(1)-vs-§108(f)(5) distinction in H2 #9 — the surface-level claim "PSLF is tax-free" is correct but the reasoning matters because IDR 20/25-year forgiveness and RAP 30-year forgiveness are NOT tax-free in TY2026+, only PSLF is.
  - **The four-pillars mental model is the load-bearing pedagogical frame.** Existing PSLF coverage usually walks the rules linearly (employer requirements, then loan requirements, then plan requirements) which obscures the simultaneity requirement. The four-pillars framing makes explicit that a month either satisfies all four pillars or counts as zero — there is no partial credit. The Graduated-plan-detour worked example in H2 #2 (24 qualifying months lost despite hitting 3 of 4 pillars) is the most actionable single example in the article because it's the failure mode borrowers can most directly choose to avoid.
  - **The RAP tier table is the single most-asked question in the post-OBBBA student-loan cluster.** Existing coverage often quotes "1% to 10% of AGI" but doesn't break out the tiers or run worked examples at typical AGIs. The 6-row table at $25K/$40K/$60K/$80K/$100K/$150K for family-of-1 vs family-of-4 makes the tier-based mechanic concrete and shows the $50/dependent reduction in dollar terms (typically $12.50/mo per dependent). The table also shows the RAP-payment shape is materially different from the legacy IDR plans (which use a discretionary-income-above-150%-FPL calculation) — at lower AGIs RAP can be slightly higher than PAYE, at higher AGIs RAP can be lower.
  - **The Diego case study is the load-bearing economic argument for PSLF.** Most career-blog PSLF coverage uses small-balance examples (e.g., $40K teacher) that produce moderate discharges and don't convey the structural advantage. Diego's $160K Grad PLUS at 8.94% on $68K civil-rights-lawyer salary produces a $185K discharge and frames PSLF as the structural difference between a sustainable public-interest career and abandoning it for a private firm within 3-5 years. The math is the realistic argument; "PSLF is the most valuable federal student-loan benefit" is the slogan, but the $185K discharge on $54K out-of-pocket is the proof.
  - **The PSLF Buyback section addresses a specific 2024-2025 cohort question.** The Eighth Circuit ruling parked millions of SAVE-enrolled borrowers in administrative forbearance for 8-14 months in 2024-2025, with no clear path to qualifying credit for those months. The FSA's confirmation that PSLF Buyback can convert those months at the IDR-equivalent payment is the single most-asked question from the 2025 cohort. The article's Diego case study integrates the SAVE-forbearance-Buyback question directly into his 120-month path (months 1-8 SAVE → forbearance buyback-rescued at month 120).
  - **The "PSLF vs refinancing" decision framework section is the single highest-leverage strategic content in the piece.** Most existing coverage treats PSLF and refinancing as separate decisions; the article frames them as a single fork that depends on three variables and produces a clear decision threshold. The "refinancing destroys PSLF eligibility permanently" callout is the single most-important warning because the refinancing decision is irreversible — once a federal loan converts to private, federal protections (including PSLF) are gone forever.

The same pairing pattern as 2026-06-23 morning blog → 2026-06-24 evening (yy) §221 calc → 2026-06-24 morning blog → tonight's (xx) forgiveness calc shows the cadence: every gold-standard blog gets its CTA'd-to calculator rebuilt within 24-48 hours when the calc has a known NAME_MISMATCH flag.
  - **The four-program clock-lookup design surfaces a counter-intuitive PSLF-pattern.** TC4 (the paid-off-before-clock edge case) demonstrates that PSLF DOES NOT deliver a benefit when the borrower's monthly payment fully amortizes the loan within 120 months. The "PSLF would not produce a discharge at this payment level" warning callout is the actionable insight: PSLF is structurally only valuable when the IDR-based payment is BELOW the standard-10-year payment. A high-earner public-service employee with a small balance who pays the standard payment for 10 years gets zero PSLF benefit — they just pay off the loan via amortization.
  - **The straight-amortization projection slightly overstates RAP forgiveness.** RAP's no-negative-amortization mechanic per OBBBA §82001 waives unpaid interest each month rather than capitalizing it. The actual RAP balance would be lower than the calc's projection, which means the actual forgiven amount under RAP is smaller and the actual federal tax owed is smaller too. The direction is conservative (the calc would never under-tell a borrower they owe more tax than they actually will), but the AUDIT block + info-section explicitly flag this. A full RAP implementation would loop month-by-month and waive `max(0, monthly_interest - monthly_payment)` each iteration. Estimated rebuild to add no-neg-amort branch: 30-45 min — flagged as new queue item (eee).
  - **The §108(f)(1) vs §108(f)(5) distinction is the single most-important policy nuance the calc surfaces.** Most existing forgiveness calculators online either treat all federal forgiveness as tax-free (incorrect for IDR post-2025) or treat all federal forgiveness as taxable (incorrect for PSLF). The tonight rebuild correctly forks: PSLF = $0 federal tax per the permanent statutory exclusion + IDR = forgiven_amount × marginal_rate per the expired ARPA exclusion. The result-display tax-line includes the inline statutory citation so the borrower sees WHY the tax is what it is.
  - **The marginal-rate lookup uses post-OBBBA TY2026 brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §3.01.** Same approach as the 2026-06-24 evening §221 calc — OBBBA made TCJA's individual-rate schedule permanent, removing the post-2025 snap-back to pre-TCJA rates. Both calcs are now consistent in using the permanent post-OBBBA bracket table.
  - **The income-vs-marginal-rate decoupling could improve.** The current calc uses CURRENT income to estimate marginal rate, but the marginal rate that actually applies to the discharge is the borrower's marginal rate IN THE YEAR OF FORGIVENESS — which could be 20-30 years from now. A 35-year-old earning $80K today might be earning $150K (in nominal terms) at age 65 when their IDR clock expires. The AUDIT block flags this. A future enhancement could add an "expected future income at forgiveness" input — flagged as new queue item (fff).

OBBBA §70433 inflation-indexes the threshold starting 2027, so this is permanent structural reset rather than a one-time bump. Reg. §301.7701-3); income flows through to the owner's Schedule C; the W-9 must show the owner's name on Line 1 and the LLC name on Line 2; the TIN is the owner's SSN (or owner's individual EIN).   - **The cascading-minimum mechanic is the load-bearing reason either strategy beats minimums.** TC2 vs TC4 shows the same loans payoff in 77 months with the cascade (snowball + $100 extra) vs 112 months without (minimums-only). The 35-month delta is NOT primarily from the $100 extra alone — it's from the $100 + $40 + $90 = $230 attacking L3 in the later years of the snowball path. Without the cascade, $100/mo extra would still meaningfully accelerate but the back-half compounding wouldn't happen.
  - **Monthly compounding is a defensible approximation but it understates federal-loan interest slightly.** HEA §455(b)(1) specifies daily compounding for Direct Loans. The monthly approximation in this calculator produces interest figures that are 0.2-0.5% below the "true" daily-compound value over a 5-15 year horizon — directionally always lower (because daily compounding earns slightly more interest per dollar than monthly). Flagged in the AUDIT block + footer note. Considered switching to daily but the additional 30× iteration cost in the JS loop wasn't worth the precision delta for a strategic-comparison tool; the relative ranking of snowball vs avalanche is unaffected.
  - **The 5-row fixed input grid is a UX simplification over an "add row" dynamic UI.** Production debt calculators (Bankrate, NerdWallet) typically use dynamic row addition, which would require event handlers + DOM manipulation. Five fixed rows handles 95%+ of borrower scenarios (the median federal-loan portfolio has 2-4 disbursements consolidated into 1-3 active accounts; private add-ons rarely push the count above 5). Flagged as future-enhancement if usage data shows we're capping out at 5.

  - **The March 16 2026 ICE fact-sheet revision is the single most consequential 2026 update for I-9 compliance.** The 1997 Virtue Memorandum had governed the substantive-vs-technical distinction for nearly 30 years; the March 2026 revision reclassified more than ten previously-curable categories as substantive, meaning the fine is immediate and the 10-day cure period vanishes. Late Section 2 (the single most common I-9 defect) is now substantive on day one. Practitioners reporting on the change estimate that average per-audit fines will roughly double under the new framework. The piece surfaces this as an explicit warning callout in the Section 2 explanation.
  - **The penalty asymmetry between I-9 and W-4 is the load-bearing narrative insight.** Most existing content treats the two forms as similar-looking onboarding paperwork with comparable importance. The piece centers the asymmetry: the W-4 has effectively zero employee-side penalty (default to single-no-adjustments + employee reclaims via tax return) and modest employer-side IRC §3403 liability. The I-9 has up to $28,619 per worker for knowingly-hiring violations, and per-form paperwork fines aggregate. A 1,000-employee company with a 25% defect rate is in seven-figure-fine territory. The "$28,619 penalty if you get it wrong" anchor in the title and deck is the highest-leverage 2026 hook for search and CTR.
  - **The alternative remote inspection procedure is the most actionable employer-side change in three years.** Effective Aug 1 2023 and codified at 8 CFR §274a.2(b)(1)(vi), it substantially reduced the practical friction of hiring fully remote employees who never visit the worksite — but only for E-Verify enrollees in good standing. The piece pairs the regulation citation with the E-Verify enrollment landscape so the reader understands both the eligibility and the operational benefit. Many small employers still don't know the procedure exists; surfacing it for them is one of the higher-leverage editorial moves available in the I-9 cluster.

  - **The tax-form sub-cluster is now structurally a trilogy, not a pair.** With this morning's 1099-K-vs-1099-NEC piece, the cluster opened 2026-06-27 by W-9-vs-W-4 and extended 2026-06-29 by I-9-vs-W-4 now covers all three temporally distinct points where federal tax-form confusion bites: at-the-offer (W-9 vs W-4: which form is the payer handing me, and what does that mean about my classification?), at-the-start-date (I-9 vs W-4: which boxes do I check on which form, and what are the deadlines?), and at-year-end (1099-K vs 1099-NEC: which forms should I expect to receive, and how do I reconcile them on my return?). Each piece anchors on /calc/paycheck-calculator.html and/or /calc/1099-tax-calculator.html, deliberately reinforcing the cluster's internal-link graph for both user navigation and topical-authority signals.
  - **The OBBBA §70432/§70433 paired reversal is the highest-leverage 2026 tax-form story Congress passed.** Both sections changed thresholds, but in opposite directions: §70433 RAISED the 1099-NEC threshold from $600 to $2,000 (less paperwork for payers, fewer year-end forms for low-dollar contractors), and §70432 RESTORED the 1099-K threshold from the planned $600 / phased $5K-$2.5K to the pre-ARPA $20K-AND-200-transactions (less paperwork for platforms, fewer year-end forms for low-volume sellers). The piece centers this asymmetry rather than treating the two threshold changes as separate events. Most existing online content on either form covers one or the other in isolation; the piece's value-add is the unified treatment.
  - **The §6045(f) attorney-payment carve-out is the most likely 2026 payer-side foot-fault.** OBBBA §70433 raised general 1099-NEC reporting to $2,000 but did not amend the §6045(f) special rule for attorney payments, which remains at $600. Small-business payers reading the OBBBA headline summaries are very likely to assume the new $2,000 floor applies universally and skip 1099-NEC issuance to attorneys paid between $600 and $1,999. The piece's "6 mistakes" section calls this out explicitly, and the FAQ surface area mirrors it.
  - **The IRC §6050W(c)(1) personal-payment carve-out is the highest-leverage 2026 recipient-side surprise-tax-form prevention.** When the ARPA $600 1099-K threshold was looming, the Venmo/PayPal/Cash App platforms had to build infrastructure to distinguish personal from business transactions (PayPal's "Friends and Family" vs "Goods and Services" toggle, Venmo's business-profile separation). That infrastructure remains in place after the OBBBA reversion. Most users still don't know that misclassifying a personal transfer as "Goods and Services" can pull it into the 1099-K stream — the piece surfaces this prominently in the FAQ and the "6 mistakes" section.
  - **Zelle exemption from 1099-K reporting** is one of the lesser-known 1099-K trivia points that the piece surfaces because Zelle doesn't hold funds in transit (bank-to-bank settlement without a settlement-organization intermediary), so §6050W's "payment settlement entity" definition simply doesn't apply. For high-volume Zelle users who would otherwise be alarmed by the OBBBA reversion math, this is meaningful clarity.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The IDR calc's previous TC2 RAP overstatement was 6× because the straight-amortization formula compounds the unpaid interest at 7.94% for 360 months while the no-neg-amort waiver freezes the balance.** The straight-amort projection gives $120K × (1.006617)^360 - $383.33 × ((1.006617)^360 - 1)/0.006617 = $724,637. The actual no-neg-amort outcome is just $120,000 (balance frozen for 360 months). The 6× ratio is roughly the ratio of `(1+r)^n` (≈10.8x growth at 7.94% over 30 years) to the partial offset from the constant payment. For lower rates or shorter clocks the multiple is smaller, but the structural overstatement is always non-trivial when payment < interest.
  - **The (ggg) "deps separate from family-size" fix is editorially load-bearing for childless couples on RAP.** A married childless couple filing MFJ enters family_size=2 for FPL purposes (correct) but had been getting credited with 1 "dependent" for the $50/mo RAP reduction (wrong — the spouse is not a tax dependent). That's a $50/mo × 360 months = $18,000 lifetime overstatement of forgiven amount + tax (since lower payment → less principal reduction → more forgiven → more tax). The new "Tax Dependents (excluding spouse)" input lets the user enter 0 for the childless case, eliminating the overstatement.

### 2026-07-02 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 site-wide SS wage-base cap sweep (closes queue item (uuu), the highest-magnitude single-batch math fix in the SE-tax family)

- **Slot:** evening (6 PM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** Queue item (uuu) — site-wide FICA cap audit sweep flagged as HIGHEST-PRIORITY EVENING WORK in the 2026-07-01 evening log after the same SS-cap bug family surfaced on `/calc/estimated-quarterly-tax-calculator.html`. The bug pattern: SE tax computed as `netProfit * 0.9235 * 0.153` applies a flat 15.3% to unlimited SE earnings, ignoring the Social Security wage-base cap (IRC §1401(a) OASDI is capped; only IRC §1401(b) Medicare is uncapped). At $300K SE income this overstates SE tax by $11,476.20/yr; at $500K by ~$27K/yr. Same bug family as (tt) closed on `/calc/paycheck-calculator.html` on 2026-06-22 evening (W-2 flavor) and closed on `/calc/estimated-quarterly-tax-calculator.html` on 2026-07-01 evening (SE flavor, one file). This morning's log recommended the /calc/1099-tax-calculator.html audit, but tonight's site-wide sweep is higher-leverage: 7 files fixed vs 1.

- **Files touched (7 calcs + OPERATIONS.md):**
  - **`/self-employment-tax-calculator.html`** — flagship SE tax calc. Added full AUDIT block + fixed SS cap. Below-cap TCs identical to pre-fix; TC3 above-cap now correct.
  - **`/1099-tax-calculator.html`** — 1099 contractor variant of shared template. Added AUDIT block + fixed SS cap.
  - **`/llc-tax-calculator.html`** — single-member LLC Schedule C variant. Added AUDIT block + fixed SS cap. Note: multi-member LLCs and S-corp-electing LLCs need separate models (documented in AUDIT block).
  - **`/quarterly-tax-calculator.html`** — updated existing 2026-06-14 AUDIT block to reflect the SS-cap fix; other NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW flags (stale TY2023 brackets, missing HoH, no std deduction) remain open as separate future item.
  - **`/s-corp-tax-calculator.html`** — the most nuanced file tonight. Added a detailed AUDIT block flagging NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW because the underlying model is semantically wrong: S-corp shareholders do NOT pay SE tax on their K-1 distributive share (per Rev. Rul. 59-221 and IRC §1402(a)) — only reasonable-comp W-2 wages incur FICA. The whole point of S-corp status is to convert Schedule C SE-taxable income into distributions that escape SE tax; a calculator that applies 15.3% to S-corp net profit tells the opposite story from the correct tax outcome. Correct model requires TWO inputs (W-2 wages + K-1 distribution). PARTIAL FIX 2026-07-02 evening: SS cap applied on the SE-tax leg for consistency with the family; this reduces the wrong-model overstatement magnitude on high earners but does not fix the model. Full rebuild deferred (~1 evening).
  - **`/quarterly-tax.html`** — the simplest, most out-of-date variant. Had two math bugs stacked: (a) missing the §1402(a)(12) 92.35% factor entirely (over-taxed all earners by ~8.3% of the SE-tax leg beyond the SS-cap issue), (b) missing SS cap. Both fixed tonight + added AUDIT block noting remaining NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW for the flat-22%-federal / TY2023-std-deduction / no-filing-status-branching layer.
  - **`/calc/1099-tax-calculator.html`** — the well-audited `/calc/` variant (originally audited 2026-06-14). Live code had `let seTax = seTaxBase * 0.153` on line 616 — same bug. Fixed line 616 to split into `min(seBase, 184500) * 0.124 + seBase * 0.029` + updated the 2026-06-14 AUDIT header to reflect the fix. TC3 (head, seBase=147760, below cap) unchanged by the fix.

- **The fix (identical shape across all 7 files):**
  ```js
  // Pre-fix (buggy):
  const selfEmploymentTax = netProfit * 0.9235 * 0.153; // 92.35% of net profit × 15.3%

  // Post-fix:
  const seTaxBase = Math.max(0, netProfit) * 0.9235; // §1402(a)(12) - 92.35% of net profit
  const SS_WAGE_BASE = 184500; // TY2026 SS wage base per SSA Press Release Oct 24 2025
  const socialSecurityTax = Math.min(seTaxBase, SS_WAGE_BASE) * 0.124; // §1401(a) OASDI (capped)
  const medicareTax = seTaxBase * 0.029; // §1401(b) Medicare (uncapped)
  const selfEmploymentTax = socialSecurityTax + medicareTax;
  ```
  Two behavioral guarantees: below-cap outputs are algebraically identical to the pre-fix ($40K net → seBase=$36,940, pre-fix = post-fix = $5,651.82); above-cap outputs are correctly reduced (e.g., $300K net → seBase=$277,050, ssTax caps at $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00, pre-fix was $34,354.20). Also: `Math.max(0, netProfit)` clamps negative net income to $0 SE tax (pre-fix returned negative values for a loss).

- **Test cases (all Node-verified vs Python hand-derivation, exact-cent match — see `/tmp/claude-0/.../scratchpad/verify_secap.js` and `/tmp/.../verify_live.js`):**
  - **TC1 low_below_cap** (gross=$50K, expenses=$10K): netProfit=$40,000, seBase=$36,940, ssTax=$4,580.56, medTax=$1,071.26, seTax=**$5,651.82** (pre-fix=$5,651.82, delta=$0.00) — below cap, identical output. Confirms below-cap behavior preserved.
  - **TC2 mid_below_cap** (gross=$100K, expenses=$20K): netProfit=$80,000, seBase=$73,880, ssTax=$9,161.12, medTax=$2,142.52, seTax=**$11,303.64** (pre-fix=$11,303.64, delta=$0.00) — below cap, identical.
  - **TC3 high_ABOVE_SS_CAP** (gross=$300K, expenses=$0): netProfit=$300,000, seBase=$277,050, ssTax=min($277,050, $184,500)×0.124=**$22,878.00** (CAP BINDS — pre-fix ssTax portion was $34,354.20), medTax=$8,034.45, seTax=**$30,912.45** (pre-fix=$42,388.65, delta=**-$11,476.20/yr more accurate**). This is the core fix and the highest-visibility per-user improvement.
  - **Edge negative_net_profit** (gross=$20K, expenses=$30K): netProfit=-$10,000, seBase=$0 (Math.max clamp), seTax=**$0.00** (pre-fix=-$1,412.95, delta=+$1,412.95). Confirms losses no longer produce negative SE tax values.
  - **TC5 exactly_at_cap** (gross=$199,784.51, expenses=$0): seBase=$184,500.99 (just over cap), post-fix seTax=$28,228.53 vs pre-fix $28,228.65 (delta -$0.12). Confirms cap kicks in smoothly at the boundary.

- **/quarterly-tax.html additional bug (worth calling out):** This file was the WORST of the seven — its pre-fix formula was `netIncome * 0.153` without the §1402(a)(12) 92.35% factor at all. So pre-fix, a $10K net earner was over-taxed by (10000 × 0.153) - (10000 × 0.9235 × 0.153) = $1,530 - $1,412.96 = **$117 above the correct-uncapped formula, ON TOP OF** the SS-cap issue at high incomes. TC3 example: $300K → pre-fix `300000 × 0.153 = $45,900`; post-fix `$30,912.45` — a **$14,987.55/yr overstatement** at $300K. Below cap: $40K → pre-fix `40000 × 0.153 = $6,120`; post-fix `$5,651.82` — a **$468.18/yr overstatement** even at $40K. Bug family is arguably worse than the SS-cap issue at low incomes (proportionally larger error). Both bugs fixed atomically tonight.

- **/s-corp-tax-calculator.html semantic-model flag (worth calling out):** The whole file is applying the wrong tax model. S-corp shareholders don't pay SE tax on distributions; they pay FICA only on reasonable-comp W-2 wages. Per Rev. Rul. 59-221 and IRC §1402(a), K-1 distributive share is EXCLUDED from net earnings from self-employment. A calculator that applies 15.3% to S-corp net profit demonstrates the exact opposite of the S-corp tax advantage. Correct model requires two inputs (wages + K-1); optional Sole-Prop vs S-corp savings comparison is the primary user value-prop. Documented in the AUDIT block; SS-cap partial fix applied for consistency with the sibling family; full rebuild deferred as a separate ~1-evening item.

### 2026-07-03 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 FULL REBUILD of `/s-corp-tax-calculator.html` (closes queue item (vvv), the single most user-misleading calc surfaced by 2026-07-02 evening's SS-cap sweep)

- **Slot:** evening (6 PM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** Queue item (vvv) — full rebuild of `/s-corp-tax-calculator.html` flagged 2026-07-02 evening as the highest-priority remaining TIER 3 tax-cluster fix. The pre-rebuild file applied SE tax to S-corp net profit — the exact opposite of the S-corp tax advantage. Per IRC §1402(a) and Rev. Rul. 59-221, S-corp K-1 distributive share is EXCLUDED from net earnings from self-employment; only the reasonable-compensation W-2 wages paid to a shareholder-employee incur FICA. The pre-rebuild calc showed $0 savings vs sole prop; the correct model shows ~$14K/yr savings for a typical $200K/$80K MFJ case. Both this morning's and last night's logs listed this as the top evening-slot recommendation.

- **Files touched (2):**
  - **`/s-corp-tax-calculator.html`** — full rewrite (393 → 616 lines). Complete new AUDIT block, new inputs, new script logic, new results UI, FAQPage + BreadcrumbList JSON-LD added.
  - **`OPERATIONS.md`** — Current State header date + calculator-with-verified-math description updated to reflect the file's promotion from PARTIAL/NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW to VERIFIED; this Daily Log entry appended.

- **The correct-model rebuild — what changed:**
  - **Inputs:** Old 3 inputs (income, expenses, filing) → New 3 inputs (**netProfit**, **wages** [reasonable comp], **filing**). The prior "gross income - expenses = netProfit" flow presumed a Schedule C model; the new flow accepts netProfit directly since S-corps file 1120-S with their own P&L and the user-facing question is really "how do I split netProfit between wages and distribution."
  - **Filing status:** Added HoH branch (was single/married only). All 3 statuses now have their own TY2025 brackets + standard deduction + Additional Medicare threshold per IRC §3101(b)(2) — single/HoH $200K, MFJ $250K.
  - **S-corp side computation:**
    - `employerFICA = min(wages, $184,500) × 6.2% + wages × 1.45%` (deductible by S-corp business, reduces K-1)
    - `employeeFICA = min(wages, $184,500) × 6.2% + wages × 1.45% + max(0, wages - AddlMedThresh) × 0.9%`
    - `totalFICA = employerFICA + employeeFICA` (both halves paid by owner economically)
    - `distribution = max(0, netProfit - wages - employerFICA)` — K-1 pass-through
    - `agi = wages + distribution` (both flow through to owner's 1040)
    - `taxable = max(0, agi - stdDeduction[filing])`
    - `fedTax = progressive bracket lookup TY2025 Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01`
    - `scorpTotal = totalFICA + fedTax`
  - **Sole-Prop comparison (computed in parallel on same netProfit):**
    - `seBase = netProfit × 0.9235` (§1402(a)(12))
    - `ssTax = min(seBase, $184,500) × 12.4%` (§1401(a) capped)
    - `medTax = seBase × 2.9%` (§1401(b) uncapped)
    - `addlMed = max(0, seBase - AddlMedThresh) × 0.9%`
    - `seTax = ssTax + medTax + addlMed`
    - `seDeduction = (ssTax + medTax) / 2` (§164(f) — Additional Medicare is NOT deductible)
    - `taxable = max(0, netProfit - seDeduction - stdDeduction[filing])`
    - `fedTax = same bracket lookup`
    - `spTotal = seTax + fedTax`
  - **Savings = spTotal - scorpTotal** — the primary user-facing output, shown as a green hero card when positive and a red "S-corp costs MORE" card when negative.
  - **UX warnings surfaced when the calc would mislead:**
    - **wages > netProfit** → red hero card + warning: "Reasonable-comp exceeds net profit. You cannot pay yourself more in wages than the business earns." Distribution clamps to $0.
    - **wages < 30% of netProfit AND netProfit ≥ $50K** → warning about IRS scrutiny under the reasonable-compensation doctrine, citing Watson v. US (8th Cir. 2012) and pointing to RCReports + BLS OES as comparable-salary databases.
    - **netProfit < $40K** → warning that compliance costs (Form 1120-S ≈ $800-$2K, payroll ≈ $300-$800, state franchise fees) typically exceed the FICA savings at that scale.

- **Test cases (all Node-verified via `/tmp/.../scratchpad/verify_scorp.js` + live-code re-verification via `/tmp/.../scratchpad/verify_live_scorp.js` — exact-cent match Python hand-derivation = standalone-JS = live-in-page-JS):**
  - **TC1 low_single** (netProfit=$50K, wages=$30K, single): S-corp employerFICA=$2,295.00, employeeFICA=$2,295.00 (addlMed=$0), totalFICA=$4,590.00, distribution=$17,705.00, taxable=$32,705.00, fedTax=$3,686.10, **S-corp TOTAL=$8,276.10**. Sole-Prop seBase=$46,175.00, seTax=$7,064.77, seDed=$3,532.39, taxable=$31,467.61, fedTax=$3,537.61, **SP TOTAL=$10,602.39**. **SAVINGS=$2,326.29** — modest at low income; still positive because SE-tax on $46K vs FICA on $30K.
  - **TC2 mid_married** (netProfit=$200K, wages=$80K, MFJ): S-corp totalFICA=$12,240.00, distribution=$113,880.00, taxable=$163,880.00, fedTax=$25,882.60, **S-corp TOTAL=$38,122.60**. Sole-Prop seBase=$184,700.00 (SS cap binds), seTax=$28,234.30, seDed=$14,117.15, taxable=$155,882.85, fedTax=$24,123.23, **SP TOTAL=$52,357.53**. **SAVINGS=$14,234.93** — the sweet spot: wages well below SS cap ($80K vs $184.5K) but netProfit at SS cap means the sole-prop side pays maximum SS ($22,878) while the S-corp side pays SS only on $80K = $9,920 (both halves). The ~$13K FICA-on-distribution differential drives the $14K savings.
  - **TC3 high_single_cap** (netProfit=$300K, wages=$200K, single): S-corp employerFICA=$14,339 (SS capped at $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439; Medicare uncapped $200K × 1.45% = $2,900), employeeFICA=$14,339 (addlMed=$0 because wages exactly at $200K threshold, IRS uses > not ≥), totalFICA=$28,678, distribution=$85,661, taxable=$270,661, fedTax=$64,278.60, **S-corp TOTAL=$92,956.60**. Sole-Prop seBase=$277,050, seTax=$31,605.90 (incl. $693.45 addlMed on seBase-$200K), seDed=$15,456.23, taxable=$269,543.78, fedTax=$63,887.57, **SP TOTAL=$95,493.47**. **SAVINGS=$2,536.87** — small because $200K wages nearly maxes the SS cap ($184.5K), leaving only Medicare-side savings ($277K vs $200K × 2.9% ≈ $2,234) plus the Additional Medicare surtax the sole-prop pays. Demonstrates the "wages too high erodes S-corp benefit" pattern the calc's warnings surface.
  - **TC4 hoh_mid** (netProfit=$150K, wages=$60K, HoH): S-corp totalFICA=$9,180.00, distribution=$85,410.00, taxable=$122,910.00, fedTax=$20,606.40, **S-corp TOTAL=$29,786.40**. Sole-Prop seBase=$138,525.00, seTax=$21,194.32, seDed=$10,597.16, taxable=$116,902.84, fedTax=$19,164.68, **SP TOTAL=$40,359.01**. **SAVINGS=$10,572.61** — confirms HoH branch wires correctly (uses $22,500 HoH standard deduction and $17K/$64,850/$103,350 HoH brackets, distinct from single).

- **What the piece covers (H2 map + editorial spine):**
  - **H2-1 Fundamental difference.** SEP-IRA is one bucket (employer, IRC §408(k)); Solo 401(k) is two buckets (employee elective deferral IRC §402(g) $24,500 + employer profit-sharing 25%/20%, both aggregating to §415(c) $72,000). Frames the entire piece: the elective deferral IS the entire structural distinction, and it's worth ~$24,500/yr of extra shelter for anyone under ~$325K Schedule C.
  - **H2-2 2026 contribution limits table.** 13-row side-by-side table anchored on IRS Notice 2025-67 + IR-2025-111 covering §402(g) $24,500 elective deferral, §415(c) $72,000 DC limit, §414(v) $8,000 age-50 catch-up, SECURE 2.0 §109 $11,250 age-60–63 super catch-up, §401(a)(17) $360,000 compensation cap, Roth availability (including SECURE 2.0 §601 Roth SEP), §408(d)(2) pro-rata aggregation, IRC §72(p) loan availability, and IRC §6058 Form 5500-EZ trigger at $250K plan assets.
  - **H2-3 The math (25%→20% algebra).** Full derivation of the IRC §401(c)(2) circular definition — C = 0.25 × (NE − ½SE − C) resolves to C = 0.20 × (NE − ½SE). Flags the excise tax under IRC §4973 (6%/year on the excess) for over-contributors. Full all-in formula for a 2026 Schedule C sole proprietor with the SSA-Oct-2025 $184,500 SS wage base and IRC §164(f) half-SE-tax exclusion of the Additional Medicare 0.9%.
  - **H2-4 Three case studies with full hand-derived numbers.**
    - **Case 1 Jasmine, $50K SC / age 34:** SEP $9,293.52 vs Solo 401(k) $33,793.52 — Solo shelters 3.6× more, $24,500 delta compounded to $2.28M at 31 years / 7% real.
    - **Case 2 David, $180K SC / age 52:** SEP $33,456.68 vs Solo 401(k) $65,956.68 (includes age-50 catch-up); $32,500 delta = ~$7,800 current-year federal tax savings at 24% marginal.
    - **Case 3 Priya + Ravi, $340K SC / spouse-in-business:** Priya alone hits §415(c) $72,000 ceiling; Ravi's $22K W-2 gets $27,500 sheltered as second Solo participant. Household total $99,500 vs SEP household total $65,628 — $33,872 delta.
  - **H2-5 The 2026 deadline calendar.** 6-row side-by-side deadline table with the key structural asymmetry: SEP-IRA can be BOTH established AND funded through the extended tax return due date (Oct 15, 2027 for TY2026), while Solo 401(k) PLAN must exist by Dec 31, 2026. Cites SECURE Act §201 for the employer-contribution deadline extension.
  - **H2-6 SECURE 2.0 §603 Roth catch-up.** IRC §414(v)(7) mandate that catch-up contributions from participants with prior-year FICA wages > $150,000 (per Notice 2025-67 threshold, indexed from statutory $145K) be designated Roth. Notes that sole proprietors are NOT subject (Schedule C is not IRC §3121 wages), but S-corp shareholder-employees ARE. Cites the IRS final regulations release + the Franklin Templeton / Trucker Huss / Thomson Reuters coverage of the two-year good-faith transition.
  - **H2-7 The backdoor Roth pro-rata trap.** Concrete example: $50K SEP + $7.5K fresh nondeductible Traditional IRA = $6,522 of a $7,500 backdoor conversion taxed. Solo 401(k) escape via IRC §408(d)(2) exclusion of §401(a) plan balances. Notes that rolling an existing SEP into a Solo 401(k) before Dec 31 is the single-most-valuable one-time move for high-earning freelancers with ongoing backdoor-Roth strategy.
  - **H2-8 Setup friction + admin burden.** SEP is Form 5305-SEP boilerplate + 15 minutes at Fidelity/Schwab/Vanguard/E*TRADE, no ongoing filing. Solo 401(k) is: adopt plan document (30–45 min), get EIN (10 min), document elective-deferral election contemporaneously, file Form 5500-EZ once plan assets > $250K (July 31 deadline, IRC §6058).
  - **H2-9 Six mistakes.** (1) Contributing 25% of gross SC instead of 20% of net-earnings-after-half-SE. (2) Assuming Solo 401(k) elective deferral is percentage-based. (3) Opening a SEP in July 2027 for TY2026 without checking backdoor-Roth pro-rata impact. (4) Missing the Dec 31, 2026 Solo 401(k) plan-adoption deadline. (5) Hiring a common-law employee mid-year (SEP §408(k)(2) coverage cascades; Solo 401(k) §401(k)(15) LTPT rules). (6) Confusing $360K comp cap with contribution ceiling.
  - **H2-10 Action checklist.** 8 items tied to the calc family + the deadline calendar + the backdoor-Roth rollover move + the July 31 5500-EZ reminder.
  - **H2-11 FAQ.** 10 questions mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim, covering the "biggest difference," the 2026 limits, the 25%→20% algebra, the Roth catch-up applicability, the deadline structure, the low-income Solo 401(k) crush, the two-business SEP+Solo combo, the admin burden, the hire-an-employee scenario (including the spouse-participation exception), and the backdoor-Roth pro-rata trap.

  - **The 25%→20% algebra is derived, not just asserted.** Most competing pieces state "25% of comp = 20% of Schedule C" as a fact without showing where it comes from. This is the exact interaction that most freelancer-facing comparison content skips.
  - **The SECURE 2.0 §603 Roth catch-up sole-prop exemption is explicitly cited to IRC §3121.** Because Schedule C income is not FICA wages, the §414(v)(7) trigger cannot be met.   - **The backdoor Roth pro-rata trap gets a concrete $6,522 tax-cost example** — most pieces mention the trap but don't quantify. Ours gives the exact math (§408(d)(2) aggregation × conversion amount / total IRA balance) and offers the Solo 401(k) rollover escape.

This is the practical decision-driver that most comparison content buries as a footnote.

### 2026-07-05 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 3 #37: Backdoor Roth IRA in 2026 (retirement sub-cluster continuation from #36 SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k))

- **Slot:** morning (6 AM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** TIER 2 Round 3 #37 — "Backdoor Roth IRA in 2026: the pro-rata trap, mega backdoor variant, and every mistake to avoid." Direct continuation of yesterday's #36 SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) piece, which flagged the IRC §408(d)(2) pro-rata trap as the single most important reason a high-earning freelancer would choose Solo 401(k) over SEP. Today's piece is the deep-dive companion on that trap plus the entire mega backdoor Roth mechanic — the two highest-leverage tax-shelter moves for households above the $153K/$242K direct-Roth phaseout.

- **Files touched (2):**
  - **`/blog/backdoor-roth-ira-2026.html`** — new gold-standard post, 6,704 words, 16 primary sources, 12 H2 sections, TOC sidebar, 3 JSON-LD blocks (Article + BreadcrumbList + FAQPage — all Python-`json.loads` verified), 8-item action checklist, methodology footer with full source list.
  - **`OPERATIONS.md`** — Current State header date bumped to 2026-07-05 by morning-routine, queue item #37 added and checked, this Daily Log entry appended.

- **What the piece covers (H2 map + editorial spine):**
  - **H2-1 What the backdoor Roth actually is.** Framed as two sequential operations each fully authorized by statute — nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution under IRC §408(a)(1), then Roth conversion under the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 which permanently removed the pre-2010 $100,000 MAGI cap on conversions. Notes IRS 2018 acknowledgment that the step-transaction doctrine does not apply to sequential contributions and conversions each independently permitted by statute.
  - **H2-2 2026 income limits.** Full IRS Notice 2025-67 MAGI phaseout table: single/HoH $153,000-$168,000, MFJ/QW $242,000-$252,000, MFS (living with spouse) $0-$10,000 (unchanged, not indexed). Cross-references 2025 was $150K-$165K single / $236K-$246K MFJ — the ~2%/2.5% inflation bump. Reduced-contribution formula from §408A(c)(3) with worked example: single with MAGI $160,000 gets $7,500 × (($168K − $160K) / ($168K − $153K)) = $4,000 reduced direct contribution.
  - **H2-3 The pro-rata trap (§408(d)(2)).** Full worked math: $50,000 SEP + $7,500 fresh Traditional = $57,500 denominator, taxable ratio 86.96%, taxable portion of $7,500 conversion = $6,522. At 24% marginal = $1,565 unexpected federal tax. Three defusing options: (a) roll pre-tax IRA into employer 401(k) or Solo 401(k) before Dec 31 (qualified plan balances under IRC §401(a) are excluded from §408(d)(2) aggregation), (b) convert entire pre-tax balance in a low-income year, (c) skip backdoor entirely and use mega backdoor through a 401(k). Also flags the spouse-escape: pro-rata is applied per taxpayer not per couple, so a spouse with zero pre-tax IRA balance can execute a clean backdoor even if the other spouse is contaminated.
  - **H2-4 The 5-step process.** Step 1 verify MAGI (don't backdoor if direct contribution is available). Step 2 confirm zero pre-tax IRA balance at every custodian ever used. Step 3 nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution. Step 4 convert to Roth within a few business days. Step 5 file Form 8606 Part I + Part II. Includes explicit fix instructions for forgotten prior-year Form 8606s (stand-alone filing + $50 penalty per year, don't try to bury in current-year filing).
  - **H2-5 The mega backdoor Roth.** The separate maneuver inside a 401(k) plan (not IRA). Formula: §415(c) $72,000 − $24,500 elective deferral − employer match = after-tax room. Worked example: $150K salary with $24,500 deferral + 4% employer match = $41,500 remaining after-tax room. Distinguishes after-tax (grows taxable) vs Roth (grows tax-free) vs pre-tax buckets — the mega backdoor works by rapid in-plan conversion of after-tax → Roth. Notes PSCA data on plan-feature prevalence: ~30% of plans allow after-tax contributions, ~50% of those also allow in-plan Roth conversions, so ~15% of employees have full mega backdoor capability out of the box. Explicit note on Solo 401(k) mega backdoor for freelancers: Fidelity + E*TRADE Solo 401(k) plan documents permit it, Schwab/Vanguard often do not.
  - **H2-6 The two 5-year rules.** Two SEPARATE rules under IRC §408A(d)(2) (account-open, first-ever Roth contribution starts a lifetime clock) and IRC §408A(d)(3)(F) (per-conversion, each conversion has its own 5-year clock for penalty purposes under §72(t)). Ordering rules under IRC §408A(d)(4): contributions come out first (never taxable/penalized), then conversions FIFO (basis-recovered but 10%-penalized if under 59½ and within 5 years), then earnings (taxable + penalized if not qualified). Links to `blog/roth-conversion-ladder-early-retirement-2026.html` for the strategy that exploits the per-conversion rule.
  - **H2-7 Three case studies with full numbers.**
    - **Case 1 Priya, 32, single, $180K salary:** clean backdoor, taxable amount at conversion ~$2 (a few days of interest on $7,500), federal tax owed on conversion ~$0.64. Projected forward at 7% real return: $7,500/yr × 33 years = ~$875,000 tax-free retirement, ~$210K in avoided future tax at 24% blended marginal.
    - **Case 2 Marcus, 45, single, freelancer with $50K SEP-IRA:** contaminated backdoor. Before fix: $6,522 taxable, $2,087 federal tax at 32%. Fix: open Fidelity Solo 401(k), roll $50K SEP → Solo 401(k) in September 2026, then clean backdoor in December. After fix: $2 taxable, ~$0 tax. One-time move saves $2,087 year one plus ~$40K over 20 years of future backdoors.
    - **Case 3 Chen household MFJ $310K:** both spouses execute clean backdoor ($15K combined). Anna's Meta 401(k) allows mega backdoor at $72K − $24,500 − 4% × $185K match ($7,400) = $40,100 after-tax room, auto-converted daily to Roth 401(k). Household total 2026 Roth capacity: $15K + $40.1K = $55,100. Compared to a household without mega backdoor access: limited to $15K. Plan-feature availability alone is worth ~$4.0M in extra tax-free retirement assets over 30 years at 7% real.
  - **H2-8 Form 8606 in exact detail.** Line-by-line table (Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15c) with typical backdoor Roth values. Notes cross-year basis tracking (each year's 8606 references prior year's), permanent-storage recommendation (IRS may audit 20+ years later), and a spreadsheet-plus-8606 dual-record pattern.
  - **H2-9 State tax treatment.** Most states follow federal (California +9.3% on the taxable pro-rata portion). Pennsylvania exception: no state tax on Roth conversions of basis at all — even a contaminated backdoor has zero PA state cost. Other states with retirement income exemptions (IL/MA/MI). Nine no-income-tax states.
  - **H2-10 Seven mistakes.** (1) Doing backdoor with $50K+ pre-tax IRA without checking pro-rata. (2) Forgetting Form 8606. (3) Withdrawing converted principal within 5 years under 59½. (4) Confusing "after-tax" vs "Roth" contributions for mega backdoor. (5) Contributing above annual IRA limit thinking backdoor is a separate track. (6) Missing the Dec 31 IRA balance zero requirement. (7) Doing backdoor when direct-contribution was still permitted.
  - **H2-11 Action checklist.** 8 items tied to the 2026 numbers + Form 8606 + plan-feature check + mega backdoor payroll election.
  - **H2-12 FAQ.** 10 questions mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim, covering "what is a backdoor Roth," "what are the 2026 limits," "what is the pro-rata rule," "what is the mega backdoor," "what are the 5-year rules," "contributions vs conversions," "SECURE 2.0 impact," "how to avoid pro-rata with a big SEP-IRA," "spousal backdoor Roth," "same-year vs cross-year timing."

- **What this piece specifically fixes vs the average online backdoor Roth guide:**
  - **The pro-rata math is derived with actual numbers, not asserted.** Most competing pieces mention the pro-rata rule but skip the algebra. Ours writes out the $50,000 / $57,500 = 86.96% ratio, computes the $6,522 taxable portion, applies the 24% marginal rate to get $1,565 unexpected federal tax, and notes the persistent basis-remainder problem that contaminates future years. This is the depth that separates gold-standard content from AdSense-rejection-triggering summary content.
  - **The mega backdoor math is derived, including the "after-tax ≠ Roth ≠ pre-tax" distinction.** Most competing pieces conflate the three 401(k) buckets. Ours explicitly separates them in a callout, then shows the exact §415(c) $72,000 − $24,500 elective − employer match arithmetic with worked numbers for a $150K/$185K salary. Includes PSCA data on plan-feature prevalence to give readers a realistic expectation about whether their plan supports the strategy.
  - **The Form 8606 line-by-line table is a durable operational reference.** Most competing pieces say "file Form 8606" without saying what goes on which line. Ours gives a table with Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15c and typical backdoor values, which is what a reader actually needs when they're staring at TurboTax or Drake in April.
  - **The state tax treatment section calls out the Pennsylvania exception.** Most pieces treat state tax as "check your state" boilerplate. Traditional wins by 15% in the peak-earner scenario; Roth wins by 13% in the early-career scenario; the middle-bracket tie is the mathematical result of the ratio formula.

  6. **SECURE 2.0 §603 — the mandatory Roth catch-up for high earners** — the trigger test (FICA wages, prior year, per-employer), the exempt-employee carve-out (zero prior FICA wages → new hires, Schedule C sole proprietors, Solo 401(k) sponsors), the plan-that-doesn't-offer-Roth trap (catch-up capped out entirely), the practical rewrite showing $24,500 base Traditional + $8,000 Roth catch-up = $32,500 total. Verified against IRS Notice 2023-62 delay to 2026 and PSCA plan-feature adoption data.

When Roth match makes sense (three conditions). W-2 mechanics side-by-side showing Box 1/3/5/12 differences between $10K Traditional vs $10K Roth deferral at $100K salary with 5% match.

Worked-numbers Uniform Lifetime Table divisor showing $2M Traditional RMD at $75,472 in year one triggering IRMAA cliffs and 12%→24% bracket jump. Roth 401(k) faces none of it. 5-year-rule clock does not transfer on Roth 401(k) → Roth IRA rollover callout.

- **Structure of the piece (13 H2 sections):**
  1. **What Form 8606 actually is (and why the IRS made you write it)** — the running tally that separates pretax from after-tax dollars in the Traditional/SEP/SIMPLE IRA pool. Load-bearing definition of basis. Key callout with the one-sentence purpose.
  2. **Who is required to file it in 2026** — the four trigger events from the 2025 Instructions for Form 8606 mapped to which Part of the form each triggers, with the statutory anchor for each (IRC §408(o), §408(d)(1)-(2), §408A(d)(3), §408A(d)(2)-(3)). Includes the two nuances: per-spouse SSN filing and the Roth 401(k) exclusion, plus the after-tax 401(k) rollover exception under IRS Notice 2014-54.
  3. **The three trigger events, in the order they arise on a real return** — the typical annual sequence for a backdoor-Roth executor: nondeductible contribution → conversion → year-end balance snapshot. Explicitly notes that a single Form 8606 covers both Part I and Part II for the same tax year.
  4. **Part I line by line** — Lines 1-15c walked individually. Line 1 (this year's nondeductible contribution with the $7,500 / $8,600 2026 limits from IRS Notice 2025-67), Line 2 (prior-year basis carry-forward from Line 14 of most recently filed 8606), Line 3 (cumulative basis pre-distributions), Lines 4-5 (branch for whether to continue), Line 6 (December 31 aggregate value across every Traditional/SEP/SIMPLE — with the callout that Roth IRAs and Roth 401(k)s do NOT go on Line 6), Lines 7-9 (denominator pieces), Line 10 (nondeductible ratio to six decimals per IRS instructions), Lines 11-15c (applying the ratio to distributions and conversions).
  5. **Part II line by line — the backdoor Roth's home** — Line 16 (total converted, matches 1099-R Box 1 with Distribution Code 2 or 7), Line 17 (basis used from Part I Line 11), Line 18 (taxable portion flowing to Form 1040 Line 4b). Includes the "clean backdoor" tip callout that Line 18 = 0 is the entire game.
  6. **Part III line by line — nonqualified Roth IRA distributions** — the three-tier ordering rule from IRC §408A(d)(4): regular contributions first, conversions next (oldest first), earnings last. Lines 19-25c walked. Explicit note that qualified Roth IRA distributions (59½ + 5-year clock) don't touch Form 8606 at all.
  7. **The pro-rata trap in dollar terms** — two identical taxpayers (Ravi $0 balance / Meera $270K rollover balance) executing what looks like the same $7,500 backdoor. Ravi's Line 18 = $7.12 → $1.71 federal tax at 24%. Meera's Line 18 = $7,304.26 → $1,753 federal tax at 24% + ~$365 state = ~$2,118 total. Explicit formula box for the ratio calculation. Warning callout that the pro-rata rule cannot be gamed by picking accounts.
  8. **The one-day rollover fix** — IRC §408(d)(3)(A)(ii) reverse rollover to a workplace 401(k) that accepts incoming rollovers. Only pretax dollars are eligible. 5-step mechanical playbook with the critical December 31 deadline note. Key callout for 2026 tax year timing.
  9. **Common 8606 mistakes that cost basis (and money)** — six failure modes: missing an 8606 in a nondeductible contribution year, filing Line 2 as zero when prior basis exists, forgetting an old rollover IRA on Line 6, skipping Part II when a conversion happened, confusing Roth 401(k) basis with Roth IRA basis, filing joint 8606s under one SSN.
  10. **Amending prior 8606s to reclaim missed basis** — the standalone-Form-8606 amendment path (do NOT use Form 1040-X unless taxable income changes). §6511 3-year statute of limitations does NOT attach because basis correction is not a refund claim. §6693(b) $50 late-filing penalty exposure with the practical note that reasonable-cause waivers are routinely granted. Cross-reference to the §6501(e) 6-year rule and the mirror-image §6511 3-year refund window for the distribution-year 1040-X.
  11. **Form 8606 for inherited IRAs, spousal, and after death** — inherited IRA basis is a separate pool under IRC §408(d)(2)(B), does NOT mix with own-IRA basis. Spousal §402(c)(9) exception. SECURE Act 10-year rule for non-spouse beneficiaries after 2019.
  12. **Your 8-item Form 8606 checklist for 2026** — pull every 5498, compute Line 6 correctly, confirm Line 2 chain integrity, verify Part II Line 16 matches 1099-R, model pro-rata before filing via the CalcLeap backdoor Roth calculator, execute the reverse rollover before December 31, file separate 8606s per spouse, retain every filed 8606 indefinitely.
  13. **FAQ** — 10 questions matching the FAQPage JSON-LD schema.

  - **§2 The three qualified formulas** — basic match (100%×first 3% + 50%×next 2%, 4% cap) with tier-by-tier table; enhanced match at least as generous at every tier (commonly 100%×4/5/6%); 3% nonelective to every eligible employee including the six-percent enhanced-match ceiling from Treas. Reg. §1.401(m)-3(d)(3).
  - **§3 QACA** — §401(k)(13) with mandatory auto-enrollment 3%→6%+ escalation capped at 15% under SECURE 2.0 §101; 3.5% employer-cost formula (100%×1%+50%×5%); the ONLY safe harbor formula permitting a 2-year cliff vesting on the safe harbor contribution; SECURE 2.0 §101 making auto-enrollment mandatory for essentially all new 401(k) plans established after Dec 29, 2022.

  - **§5 ADP/ACP exemption mechanics** — traditional 1.25-or-2%-rule test structure the safe harbor replaces; §401(m)(11) parallel ACP exemption on employer match; ACP still runs on employee after-tax contributions (which is why "mega backdoor Roth" is hard at small employers without a QNEC to NHCEs).
  - **§6 §416(g)(4)(H) top-heavy exemption and its narrow limits** — §416 60% key-employee test; the exemption breaks the moment a discretionary match / profit sharing / forfeiture reallocation is added; a 3% nonelective safe harbor satisfies BOTH ADP exemption AND top-heavy minimum in one contribution.

This is a P0 credibility bug — a reader who lands from a search for "backdoor Roth calculator" and sees a medical disclaimer immediately loses trust in the site.
  - **`toFixed(2).toLocaleString()` NO-OP BUG.** Same silent bug family found in `/simple-ira-calculator.html` and `/sep-ira-calculator.html` pre-fix. `Number.prototype.toFixed(2)` returns a string, and `String.prototype.toLocaleString()` on a string is a no-op that returns the same string — so the intended thousand-separator formatting never applied. The calc displayed `202889.929454783` instead of `$202,889.93` for large numbers. Migrating to `Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', {style:'currency', currency:'USD'})` fixes it site-consistently.

- **Post-fix design:** Full rebuild patterned exactly on the 2026-07-06 (SIMPLE-IRA), 2026-07-07 (SEP-IRA), and 2026-07-08 (401(k)) evening rebuilds. Uses the same visual scaffold — Apple-tokens palette, `.calc-box`, `.result-box`, `.info-section`, `.form-grid`. Form now has 9 fields:
  1. Filing status (Single / MFJ / HoH / MFS)
  2. Age (unlocks $1,100 catch-up at 50+)
  3. Taxable income excluding conversion ($) — for marginal-rate inference
  4. State marginal tax rate (%) — flat
  5. Nondeductible contribution this year ($) — Form 8606 Line 1
  6. Prior-year basis ($) — Form 8606 Line 2
  7. Total pretax Trad/SEP/SIMPLE IRA balance ($) — feeds Line 6
  8. Amount converted to Roth ($) — Form 8606 Line 8
  9. Reverse-rollover fix applied? (Yes/No) — IRC §408(d)(3)(A)(ii) toggle

- **Formula (IRC §408(d)(2) per 2025 Instructions for Form 8606):**
  - Line 5 = Line 1 + Line 2 (total basis available for pro-rata).
  - Line 6 = pretax balance (forced to $0 if reverseRolloverFix === 'yes' per §408(d)(3)(A)(ii)).
  - Line 9 = Line 6 + Line 7 + Line 8 = pretax + 0 + conversion (denominator of the pro-rata ratio).
  - Line 10 = min(1, Line 5 / Line 9), rounded to 6 decimals for DISPLAY per IRS instruction but computed at unrounded floating-point precision INTERNALLY for maximum accuracy in the downstream tax math.
  - Line 11 = Line 8 × (Line 5 / Line 9) at unrounded ratio (tax-free portion of conversion).
  - Line 18 = Line 8 − Line 11 (taxable portion — flows to Form 1040 Line 4b).
  - Line 14 = Line 3 − Line 11 (basis carryforward to next year's Form 8606).
  - fedAddl = fedTax(income + Line 18, filing) − fedTax(income, filing) using the four-filing-status TY2025 brackets from Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01 (single/MFJ/HoH/MFS) — the CORRECT bracket-stacking method that handles conversions that cross bracket boundaries, same method as `/calc/capital-gains-tax-calculator.html` (2026-06-20 evening) and `/calc/hsa-contribution-calculator.html` (2026-06-21 evening).
  - stateAddl = Line 18 × stateRate (flat marginal — see caveat (f)).
  - totalAddl = fedAddl + stateAddl.

  - **Earnings drag formula:** `drag = afterTax × (return/100) / (2 × sweeps_per_year)`. Same-day sweep → drag = 0. Monthly (12/yr) → drag = $158.33/yr on $47.5K at 8%. Quarterly (4/yr) → $475/yr. Annual (1/yr) → $1,900/yr. Formula derives from continuous-contribution linear-accumulation avg-balance × rate × period = C × rate / (2n).

- **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The $150,000 threshold is precisely defined against Form W-2 Box 3 (Social Security wages), NOT Box 1 or Box 5.** Competing web content routinely conflates "wages" or uses "compensation" — imprecise language that leaves readers guessing whether their pretax 401(k) deferrals reduce the number. This piece names Box 3 specifically and walks the arithmetic: Box 3 = gross wages up to the Social Security wage base ($176,100 for 2025), NOT reduced by pretax 401(k) deferrals (which reduce Box 1 for federal income tax purposes but NOT Box 3 for Social Security tax). The wage-comparison table (Section 2) concretely shows why a $155,000 earner cannot avoid §603 by ramping their pretax deferral: Box 3 stays at $155,000 regardless.
  - **The mid-year job change one-year exemption is quantified and defended as a legitimate reading of the statute.** Competing content mostly ignores this scenario or dismisses it as a "loophole." This piece explicitly names it as a byproduct of the per-employer, per-prior-year measurement design and cites Section III.C of Notice 2023-62 as the IRS's own operational endorsement of the per-employer measurement. Concrete number: a $200,000 earner at Employer A in 2025 who moves to Employer B in January 2026 has $0 Box 3 wages at Employer B for 2025 → not §603-covered at Employer B for 2026 → pretax catch-up election available at Employer B for one calendar year. Similarly for self-employment-to-W-2 transitions and return-from-leave scenarios.
  - **The plan-must-offer-Roth-or-no-catch-up mechanic is quantified with PSCA + NAGDCA adoption statistics.** §414(v)(7)(B) is the sharpest edge of §603 — a plan without a designated Roth source cannot make any catch-up for §603-covered participants — but competing content routinely glosses over the pre-transition adoption gap. This piece names the numbers: 82% of §401(k) plans had Roth at year-end 2023 (PSCA 66th Annual Survey), 55% of §457(b) plans (NAGDCA 2024), meaning ~18% of §401(k) plans and ~45% of §457(b) plans faced a forced-choice window during 2024-2025 to add Roth or lose catch-up capacity. This concrete framing helps readers understand why 2024-2025 saw a wave of plan amendments and why some smaller / governmental plans may still be non-compliant in 2026.
  - **The S-corp W-2-vs-K1 planning arbitrage under Notice 2023-62 §III.C is a "gray-hat" data point.** Competing content universally assumes §603 applies to all high-income Solo 401(k) participants. This piece names the sole-proprietor exemption (Schedule SE income is not FICA wages under §3121(a) so pure sole props escape §603 regardless of income) and the S-corp shading (W-2 wages count but K-1 distributions do not, subject to the §162 reasonable-compensation constraint).
