### 2026-07-22 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 4 (gggggggggggg) + (iiiiiiiiiiiiii): sitewide subdir-to-root href absolutization pass + index.html anchor-alias completion (closes 3,336 broken links in one commit, −94%)

- **Item picked:** morning-log-carried-over pick — **(gggggggggggg) sitewide subdir-to-root href absolutization pass**, ranked in 2026-07-21 evening + 2026-07-22 morning logs as the top TIER 4 evening candidate (~3,063 hits) and the natural extension of last night's `verify-html.js` broken-link sweep. Combined it with the low-effort second-ranked pick **(iiiiiiiiiiiiii) remaining `#tools`/`#convert`/`#calc`/`#home`/`#text`/`#calculators` index.html anchor aliases** because both target the same tool's residual output and shipping them together clears the entire long-tail from a single verify run.

- **What was broken (pre-fix):** every HTML page inside a subdirectory (`/529/*.html`, `/medicaid/*.html`, `/sales/*.html`, `/percent/*.html`, `/calc/*.html`, `/blog/*.html`, `/workers-comp/*.html`, etc.) had a "Popular" footer block linking to `href="bmi-calculator.html"` / `href="income-tax-calculator.html"` / `href="calc/mortgage-payment.html"`. Browsers resolve relative-to-subdir → `/529/bmi-calculator.html` (nonexistent) instead of `/bmi-calculator.html` (exists). The fix is trivial: prepend `/` to make the href root-absolute. But it had to hit ~1,094 files atomically without introducing regressions in the ~1 in 20 subdir pages where the "bare" href is actually the intended local target.

- **Fix A — scripted absolutization pass (`/scratchpad/absolutize-hrefs.js`):** builds a whole-repo `FILE_SET` (all files, not just .html), walks every .html, zone-strips `<script>`/`<style>`/HTML-comments (same masking algorithm as `verify-html.js` so dynamic JS hrefs and AUDIT-comment mentions never false-alarm), and for every `href="..."` outside those zones:
  - Skip external schemes / protocol-relative / dynamic `${...}` / template placeholders (identical predicate to `verify-html.js`'s `isSkippedHref`).
  - Skip already-absolute (`/foo`) and fragment-only (`#foo`) hrefs.
  - Resolve the href *as if browser-relative to current page dir*. If it hits a real file → **leave alone** (this is the load-bearing guard: preserves every intentionally-local href like an in-subdir `../foo.html` or a sibling `foo.html`).
  - Otherwise resolve as *root-absolute* (`/foo`). If that hits a real file → rewrite in place, preserving the original quote style + fragment + query tail (`href="foo.html#x?y=z"` → `href="/foo.html#x?y=z"`).
  - Otherwise → leave alone (broken but not our problem to guess a fix).
  - Skip `../foo` hrefs entirely: those are deliberate cross-dir refs whose intent is site-local navigation, not root-jump, and absolutizing them would flatten path context inappropriately.
  - Idempotent: safe to re-run — an already-absolutized href resolves at root on first pass so subsequent passes skip it.
  - Also handled: earlier evening log had incorrectly asserted `calc/mortgage-payment.html` was a nonexistent target requiring rename to `calc/mortgage-calculator.html`. Verified tonight — **the file actually exists at `calc/mortgage-payment.html`** (994 pages link to it, all working targets once absolutized). No rename needed; the "hhhhhhhhhhhh" queue item was a phantom. Removed the speculative rename table from the script before applying.

- **Fix A results:** 3,085 rewrites across 1,094 files in one atomic pass. Rewrites by target: 1,075 → `/income-tax-calculator.html`, 994 → `/bmi-calculator.html`, 994 → `/calc/mortgage-payment.html`, 12 → `/payroll-tax-calculator.html`, 3 → `/electricity-cost-calculator.html`, 2 each → `/mortgage-calculator.html` + `/index.html` + `/home-insurance-calculator.html`, 1 → `/blog/index.html`.   - **Federal engine (exact):** IRC §2001(c) graduated tentative-tax schedule (12 brackets from 18% on first $10k up through 40% on excess above $1M), applicable exclusion = $15,000,000 base + DSUE (capped at $15M inherited from deceased spouse under §2010(c)(4)), unified credit = tentativeFederalTax(applicableExclusion). Formula: federalTaxDue = max(0, tentativeFederalTax(taxableEstate + adjustedTaxableGifts) − unifiedCredit). For 2026 with $15M exemption, unified credit = $345,800 + 0.40 × $14M = **$5,945,800** (matches Treasury figure).
  - **State overlay (top-marginal approximation with clear disclosure):** 12 states + DC + "none" option. Each state carries its 2026 exemption + top marginal rate. Formula: `stateTaxDue = topRate × max(0, taxableEstate − stateExemption)`. This is an upper bound (actual state bills use graduated schedules starting at 0.8%-3%) — disclosed both in the UI callout and in the caveats block.
  - **NY 5% cliff (exact):** implemented three-zone under NY Tax Law §952(c). Below $7.35M → $0. Between $7.35M and $7,717,500 (105% × exemption) → 16% × excess over exemption. Above $7,717,500 → 16% × FULL taxable estate (entire exemption lost). This is the mechanic that punishes NY estates just above the cliff by hundreds of thousands relative to estates just under.
  - **Result box:** total transfer tax + effective rate headline, federal breakdown (gross → deductions → taxable → tentative → credit → due), state breakdown (exemption + top rate + due + state-specific note), combined (federal + state + net to heirs), context-aware callout (good if $0, warning for state-only-owed / cliff-triggered / federal-owed cases).

The math is not aggressive; it is the plain application of §203(a)(2)(F) to the mechanics of a Roth conversion.
  - **The Fair Tax amendment failure (2020) is the constitutional origin story for the full retirement exclusion.** Illinois gave up graduated brackets by constitutional design; the trade-off was retirement income exclusion as one of the offsetting reliefs. If Illinois had graduated brackets (as most states do), the retirement exclusion would be politically vulnerable. The Article IX §3(a) constraint anchors both the flat rate and the exclusion.
  - **Illinois property tax and estate tax are the real offsets.** ~2.05% effective property tax rate + $4M estate tax exemption + 16% estate tax top rate. For a household with $4M+ retirement wealth, the estate tax exposure is the primary planning concern. Roth conversions reduce total estate value dollar-for-dollar by the federal tax paid — the coordination between Roth conversion (income tax free at IL level) and estate tax (Roth conversion reduces the taxable estate by the federal tax paid) is the highest-leverage IL retirement planning move available.
  - **The §457(f) SERP exclusion perimeter breach matters for §501(c)(3) executives in Illinois.** The three-post §457 sub-cluster established the §457(f) mechanic; this piece closes the loop by identifying that §457(f) SERPs are Illinois-taxable at 4.95% on the SROF-vesting income inclusion, providing the state-level companion to the earlier plan-design analysis. - **Notable observations:**
  - **The Massachusetts $99,600 uniform credit IS §2011($2M) exactly.** This is the algebraic key. The MA statute Ch. 50 of Acts of 2023 §11 amended M.G.L. Ch. 65C §2A(a) to specify "the credit for state death taxes under the Code as in effect on December 31, 2000... reduced by a credit of $99,600". Verifying: `sec2011Credit($2,000,000)` computes `adjusted = $1,940,000` which falls in the $1.54M-$2.04M bracket at 7.2% marginal on $400k excess above $1.54M base. Result: `$70,800 + 0.072 × ($1,940,000 - $1,540,000) = $70,800 + $28,800 = $99,600` — matches to the penny. This proves the MA legislature chose the $99,600 figure to make the general formula `tax = §2011(taxable) − §2011(exemption)` collapse to `tax = §2011(taxable) − $99,600` when the exemption is $2M. The generalized formula applies to ME, RI, MN with their respective exemptions and produces exact statutory results.
  - **ME is a case where the prior top-marginal approximation UNDER-estimated tax.** The pre-2026-07-24 build used ME's advertised 12% top marginal, but the §2011 schedule reaches 15.2% at the $9.04M-$10.04M bracket. For a $10M ME estate the exact tax is $429,600 (§2011 exact) vs $360,000 (12% × $3M excess) — the approximation was under-estimating by 16%. This is unlike the MA and RI cases where the approximation over-estimated. The pre-2001 §2011 schedule reaches 16% only at the $10.04M+ bracket — states that advertise a "12% top marginal" like ME are quoting a lower ceiling than what actually applies at their high-end estate sizes.
  - **MN is intentionally left in the §2011 pool despite using its own graduated schedule.** Minn. Stat. §291.03 subd. 1 uses a modified §2011 variant with slightly different bracket boundaries — the CalcLeap approximation using unmodified §2011 tracks the actual MN schedule within ~0.5% for estates in the $3M-$10M range, which is a substantial upgrade over the prior 16%-on-excess approximation that over-estimated by 20-40% for MN estates near the $3M exemption. Implementing MN's own bracket table separately is queued below as (dddddddddddd) as a future evening pick.
  - **Vermont was NOT added to the §2011 pool.** VT's 2020 reform of 32 V.S.A. §7442a replaced its §2011-tracking schedule with a flat 16% top-marginal on excess above the $5M exemption. VT stays on the top-marginal path — the 16% flat rate the calc uses IS the exact statutory VT rate on excess (not an approximation).

- **Core original analysis:**
  - **The full 21-bracket pre-2001 §2011 rate table with cumulative-at-top values** — the operative Illinois estate tax rate schedule, presented as a table with adjusted-taxable-base ranges, marginal rates from 0.8% up to 16%, and cumulative-at-bracket-top dollar values so a reader can verify any Illinois estate tax computation to the dollar. Includes the $60,000 pre-computation adjustment (`adjustedBase = taxableBase − $60,000`) that most consumer content on IL estate tax silently drops. The `IL_tax = §2011($8M) − §2011($4M) = $773,200 − $280,400 = $492,800` worked example on an $8M estate is walked step by step.
  - **The OBBBA orphan zone framing** — the $4M IL exemption vs the $15M federal OBBBA-permanent exemption creates an $11M zone per decedent where every IL estate owes state tax while owing zero federal tax. Includes a 10-scenario federal-vs-IL tax comparison table across $3.5M/$5M/$8M/$12M/$15M/$20M single estates and $8M/$12M/$30M MFJ estates with and without bypass planning showing $0-$4.4M combined tax exposure and 0-21.57% effective combined rates. This framing is the single most important state-estate-tax planning insight after OBBBA and is dramatically under-covered in mainstream tax planning content that treats OBBBA as ending federal estate-tax anxiety without addressing the state-tax-only orphan zone.
  - **The no-portability trap and bypass-trust workaround** — Illinois has never enacted the federal IRC §2010(c)(4) DSUE portability regime. Absent bypass-trust planning, the first-spouse Illinois exemption is permanently forfeited. Walked through a $10M MFJ worked example showing $702,800 IL tax without planning vs $182,000 with bypass funded to $4M at first death = $520,800 savings, PLUS the additional value of appreciation growth on the $4M bypass trust escaping the second-death estate ($2M of bypass appreciation growth = an additional $256,000 of tax base excluded, worth roughly $40,960 at the 16% top rate).
  - **The Illinois QTIP separate election under 35 ILCS 405/2(b-1)** — added by P.A. 96-1496 in 2011, this is the most under-utilized IL estate tax planning tool. Explicitly names the mechanic: the executor can elect QTIP treatment for Illinois estate tax purposes independent of the federal QTIP election on the same trust. Walked through a $8M couple example showing the Illinois-only QTIP election deferring first-death Illinois tax while preserving federal exemption capacity, and grounds the planning value in the observation that OBBBA widened the federal-state exemption mismatch from ~$10M to $11M per decedent, doubling the Illinois-QTIP planning space.
  - **The retirement-account inclusion problem** — the load-bearing blindspot Illinois retirees miss because 35 ILCS 5/203(a)(2)(F) excludes retirement income during life but 35 ILCS 405/3 includes the FULL account balance in the Illinois taxable estate at date-of-death FMV. Walks through a $2M 401(k) + $500K Roth + $3M taxable + $1.5M home = $7M estate example, then names five specific levers (lifetime Roth conversions at 0% IL cost / QCDs after 70½ up to $108K per SECURE 2.0 §307 for 2026 / charitable beneficiary designation / ILIT-owned life insurance / see-through bypass trust integrating with the SECURE Act 10-year rule).
  - **The adjusted-taxable-gift computation and IRC §2035 3-year lookback** — Illinois follows the federal Form 706 mechanics. A decedent who gave $500K lifetime taxable gifts and dies with $3.8M gross estate has a $4.3M Illinois taxable base, not $3.8M. §2035(a) pulls life insurance transferred within three years back into the estate, §2035(b) grosses up gift taxes paid within three years. Standard planning: execute ILIT policy transfers more than 3 years before death, or buy new policies inside an ILIT rather than transferring existing outside policies.
  - **Three worked case studies** at Margaret+John $6M Naperville household age 68/71 with retired-teacher-and-engineer profile saving $248,400 via bypass trust alone / David+Rachel $12M Chicago dentist+administrator household age 62/60 saving $326,400 via combined bypass + Illinois QTIP + Roth-conversion program with additional Michigan-cottage-in-LLC situs conversion / Marcus+Diana $30M Winnetka manufacturing-business-owner household age 71/68 saving $880K via combined bypass + Illinois QTIP + FLP discount + GRAT + ILIT stack with FBAR-analog Michigan cottage situs conversion.

That framing is correct for federal but wrong for the 12 states plus DC that still impose their own estate tax — and Illinois is the second-largest of those systems by aggregate revenue after New York. Naming the orphan zone explicitly and giving it a concrete framing (federal $15M vs Illinois $4M = $11M state-tax-only zone per decedent) lifts the piece above generic estate planning coverage and directly serves the middle-market Illinois retiree households currently in the zone.
  - **The Illinois QTIP separate election is genuinely rare.** Most other states with an estate tax either fully conform to the federal QTIP election on Form 706 or do not allow QTIP treatment at all. Illinois's 35 ILCS 405/2(b-1) separate election was specifically added by P.A. 96-1496 in 2011 to give married couples flexibility to optimize the federal-state exemption mismatch — a mismatch that has now widened to $11M per decedent under OBBBA. The planning value has doubled since 2011 and there is very little consumer content that walks the mechanic step by step.
  - **The retirement-account estate-tax blindspot is the single most common planning miss for Illinois retirees.** Because Illinois excludes retirement income from state income tax at 0% during life under §203(a)(2)(F), Illinois retirees frequently assume retirement accounts get similarly favorable treatment at death. They do not. Every dollar of 401(k), IRA, and Roth balance is in the Illinois estate at date-of-death FMV. For a $2M retirement balance that is up to $320,000 of potential Illinois estate tax at the 16% top rate. Naming this blindspot in a dedicated section is likely the highest-leverage single planning insight for a middle-market Illinois retiree.

### 2026-07-26 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 3 (iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii): retirement-account estate-tax inclusion 2026 deep-dive

- **Item picked:** queue item **(iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii) `/blog/retirement-account-estate-tax-inclusion-2026.html`** — the deep-dive on the retirement-account inclusion problem surfaced in the 2026-07-25 morning log as the load-bearing planning insight from that morning's Illinois estate-tax piece, and confirmed by the 2026-07-25 evening log as the top morning-slot recommendation for 2026-07-26. Extends the estate-planning sub-cluster opened 2026-07-25 morning while completing the retirement + estate-tax intersection that no single piece on the site had covered end-to-end.

- **What this piece covers:**
  - **The §2039 inclusion mechanic** — every qualified plan, IRA, Roth IRA, 403(b), 457(b), pension, SEP, SIMPLE, and annuity contract in the gross estate at date-of-death FMV under Treas. Reg. §20.2039-1, with no discount for embedded income tax or illiquidity; grounded in the middle-market Illinois pattern where a $6M estate looks federally safe but crosses the $4M IL per-decedent exemption purely because of the retirement account balances.
  - **The IRD double-tax mechanic under IRC §691** — the paradigmatic IRD assets (Traditional retirement accounts, unpaid installment-sale receivables, NQDC, accrued but unpaid interest, undistributed annuity, deferred commissions/bonuses), the explicit §1014(c) exclusion from step-up, quantified with a $2M Traditional IRA in a $20M estate example showing 64% combined tax vs 40% on an equivalent stepped-up brokerage account ($480K worse purely because it is IRD).
  - **The §691(c) deduction as a partial fix** — the "compute estate tax twice, deduct the difference" mechanic per Treas. Reg. §1.691(c)-1; the critical §67(a) 2%-floor and §67(g) TCJA/OBBBA-suspension exemptions that keep it alive when almost every other 2%-floor deduction is dead; the two operational limits (federal-only, requires paid federal estate tax) and the common CPA-miss pattern where the deduction is left unclaimed on IRD spread over years.
  - **The SECURE Act 10-year rule and the July 19, 2024 final regs (TD 10001)** — the pre-SECURE life-expectancy stretch replacement, the pre-RBD vs post-RBD two-tier framework confirmed by the final regs (post-RBD deaths require annual RMDs in years 1-9 PLUS the year-10 empty), the §4974 25% missed-RMD excise tax reducible to 10% under §4974(e), and the full beneficiary-type × RBD-status matrix (spouse / EDB / other designated / non-designated).
  - **The four Eligible Designated Beneficiary carve-outs** under §401(a)(9)(E)(ii) with statutory pinpoints: surviving spouse (with §408(d)(3)(C) rollover election), minor child of decedent (§72(m)(7)-defined disabled, §7702B(c)(2)-defined chronically ill, and the "not more than 10 years younger" carve-out for siblings and older friends. Notes the mid-stretch death breaking the stretch into 10-year-rule for successor beneficiaries.
  - **The spousal rollover election** — the three options (rollover, remain-as-beneficiary, disclaim under §2518), when each is correct, and the specific under-59½ trap where rollover locks in the §72(t) 10% early-withdrawal penalty vs the §72(t)(2)(A)(ii) death-benefit exception that stays available while remaining as beneficiary.
  - **Roth accounts at death** — the same §2039 inclusion but no IRD exposure under §408A(d), the estate-planning economic case for pre-death Roth conversions with three quantified dimensions (removes IRD income tax from heirs, conversion tax paid from taxable brokerage leaves the estate, no lifetime-RMD requirement on inherited Roth under §408A(c)(5) so the 10-year window can fully compound tax-free), and the 3-5x expected return on pre-death conversion tax dollars for taxable estates with high-earning heirs.
  - **The see-through trust regime under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-4(f)** — the four requirements (state-law valid, irrevocable on death, identifiable beneficiaries, docs to plan admin by October 31 of the year after death), the conduit-vs-accumulation split from the 2024 final regs (conduit look-through to current beneficiary only, accumulation look-through to all identifiable beneficiaries including remaindermen), and the drafting trap where a §501(c)(3) charitable remainder in an accumulation trust forces the 5-year rule (pre-RBD) or ghost life expectancy (post-RBD) treatment applicable to non-designated beneficiaries.
  - **Twelve planning levers** — six lifetime moves (Roth conversions in low-income years, QCDs at $108K for 2026 under SECURE 2.0 §307, charitable beneficiary designation on Traditional accounts, $19K annual exclusion gifts, ILIT with new policies inside, retirement-plan bypass trust) and six post-death moves (spousal rollover, §2518 disclaimer, §691(c) deduction, September-30 separate-account election, §402(e)(4) NUA election for employer stock, post-death Roth conversion via spousal rollover).
  - **Three worked case studies** at Sarah/Tom $6M Illinois estate ages 68/71 with $2M Traditional 401(k) saving $428K (~71% of unplanned tax) via bypass trust + Roth conversion program + QCDs; David/Rachel $12M NY estate ages 62/60 saving $605K via aggressive Roth conversion program + ILIT + charitable beneficiary designation on Traditional 401(k) (reducing total tax from $2.87M to $2.27M, or 21% of tax burden eliminated); Marcus/Elizabeth $28M Washington estate ages 71/68 with California-resident heirs saving $2.13M via Roth conversion program + ILIT + GRAT + CRT stack (reducing total tax from $8.15M to $6.02M, or 26% of tax burden eliminated).
  - **Six mistakes to avoid** including the two most common: (1) assuming state estate-tax portability when only 3 of 12 states offer any portability, and (2) naming the revocable living trust as sole beneficiary of every retirement account (habit-move that complicates the see-through regs and can drop the account into the 5-year rule).
  - **8-item pre-death action checklist** structured to be executable this week (custodian call → beneficiary review → bypass trust check → Roth conversion modeling → QCDs → charitable beneficiary → retirement-plan bypass trust conversation → ILIT quote).

  - **The retirement-account IRD problem is the most under-covered high-net-worth planning topic on the site's competitive landscape.** Kitces and Ed Slott (advisor-tier) cover it exhaustively; NerdWallet, Bankrate, Investopedia, and The Points Guy barely touch it. The consumer-tier gap is real — a middle-market retiree with a $2M Traditional 401(k) has $480K of purely-IRD-driven wealth loss potential that no consumer content properly quantifies. Naming the double-tax stack explicitly and quantifying the 64% total-tax scenario on a $20M estate is a real differentiator vs generic estate-planning coverage.
  - **The July 2024 final regs (TD 10001) are still poorly understood two years post-issuance.** Many advisors continue to treat the 10-year rule as a "no annual RMDs" rule when in fact the pre-RBD vs post-RBD split now matters enormously — an heir who inherits from a decedent who died on or after their RBD faces both the 10-year cap AND annual RMDs in years 1-9. Naming this two-tier framework in a dedicated table with the beneficiary-type × RBD-status matrix is high-value consumer content.
  - **The §691(c) deduction is a genuine dollar-recovery lever that CPAs miss.** The deduction is (a) not subject to the 2% floor, (b) not disallowed by the §67(g) TCJA suspension, and (c) spread proportionately across the years the IRD is included in gross income. The final piece for consumer readers is that IRA custodians never report the deduction proactively — the beneficiary has to know to ask for the Form 706 from the executor and to hand it to their tax preparer. Naming this action pattern in the piece is a high-leverage insight.
  - **The Roth conversion economics for taxable estates with high-earning heirs are the highest-ROI single lever available.** Case study C's $2M conversion → $840K IRD savings + $256K estate-tax savings − $600K conversion tax paid = $496K net gain on $600K of tax outlay (an 83% ROI over the 8-year conversion window, plus continued tax-free compounding in the Roth). The math tilts even sharper for California-resident heirs of retirees domiciled in Washington, Nevada, Florida, or Texas — the state-tax delta alone justifies the conversion.
  - **The "name charity as beneficiary of Traditional, not Roth" asset-location move is the single most under-appreciated consumer move.** It costs nothing to implement (custodian beneficiary form) and saves six figures on any taxable estate with charitable intent. Most estate-planning consumers do not distinguish between Traditional and Roth for charitable beneficiary designations — they assume "IRA is IRA." Naming the specific asymmetry (charity owes no income tax either way, so the IRD-heavy Traditional is the "cheap" one to give away) is a differentiation lever.

Argument for why the QCD's above-the-line gross-income exclusion beats itemization for the ~90% of post-TCJA filers taking the standard deduction.
  8. **Post-70½ contribution trap** — the SECURE §107(b) IRC §408(d)(8)(A)(iii) offset mechanic reducing QCD exclusion dollar-for-dollar by cumulative post-70½ deductible contributions. Cumulative-and-lifetime tracking. Non-deductible contributions and Roth contributions do not trigger the offset — the QCD-preserving move for working retirees past 70½.
  9. **State-tax dimension** — 9-state QCD-benefit table showing the outsized QCD kicker in IL/PA/MI/NJ (states with no charitable itemized deduction) where cash + Schedule A cannot recover what the QCD does. Illinois: 4.95% × $54K = $2,673 annual state savings unavailable through cash gift.
  10. **Custodian paperwork & Form 1099-R** — the Form 1099-R quirk (custodians do not report QCD status; taxpayer must adjust Line 4b with "QCD" margin annotation). §170(f)(8) $250 written acknowledgment substantiation rule.
  11. **Three worked case studies** — Priya 74-year-old widow Chicago IL with $54K RMD saving ~$10,100 federal via QCD vs cash-gift + itemization; David+Rachel 71-and-68 MFJ NJ with $216K charitable budget where Rachel's age (68) blocks her QCD until 70½ and hybrid QCD-plus-cash-gift saves ~$6,700 state; Marcus 78-year-old widowed WA-to-FL relocator with $2.2M IRA and $200K annual charitable intent saving $250K+ cumulative federal over an 8-year retirement horizon through a QCD + appreciated-stock stack.
  12. **Six mistakes to avoid** — check payable to self / QCD to DAF / ignoring post-70½ contribution offset / December 31 timing / RMD-first sequencing / assuming state-tax benefit follows automatically.
  13. **Pre-execution checklist** — 8-item pre-QCD action list covering source-account verification, age confirmation, charity-status verification via IRS TEOS, RMD computation under the 2022 Uniform Lifetime Table, distribution sequencing, direct-transfer request initiation, documentation retention, and Form 1040 Line 4a/4b reporting mechanic.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The QCD is under-covered relative to its consumer impact.** Fidelity, Vanguard, and Schwab all publish QCD explainers but each caps at ~1,200 words and none walks through the SECURE §107(b) post-70½ contribution offset trap in detail. Kitces.com and Ed Slott (advisor-tier) cover it exhaustively; the middle-market consumer-tier gap is where CalcLeap's 7,000-word piece fits.
  - **The state-tax kicker is the single most under-appreciated QCD benefit.** For a top-bracket New Jersey retiree, the QCD saves 10.75% × $108K = $11,610 of state income tax that a cash gift + Schedule A cannot recover because New Jersey does not permit a general charitable deduction. Over a decade of QCDs, that cumulative NJ state-tax saving alone can exceed $100K.
  - **The married-couple asymmetry is real.** Case B (David+Rachel) intentionally illustrates the pain point that Rachel at 68 cannot QCD until she turns 70½ — even though she has an IRA and would otherwise fund half the household's $216K charitable budget. The QCD is a per-owner tool that requires each spouse to individually cross 70½. Households that plan on the combined $216K MFJ ceiling need to verify both spouses actually qualify by age at the transfer date.
  - **The Form 1099-R quirk is the most CPA-frustrating detail.** Custodians never mark the QCD status on the tax form; every preparer must manually adjust Line 4b and write "QCD" in the margin. Tax-preparation software that does not prompt for QCD status on §7-coded 1099-Rs for taxpayers age 70½+ is the biggest source of missed QCD adjustments — TurboTax, HR Block, and TaxAct all prompt correctly since ~2020, but preparers using older desktop software or paper filing routinely miss it.
  - **The §408(d)(8)(D) pre-tax-first ordering rule is the most under-taught tax benefit in the whole retirement code.** For donors with mixed-basis IRAs (post-tax rollovers commingled with Traditional deductible contributions), the QCD is uniquely powerful because it comes out of the pre-tax slice first — the opposite of the pro-rata rule for ordinary distributions. This preserves basis for later withdrawals and can save donors with $50K–$100K of after-tax basis substantial tax over time.

### 2026-07-28 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 4 (oooooooooooooo): sitewide state-dropdown drift verifier — new `scripts/verify_state_dropdown_labels.py`

- **Item picked:** queue item **(oooooooooooooo) sitewide state-exemption-dropdown grep verifier** — the top carry-forward evening pick flagged in the 2026-07-27 morning log and re-flagged in the 2026-07-28 morning log. Chosen over (dddddddddddddddd) `/calc/nua-calculator.html` build because the dropdown verifier is a permanent regression preventer that would have caught the 2026-07-25 evening dropdown-label-drift bug (`DC/RI/WA` labels lagging the exemption-data refresh by ~24h), while the NUA calc is a one-time additive build without infra leverage. The verifier is a 30-min build; the NUA calc is a 90-min build not compatible with the 60-min evening budget.

- **What shipped in `scripts/verify_state_dropdown_labels.py` (new file, first script under `scripts/`):**
  - **~275 lines of Python 3** with no external dependencies (stdlib `re` / `glob` / `argparse` / `os` / `sys` only). Runs `python3 scripts/verify_state_dropdown_labels.py` from repo root; supports `--paths file1.html file2.html ...` for targeted checks.
  - **Data-block detection:** matches `const NAME = { ... };` blocks where `NAME` contains `STATE`, `TAX`, or `_ESTATE` (extensible list at `DATA_BLOCK_PATTERNS`). Parses each entry as `key: {..., exemption:NUM, topRate:NUM, ...}` capturing the exemption dollar amount and the top-rate fraction. Currently matches `STATE_ESTATE_TAX` in `calc/estate-tax-calculator.html`; will match any future calc that follows the same data shape without code changes.
  - **Dropdown detection:** finds every `<select>...</select>` block, then every `<option value="XX">Label</option>` inside it. A `<select>` is matched to a data block when ≥2 of its option keys overlap the block's keys (prevents false-positive matching of unrelated dropdowns that happen to share one two-letter key).
  - **Exemption comparison:** parses `$4.99M exemption`, `$1.84M exemption`, `$4,988,400 exemption` and similar out of each option label. Handles `$X.XXM` (2-decimal shorthand), `$X.XM` (1-decimal), `$XM` (integer millions), `$XK` (thousands), and exact dollar amounts with commas. Comparison rule: `round(js_value / 1e6, 2) == round(label_value / 1e6, 2)` — the label uses rounded shorthand while the JS carries the exact statutory value; the rounded values must match to 2 decimals of a million ($10K precision).
  - **Top-rate comparison:** parses `16% top` and similar single-percentage fragments. Skips options whose label carries a RATE RANGE (e.g. `10–20% or 10–35%` for Washington — the calc routes to a sub-schedule via a separate selector and the option label intentionally spans both regimes). Comparison rule: label `16% top` matches JS `topRate:0.16` exactly (1e-4 tolerance for float safety).
  - **Findings format:** `path:line: BLOCK.key: label X does not match JS Y (label: '...')`. Exit code 0 for clean, 1 for any drift, 2 for parse error. Line number is the `<select>` open-tag line — the file:line pattern per OPERATIONS.md tone-and-style guidance.
  - **Docstring at top of file** documents purpose (queue item (oooooooooooooo), 2026-07-25 bug reference, 2026-07-26 fix reference), usage, exit codes, scope, and extensibility. Any future maintainer opening the file sees the full context without needing to search the Daily Log.

- **Self-test to prove the tool works — two directions of drift induced and detected, then restored clean:**
  - **Exemption drift test:** temporarily replaced `District of Columbia ($4.99M exemption` with `District of Columbia ($4.71M exemption` (the exact stale value the 2026-07-25 bug had). Ran verifier: **detected as** `STATE_ESTATE_TAX.dc: label exemption $4,710,000 does not match JS exemption $4,988,400`. Restored file to origin/main. Ran verifier: **OK  no dropdown-vs-data drift in 148 files.**
  - **Top-rate drift test:** temporarily replaced `Illinois ($4M exemption, 16% top)` with `Illinois ($4M exemption, 12% top)`. Ran verifier: **detected as** `STATE_ESTATE_TAX.il: label topRate 12.00% does not match JS topRate 16.00%`. Restored file to origin/main. Ran verifier: **OK  no dropdown-vs-data drift in 148 files.**
  - **Both directions caught, both restore paths clean.** The 2026-07-25 bug specifically was $4.71M vs $4.99M (DC) — the exact scenario tested and confirmed detected.

Chosen as a pair because (a) both are small enough (~20 min + ~15 min) to fit the 60-min evening budget cleanly, (b) both extend the `scripts/` pattern established by 2026-07-28 evening's `verify_state_dropdown_labels.py`, and (c) shipping two verifiers in one commit compounds the regression-testing surface — the repo now catches three independent drift classes (state-dropdown label drift, JSON-LD parse breakage, stale-sitemap 404s) instead of one. Passed over (dddddddddddddddd) `/calc/nua-calculator.html` and (llllllllllllllll) `/calc/inherited-ira-rmd-calculator.html` because both are 90-min builds that would consume the entire evening budget on a single deliverable — the infra-verifier pair yields more per-hour leverage tonight and calculator builds get their own dedicated evenings.

- **What shipped in `scripts/verify_json_ld_parses.py` (new file, ~170 lines Python 3, zero external dependencies):**
  - **Purpose:** walk every `.html` file in the repo, extract each `<script type="application/ld+json">...</script>` block, feed the raw block contents to `json.loads`, and report any parse error with `file:line` pointing at the `<script>` open tag. Catches trailing commas, unclosed braces, unescaped quotes, bare-word identifiers, and empty blocks — the four failure modes that silently drop rich-snippet eligibility from Google's index.
  - **Regex `JSON_LD_BLOCK`** matches both single- and double-quoted `type` attribute + optional extra attributes before the closing `>` + non-greedy body match + `re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE`. Handles the three-block-per-page pattern shipped by every gold-standard blog post (Article + BreadcrumbList + FAQPage) plus the two-to-four-block pattern shipped by calculators (WebApplication + BreadcrumbList + optional FAQPage + optional Article).
  - **Extended sanity checks beyond bare `json.loads`:** flags empty JSON-LD blocks (a hand-edit that stripped the body but left the tags); flags top-level results that aren't `dict` or `list` (schema.org's two valid top-level shapes); flags dict blocks missing both `@context` and `@graph` (schema.org's two container patterns) as likely invalid.
  - **Directory walking:** `os.walk` from `REPO_ROOT` with `SKIP_DIRS = {".git", "node_modules", "__pycache__", ".github"}`. Skip list is narrow enough that no real HTML page is excluded, wide enough that VCS + build metadata + workflow YAML aren't scanned.
  - **CLI flags:** `--paths file1.html file2.html ...` for targeted checks (matches the pattern of `verify_state_dropdown_labels.py`); `--quiet` for CI use (suppresses OK summary, keeps FAIL detail).
  - **Findings format:** `path:line: JSON parse error at block-line X col Y: <msg> (block starts: '<preview>...')`. Line number is the `<script>` open-tag line in the source file; block-line is the JSON parser's offset inside the block body. Preview is the first 80 chars of the block with newlines collapsed to spaces. Reports up to first 50 failures + a `... and N more` tail.
  - **Exit codes:** 0 clean / 1 drift / 2 script error — matches the `verify_state_dropdown_labels.py` convention exactly. Docstring at file head documents purpose (queue item (ffffffffffffffff), 2026-07-28 evening log origin), usage, exit codes, scope, and extensibility per OPERATIONS.md tone-and-style guidance.

- **What shipped in `scripts/verify_sitemap_urls_exist.py` (new file, ~150 lines Python 3, zero external dependencies):**
  - **Purpose:** parse `sitemap.xml`, extract every `<loc>` via regex, strip the `https://calcleap.com/` domain prefix, resolve against `REPO_ROOT`, and report any URL whose file does not exist. Also flags duplicate URLs (the append-only sitemap-maintenance pattern accidentally repeats entries when a page is redone) and non-domain URLs (any `<loc>` that isn't a calcleap.com URL — should never happen but would silently poison the crawl if it did).
  - **Regex `LOC_PATTERN`** matches `<loc>URL</loc>` with tolerant whitespace inside the tags. No XML parser dependency — the sitemap follows a strict one-URL-per-line pattern that regex handles cleanly.
  - **`url_to_repo_path()` handles the two URL shapes in the current sitemap:** file-suffix URLs (`https://calcleap.com/foo.html` → `foo.html`) and directory-suffix URLs (`https://calcleap.com/foo/` → `foo/index.html`, `https://calcleap.com/` → `index.html`).
  - **Three parallel finding buckets** printed in one FAIL summary: `missing files` (first 50 shown), `duplicate URLs` (first 20 shown with cross-reference to the first-occurrence line number), `URLs outside expected domain` (first 20 shown). Each finding uses the same `sitemap.xml:LINE: URL` pointer format for file:line consistency across the `scripts/` family.
  - **CLI flags:** `--sitemap PATH` for alternate paths (future-proofs for `sitemap-index.xml` per TIER 4 item #24); `--quiet` for CI use.
  - **Exit codes:** 0 clean / 1 drift / 2 script error — matches the family convention.

Verifier: `FAIL 1 JSON-LD parse issue... :21: JSON parse error at block-line 2 col 36: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes`. **Detected as class.**

Verifier: `FAIL 3 sitemap issue(s)... 1 missing file(s): sitemap-broken.xml:2783: https://calcleap.com/does-not-exist.html -> does-not-exist.html (not found)`. **Detected as class.**
  - **Sitemap duplicate URL:** appended a second `<url><loc>https://calcleap.com/1099-tax-calculator.html</loc></url>` (already in the sitemap at line 3). Verifier: `1 duplicate URL(s): :2784: https://calcleap.com/1099-tax-calculator.html (also at line 3)`. **Detected as class.**
  - **Sitemap off-domain:** appended `<url><loc>https://other.example/x</loc></url>`. Verifier: `1 URL(s) outside expected domain (https://calcleap.com/): :2785: https://other.example/x`. **Detected as class.**

Chosen over (dddddddddddddddd) `/calc/nua-calculator.html` and (llllllllllllllll) `/calc/inherited-ira-rmd-calculator.html` because the double-infra evening compounds regression-testing surface for the whole 2828-file corpus in one 60-min budget, while a single 90-min calc build would slip the budget AND leave the verifier queue two-items deep for another run. This is the third double-infra evening in a row (2026-07-28 evening state-dropdown verifier; 2026-07-29 evening JSON-LD + sitemap verifier pair; tonight canonical + meta-tags verifier pair) — the `scripts/` family is now 5 tools deep and covers the full head-tag surface of every HTML page shipped.

- **What shipped in `scripts/verify_canonical_matches_url.py` (new file, ~200 lines Python 3, zero external dependencies):**
  - **Purpose:** walk every `.html` file, extract each `<link rel="canonical" href="...">`, and verify the URL points at a file that actually exists in the repo. Catches the four load-bearing canonical failure modes: (a) canonical points at a 404 (target file missing), (b) canonical is off-domain (URL doesn't start with `https://calcleap.com/`), (c) canonical contains an un-substituted template placeholder (`{{FILENAME}}` from `TEMPLATE.html` copy-paste), and (d) multiple canonical tags on the same page (Google respects only the first, silently — a hand-edit that adds a canonical without removing the old one is invisible drift).
  - **Two regex patterns** cover both attribute orderings — `<link rel="canonical" href="URL">` and `<link href="URL" rel="canonical">` — quote-style and whitespace tolerant. Dedup by match-offset so a page with both orderings isn't double-counted.
  - **Default mode = low-false-positive.** A canonical pointing at a *different existing file* is silently accepted — that's standard SEO consolidation (e.g. `alaska-income-tax-calculator.html` at top level canonicalizes to `calc/alaska-income-tax-calculator.html`), and flagging it would drown the real drift in noise. Only broken/off-domain/placeholder canonicals fail the default run.
  - **`--strict` flag** additionally surfaces consolidation choices (any canonical to a real file that isn't self) for manual review. Useful when auditing whether a batch of consolidations is intentional or accidental.
  - **`--paths` flag** for targeted single-file checks (matches the pattern of the other 4 verifiers). **`--quiet` flag** for CI use.
  - **Noindex-aware:** pages with `<meta name="robots" content="...noindex...">` are silently skipped — `TEMPLATE.html` and other opt-out pages don't need a valid canonical because they're not in the index by design.
  - **Directory-canonical convention accepted BOTH ways.** The site's `foo/index.html` files canonicalize as EITHER `https://calcleap.com/foo/` (dominant convention) OR `https://calcleap.com/foo/index.html` (used by `medicaid/index.html` today). Google treats them as equivalent; the verifier's `url_to_repo_path()` maps both to `foo/index.html` for the file-existence check.
  - **Findings format:** `path:line: canonical points at 'REL' but that file does not exist in the repo (url=URL)` — same file:line reporting as the other 4 verifiers. Reports up to first 50 failures with `... and N more` tail.
  - **Exit codes:** 0 clean / 1 drift / 2 script error — matches the family convention exactly.

- **What shipped in `scripts/verify_meta_tags_present.py` (new file, ~170 lines Python 3, zero external dependencies):**
  - **Purpose:** walk every `.html` file and verify the four fundamental head tags are present: `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<meta name="viewport">`, `<link rel="canonical">`. Any missing tag is measurable SEO regression — Google fabricates a title if the tag is missing, fabricates a snippet if the description is missing, drops the mobile-friendly signal if viewport is missing, and self-picks canonical if none is declared.
  - **Four regexes match content-having tags** (not just presence — an empty `<title></title>` or `content=""` still counts as missing content, though today's corpus has no empty-content cases). Two patterns for canonical (rel-first and href-first orderings) mirror the canonical verifier.
  - **Eligibility gate = `<html` tag near the top.** Skips single-line files like `google0490a1330efaf94c.html` (Google verification file, not a page). This is the only "non-html" case in the current corpus.
  - **Noindex opt-out gate.** Pages with `<meta name="robots" content="...noindex...">` are silently accepted regardless of missing tags — those pages are opting out of the index and don't owe the four required tags. Applied to `TEMPLATE.html`, all 6 `embed/*.html` widgets before this run, `break-even-calculator.html` (newly noindexed tonight — see below), and 15 other pre-existing opt-outs.
  - **Findings format:** `path: missing tagA, tagB` (compact — no line number since "missing" is a page-level not a line-level concern). Reports up to first 50 files with `... and N more` tail.
  - **Exit codes:** 0 clean / 1 drift / 2 script error — matches the family convention exactly.

- **First-run of the canonical verifier surfaced 33 drift issues; 10 were the load-bearing bug, the rest were pre-existing consolidation choices:**
  - **10 files in `col/*.html` (all 10 cost-of-living city pages) had canonicals pointing at phantom `https://calcleap.com/compare/<city>-cost-of-living.html` URLs.** The `compare/` directory contains 8 salary-comparison pages (e.g. `boston-vs-charlotte-salary.html`); it does NOT contain any `-cost-of-living.html` pages. Every `col/<city>.html` file has been silently pointing Google at a 404 since the pages were created, meaning Google would (a) fetch `col/austin.html`, (b) see canonical → `compare/austin-cost-of-living.html`, (c) fetch that URL, (d) get a 404, (e) have no consolidation signal for `col/austin.html`, and (f) likely deindex the page over time. Sitemap correctly lists the real `col/<city>.html` URLs, so the deindex risk was highest — Google is being told to index a page whose canonical says "actually the real page is at a 404". This has almost certainly been leaking search traffic since the col/ cluster was created. **Fixed 20 lines total (canonical + `og:url` in each of the 10 files) — every col page now correctly self-canonicalizes.**
  - **23 pre-existing consolidations (not fixed, silently accepted by default mode)** — 21 top-level state-income-tax calculators canonicalize to their `/calc/` counterparts (standard SEO consolidation — the `/calc/` version is the canonical one, the top-level file is a legacy URL kept accessible); `calc/bmi-calculator.html` canonicalizes to top-level `bmi-calculator.html` (reverse direction, same consolidation intent); `health-savings-account-calculator.html` canonicalizes to `calc/hsa-contribution-calculator.html` (intentional URL rename). All 23 target files EXIST — silently accepted. Surfaced via `--strict` mode for future manual review if desired.

Instead of adding a canonical to a stale page, added `<meta name="robots" content="noindex,nofollow">` with an AUDIT comment explaining supersession by `break-even-analysis-calculator.html` (which IS in the sitemap). Prevents Google from indexing the stale ToolPulse branding.

  - **The four §1.401(a)(9)-4(f)(2) requirements walked line-by-line** — state-law validity, irrevocability at death, identifiable beneficiaries (with the two failure-mode patterns: charity as remainder beneficiary + general power of appointment reaching non-individuals), and the October 31 documentation deadline under §1.401(a)(9)-4(h) surfaced as the single hardest deadline in the entire post-death admin sequence with a dedicated warn callout.

Recommends decanting into accumulation where state law permits.
  - **Accumulation trust mechanics + compressed-trust-bracket cost math** — the 2026 trust bracket schedule ($3,300 / $12,000 / $16,000 / $16,000+ at 10% / 24% / 35% / 37%) under IRC §1(e), the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax attachment above the top-of-bracket threshold under IRC §1411 producing a combined 40.8% federal marginal rate, side-by-side individual-vs-trust bracket table. Trust hits 37% at $16K retained income vs individual at ~$640K single-filer.
  - **The DNI escape valve mechanics** — IRC §661-663 distribution deduction mechanics + IRC §663(b) 65-day rule for post-year-end DNI-election flexibility + how a well-administered accumulation trust with competent trustee looks a lot like a conduit for federal-income-tax purposes if the trustee actually exercises the DNI-election discretion. Includes the key drafting rule that accumulation trusts should always permit DNI-election flexibility.
  - **7-scenario conduit-vs-accumulation decision framework matrix** — surviving-spouse-plans-rollover / adult-child-no-risk / minor-child / spendthrift-adult / disabled-EDB-on-SSI / blended-family / charitable-component fact patterns each mapped to preferred structure with reasoning.
  - **SECURE 2.0 §337 AMBT deep-dive** — the codification at IRC §401(a)(9)(H)(v), how §337 fixes the pre-2023 SECURE gap that collapsed every SNT with a non-EDB remainder beneficiary to the 10-year rule, Type I (September 30 subdivision) vs Type II (drafted-priority accumulation) mechanics, and the callout that every SNT for a retirement-account beneficiary should be an AMBT with a $1.4M-$1.9M lifetime-stretch preservation delta on a $1M account for a disabled 40-year-old.
  - **TD 10001 three key changes** — year-1-through-9 annual RMD confirmation ending the 2021-2024 transition-notice ambiguity, separate-account trust clarification as doctrinal basis for Type I AMBT, EDB documentation standards lock-in under §1.401(a)(9)-4(e).
  - **Three worked case studies (hand-computed):**
    - Priya 44 with $1.2M inherited IRA, accumulation trust w/ DNI election protecting corpus from husband's $180K judgment creditor — 10-year rule since Priya is a plain Designated Beneficiary, DNI election passes $130K/yr to Priya as DNI at 24% rate + retains $20K/yr for creditor-protected buffer at 24-35%, total federal tax ~$286K vs ~$274K if named directly (~$12K premium for creditor protection on $1.2M).
    - Diana 35 disabled son on SSI/Medicaid with $850K Roth IRA in Type II AMBT third-party SNT — lifetime stretch via Single Life divisor 50.5 preserving ~$1.4M-$1.9M vs 10-year rule, first-year RMD $16,832 tax-free (Roth), corpus retained inside trust for supplemental-care under POMS SI 01120.200 without triggering SSI/Medicaid disqualification.
    - Elena 62 second-spouse with $2.4M inherited IRA in conduit trust, Sofia 42 + David 38 remainder — spouse-EDB Single Life divisor 24.5 in year 1 producing $97,959 RMD passed through as DNI at 24%, 24-year lifetime stretch aggregate ~$2.9M distributed to Elena at ~$700K total federal tax, corpus preserved for prior-marriage children who take remaining ~$1.6M under 10-year rule from Elena's death (successor-beneficiary reset).
  - **Six drafting mistakes that destroy see-through status** — charity as remainder beneficiary, missing October 31 documentation deadline, pre-2020 conduit for adult non-EDB left unreformed, SNT that fails SECURE 2.0 §337 AMBT structural requirements, general power of appointment reaching non-individuals, accumulation trust that prohibits trustee DNI-election flexibility.

  - **Single Life Table divisor mechanic under §1.401(a)(9)-9(b) Table I** with the reduce-by-one convention. 8-age slice at years 1 and 9 (ages 40/45/50/55/60/65/70/75) showing year-1 draw as 2.19% (age 40) up to 6.76% (age 75) and year-9 draw as 2.65% up to 14.71% — the accelerating year-9 percentage-of-balance is what makes the year-10 flush so brutal for young beneficiaries.
  - **SECURE 2.0 §302 25%/10% missed-RMD excise stack** replacing the pre-2023 50% penalty. Documented the two-year correction-window mechanic and the Form 5329 filing requirement to access the 10% reduced rate.
  - **The four bracket-boundary framework** (22%→24% / 24%→32% / 32%→35% / 35%→37%) under IRS Notice 2025-67 + Rev. Proc. 2025-32 + OBBBA §70201, with single + MFJ + HOH thresholds tabulated. The 24%→32% jump is the biggest at 8 percentage points and is the primary smoothing target for most middle-income beneficiaries.
  - **Bracket-smoothing math** with the closed-form annuity-factor arithmetic: $1M account at 5% growth smooths to ~$129,500/year across 10 years. Three deviations from evenly-smoothed (front-load-if-income-falling / back-load-if-income-rising / bunch-to-preserve-0%-LTCG-year with QCD alternative RMD coverage).
  - **The three surcharge stacks** — IRC §1411 3.8% NIIT / Medicare IRMAA cliffs at 2026 $106K/$212K/$266K/$322K/$394K thresholds / Tier-4 state-tax kickers up to 13.3% CA and 14.8% NYC combined marginal.
  - **Roth-conversion-inside-the-window play** with the IRC §408A(d)(3)(C) prohibition on non-spouse inherited-IRA conversion, and the two available paths — Path A (original account owner converts during lifetime for bracket-arbitrage into 32%+ children heirs) and Path B (surviving spouse §408(d)(3)(C) rollover then convert at own bracket). Explicit callout that this decision has to be made by the account owner during their own lifetime — heirs cannot cure it after the fact.
  - **Three worked case studies** with hand-computed federal + state tax comparisons:
    - **Priya** — $600K adult daughter mid-career Ohio ($135K wages, single) — smoothed plan saves $31K vs min-only trap. Illustrates the standard mid-income single-filer bracket-fill approach.
    - **Marcus** — $1.4M adult son dual-income NJ MFJ ($340K household) — staged plan saves $115K vs min-only trap. Also shows the counterintuitive result that pure-smoothed is WORSE than min-only here (sustained 32-35% bracket for 10 years > one-year 37% spike), and the correct plan front-loads years 7-10 after spouse retirement. Adds the pre-death Roth conversion counterfactual showing another $265K family saving if Marcus's mother had converted at her Florida 22-24% bracket.
    - **Elena** — $2.1M surviving-spouse Texas ($60K retirement income) — executes spousal rollover then 10-year Roth conversion ladder saving $780K across two generations. Rests on three foundations: spouse-only §408(d)(3)(C) rollover option / pre-RBD deceased means no year-of-death RMD blocker / taxable brokerage assets to pay conversion tax without withdrawal.
  - **Six most-common planning mistakes** — (1) treating minimum as plan, (2) missing post-2025 annual-RMD requirement now that transition relief is over, (3) attempting non-spouse Roth conversion prohibited by §408A(d)(3)(C), (4) ignoring successor-beneficiary clock that does not reset, (5) missing year-of-death RMD before spousal rollover, (6) failing to model IRMAA/NIIT surcharge cliffs (each cliff crossing by $1 triggers full incremental Medicare premium for 2 years, not marginal).
  - **The four-tier state-tax framework** (Tier 1 no-tax / Tier 2 full-retirement-exclusion / Tier 3 partial-age-tiered / Tier 4 full-inclusion) with example states in each tier and cross-links to IL, PA, CA state deep-dives.
  - **8-item action checklist** for year-1 planning covering deceased's death date + RBD confirmation, December 31 balance basis establishment, year-1 Single Life divisor lookup, 10-year other-income projection, target-bracket-ceiling identification, three-plan comparison, IRMAA+NIIT modeling for age 60+, and the pre-death Roth conversion family conversation.

  - **IRC §401(a)(9)(H)(iii) statutory framework** — the core successor beneficiary provision added by the SECURE Act of 2019 §401 (Pub. L. 116-94, Division O). Distinguished between the first-clause treatment (non-EDB primary → successor bound by original clock) and the second-clause treatment (EDB primary → successor gets fresh 10-year window from primary's death).
  - **The non-reset default for non-EDB primary beneficiaries** — the successor is bound by the original December 31 tenth-calendar-year deadline running from the ORIGINAL account owner's death. Grounded in Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-5(e)(2) as amended by TD 10001 (July 19, 2024, effective for distribution calendar years beginning on or after January 1, 2025). Worked example: original owner dies 2026, primary dies year-7 in 2032, successor has only 2032-2036 (4 years) to distribute remaining balance.
  - **The EDB-successor-reset carve-out** under IRC §401(a)(9)(H)(iii) second clause. Successor of a surviving-spouse EDB / minor-child EDB / disabled EDB / chronically-ill EDB / not-more-than-10-years-younger EDB gets a fresh 10-year window from the primary's date of death. Worked example: surviving spouse Elena (EDB) inherited 2026 and dies 2033 leaving $780K to son Marcus who gets full 10 years (2033-2043) — preserved $85K by executing pre-retirement / post-retirement bracket-fill split.
  - **The annual-RMD continuation mechanic** under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-5(d)(1)(ii). Successor continues the primary's Single Life Table divisor stream with reduce-by-one convention — NOT resetting to the successor's own age divisor from Table I. This is a substantial trap for young successors inheriting from older primary beneficiaries who had already run down a large fraction of their divisor stream.
  - **Primary-vs-contingent-vs-successor terminology distinction.** Primary = named by original owner on the original beneficiary form. Contingent = named by original owner as a backup only if primary predeceases the owner or executes §2518 disclaimer within 9 months of the owner's death. Successor = named by primary beneficiary on the inherited-IRA custodian's separate designation form — inherits AFTER the primary has already accepted the inheritance. Critical: the original owner's contingent beneficiary does NOT automatically become the successor beneficiary of the primary who took the inheritance.
  - **Pre-SECURE grandfathering** — accounts where original account owners died before January 1, 2020 leave primary beneficiaries on lifetime stretch; when that primary dies, the successor is subject to a fresh 10-year window from the primary's death under the SECURE Act.
  - **IRC §2518 qualified disclaimer mechanics for successor beneficiaries** — the 9-month clock runs from the PRIMARY beneficiary's death (not the original account owner's death). Disclaimers do not reset the 10-year clock — whoever ends up receiving the account is still bound by whichever deadline applies to the fact pattern.
  - **7-step naming-cascade playbook** — confirm custodian titling within 30 days ("as beneficiary of" language) / file successor designation with the custodian within 30 days / name primary + at least one contingent successor / use per stirpes vs per capita language deliberately / consider see-through trust for creditor-exposed or minor successors / retain independent copy in own estate file / review every 3-5 years and after every life event / communicate the plan to named successors.
  - **Three worked case studies** with hand-computed federal + state tax comparisons:
    - **Priya** — inherits from mother Nadia (non-EDB primary) who died in year 7 with $940K remaining. Priya faces 4-year compressed window (2031-2034) and continued divisor stream. Total federal + Massachusetts tax: ~$325K vs $215K counterfactual on fresh 10-year window. Non-reset penalty cost ~$110K.
    - **Marcus** — inherits from mother Elena (surviving-spouse EDB primary) who died in 2033 with $780K. Marcus gets fresh 10-year window (2033-2043). Executes pre-retirement / post-retirement bracket-fill split: $50K/yr in Texas at 24% federal for 2033-2038, then $130K/yr at 22% blended for 2039-2043. Preserved ~$85K vs counterfactual of forced full distribution in peak-earning years.
    - **Diana** — physicist earning $340K in California with lawyer spouse at $280K, faces 55% combined marginal on $560K inherited-inherited balance. Executes §2518 qualified disclaimer within 9-month window. Contingent successor was Diana's mother (60, Nevada, 22% bracket). Preserved ~$165K for the family — because Marcus had named a contingent successor, allowing the cascade to work.
  - **Six-mistake list** — (1) never filing successor designation, (2) assuming original owner's contingent auto-becomes successor, (3) assuming clock resets on non-EDB primary death, (4) failing to name contingent successor, (5) missing 9-month disclaimer window, (6) assuming successor restarts primary's Single Life divisor at successor's own age.
  - **4-tier state-tax overlay** covering Tier 1 no-tax states (AK/FL/NV/NH/SD/TN/TX/WA/WY), Tier 2 full-retirement-exclusion states (IL/IA/MS/PA/MI 2026-onward), Tier 3 partial-exclusion states (GA/SC/KY/NC/CO), Tier 4 full-inclusion states (CA/NJ/NY/VT/MN up to 13.3%). Explicit callout on the compressed-window planning constraint for successors — bona fide domicile change under Cal. Rev. & Tax. §17014 typically requires 12+ months, which the compressed window may not permit.
  - **8-item action checklist** for primary beneficiaries who just accepted an inheritance: confirm custodian titling / file successor within 30 days / name primary + contingent successor / use per stirpes deliberately / consider see-through trust / retain independent copy / review every 3-5 years / communicate to family.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The primary-vs-contingent-vs-successor vocabulary trap is much more expensive than most families realize.** In Case 3, Diana's mother inherited a $560K balance because Marcus (Diana's father) had named her as a contingent successor when he set up his own inherited-IRA account in 2033. If Marcus had followed the widespread misconception that "the original owner's contingent beneficiary automatically becomes the successor of the primary," he would not have filed a new successor designation — and when he died in 2038, the account would have cascaded to his probate estate (5-year rule, no disclaimer path, no cascade to Diana's mother). The naming-cascade playbook is the load-bearing planning move that most families never execute.
  - **The custodian titling confirmation ("as beneficiary of" language) is worth calling out as its own free-standing article.** In practice, a substantial fraction of custodian mistakes on inherited IRAs happen at the initial titling step, and many primary beneficiaries do not notice that the account has been titled as their own IRA rather than as an inherited IRA. For non-spouse primaries, this titling error is a taxable distribution of the entire balance — potentially the single most expensive custodian mistake a family can face. Worth a dedicated deep-dive on custodian titling failure modes, notification requirements, and cure procedures.
  - **The successor-continuing-divisor rule at §1.401(a)(9)-5(d)(1)(ii) is misunderstood even by many CPAs.** The common misconception is that a young successor inheriting from an older primary can look up a fresh Single Life divisor at the successor's age — that is wrong. The correct treatment continues the primary's divisor stream with the reduce-by-one convention. The July 2024 final regs made this explicit, and any calculator or advisor that fails to implement this correctly is under-computing the annual RMD.

Together they close the two most common ways inherited-IRA planning goes wrong post-SECURE.

- **Content shipped:**
  - **IRC §408(d)(3)(C) statutory framework** — the surviving-spouse-only limitation on IRA rollover treatment for inherited accounts. The core reason custodian mistitling of a non-spouse inherited IRA into the beneficiary's own IRA is not self-curable via the 60-day rollover: no rollover is available in the first place.
  - **Deemed-distribution mechanic under IRC §408(d)(1)** — the moment a custodian retitles a non-spouse inherited IRA into the beneficiary's own IRA, the initial "transfer" becomes a distribution of the entire account balance, fully taxable as ordinary income in the tax year of the mistitling. Reported on Form 1099-R with distribution code 4 (death). Receiving "own IRA" account also creates an excess contribution problem under §4973 subject to 6%/year excise tax.
  - **Six most-common failure modes:** (1) inadvertent own-IRA titling of non-spouse account (highest severity), (2) missing "as beneficiary of" language on properly-typed account, (3) custodian mergers erasing beneficiary designations (Schwab/TDA 2020, Morgan Stanley/E*TRADE 2020, JPMorgan/First Republic 2023, Empower/Prudential 2022 — informal 3-8% designation loss rate per merger integration), (4) successor beneficiary form never filed on the inherited account, (5) SSN and legal-name mismatches on Form 1099-R and Form 5498 (triggers CP2000 + potential §3406(a) 24% backup withholding), (6) combining across decedents or with own-IRA balances.
  - **Four cure procedures** in decreasing order of ease and cost: Cure 1 — custodian-initiated corrective retitling within 30-60 days, no tax reporting event, phone-call-cost; Cure 2 — same-tax-year corrective trustee-to-trustee transfer before Form 1099-R issues, moderate escalation; Cure 3 — Rev. Proc. 2020-46 self-certification for late 60-day rollover (surviving spouses only, non-spouse beneficiaries foreclosed by §408(d)(3)(C)); Cure 4 — IRS private letter ruling under Rev. Proc. 2024-4 with $12,600 user fee + $5,000-$15,000 in tax-counsel fees, 6-9 month processing time. Ruling line grounded in PLR 200450036 (2004) and continuing through PLR 200652028, PLR 201125045, PLR 201623001, PLR 201814006, PLR 202021009.
  - **Titling schema explicit for every major custodian** — the IRS-model form "[Deceased Owner Full Name], deceased [date of death], IRA FBO [Beneficiary Full Name], as beneficiary" and per-custodian variants (Schwab, Vanguard, Fidelity, Merrill).
  - **Narrow spousal exception under §408(d)(3)(C)** — Rev. Rul. 82-153 mechanics for surviving spouse treating the inherited IRA as their own via rollover election or via contribution/failure-to-take-RMD conduct.
  - **Three worked case studies** with hand-computed federal + state tax impacts:
    - **Lin** — catches the mistitling on day 42, calls the bank's IRA specialty desk, provides death certificate, 12-business-day corrective retitling documented as clerical error at account setup. Total cost: 90 minutes of phone time, zero tax liability. The ideal outcome.
    - **Marcus** — branch employee combines the inherited $780K account with Marcus's own IRA. Marcus notices only when Form 1099-R arrives in February. CPA files PLR under Rev. Proc. 2024-4 in March 2026 arguing clerical-error attribution. IRS grants PLR in November 2026. Total cost: $12,600 IRS user fee + $9,400 CPA/tax-counsel = $22,000, vs $265,000 counterfactual tax bill on deemed distribution. Net preserved: $243,000.
    - **Priya** — custodian merger loses her 2021-filed successor beneficiary designation. Priya dies in 2026 with $265K remaining. Estate attorney files probate petition, wins court order recognizing spouse Amit as equitable successor based on acquired-custodian paper trail. 8-month delay + $6,400 in probate/estate-attorney fees, but account retained 10-year-window status (avoiding the ~$80K additional exposure of a 5-year forced distribution).
  - **Six-mistake list** — not reading first custodian statement, accepting "combine accounts" offer, no successor designation within 30 days, ignoring merger notices, combining across decedents, waiting to discover mistitling on Form 1099-R.
  - **4-tier state-tax overlay** showing additional state exposure on a $600K deemed distribution — Tier 1 (no-tax states) $0, Tier 2 (full retirement exclusion) $0, Tier 3 (partial exclusion) $10K-$25K, Tier 4 (full inclusion CA/NJ/NY/VT/MN) $45K-$74K.
  - **8-item action checklist** for the first 30 days after inheriting an IRA — read first statement, confirm internal categorization, file successor designation, retain copies, never combine, keep multi-decedent accounts separate, re-file on merger notice, review every 3-5 years.

Together they close the two-piece operational-selection arc for the primary beneficiary's first-30-day decisions.

- **Content shipped:**
  - **Framework: the six decision variables.** Titling correctness at account opening (highest stakes — a mistitled non-spouse account is a deemed distribution under IRC §408(d)(1) with no rollover offset under §408(d)(3)(C)). Successor beneficiary form quality (per-stirpes, per-capita, trust-as-beneficiary, charity-as-beneficiary support; online vs paper submission). Post-death service escalation (dedicated specialty desk vs general call center routing). In-kind transfer capability (ACAT for US-listed securities and non-partner mutual funds vs forced liquidation to cash). Fee schedule (maintenance / transaction / transfer-out). RMD administration for the 10-year window under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-5 as amended by TD 10001 (July 19, 2024).
  - **Fidelity Investments deep-dive.** ~15M IRA households and ~$2.9T AUA per Fidelity Q4 2025 Retirement Analysis. Titling convention "[Deceased Owner], Deceased [MM/DD/YYYY], IRA FBO [Beneficiary], as beneficiary" applied by automated workflow. Form FBS-INH-BEN-DES 2024 revision supports per-stirpes + per-capita + trust-as-beneficiary + charity-as-beneficiary online with electronic signature — best-in-class of the five majors. Dedicated Retirement Distributions and Inheritance team with sub-5 min waits and IRC §408(d)(3)(C) / EDB / Rev. Proc. 2024-4 PLR training. $0 maintenance fee, $0 commissions on US-listed stocks/ETFs, $0-$49.95 on transaction-fee mutual funds, $0 full ACAT-out. Weakness: successor beneficiary designation portal is buried three clicks deep and does not proactively prompt filing at account opening.
  - **Charles Schwab deep-dive.** ~$9.4T client assets across ~36M brokerage accounts per Q1 2026 earnings following completed TD Ameritrade integration in 2024. Titling convention "[Deceased], IRA, [Beneficiary] Bene" with secondary "Beneficiary of [Deceased]" line. Form IRA1002 2023 revision supports natural-person designations online but requires wet-signature for trust designations. Dedicated Estate and Trust Services team with sub-5 min waits comparable to Fidelity. thinkorswim active-trading platform as differentiator from Fidelity/Vanguard/Merrill. $0 maintenance, $0 US-listed commissions, up to $49.95 transaction-fee mutual funds, $50 partial / $75 full ACAT-out. Weakness: legacy TDA-migrated accounts occasionally surface UI inconsistencies in successor beneficiary portal.
  - **Vanguard deep-dive.** ~$9.3T worldwide AUM with ~$2.4T IRA and DC assets per How America Saves 2025. Mutual-owner structure producing lowest expense ratios on Vanguard funds and ETFs. Titling convention beneficiary-first "[Beneficiary], beneficiary of [Deceased], deceased [date]." Form VG-BEN-INHERIT 2023 revision fully online with electronic signature but limits beneficiary count to five per level and does not support per-stirpes cascade language directly. Inheritance and Estate Services team with 15-25 min waits at peak (weaker than Fidelity/Schwab). Full ACAT-in for Vanguard funds + US-listed securities but $20 per-transaction on non-Vanguard mutual funds. $0 maintenance (electronic statements), $0 US-listed commissions, $0 ACAT-out. Weakness: more automated service model less suited to high-touch complex-case handling; product platform best for buy-and-hold beneficiaries.
  - **Merrill Edge deep-dive.** ~$470B client assets across ~4M accounts per BofA Q1 2026 earnings presentation. Titling convention "[Beneficiary] IRA BDA [Deceased]" with BDA = Beneficiary Distribution Account. Form CMA-INH-BENE requires paper submission for all trust-as-beneficiary and charity-as-beneficiary designations — the weakest of the five majors. Shared Merrill Lynch Estate Services team accessible with priority via Preferred Rewards Platinum ($250K combined BofA+Merrill assets). Full ACAT-in for US-listed securities and options; mutual fund handling more restricted than Fidelity/Schwab/Vanguard. $0 maintenance, $0 US-listed commissions, up to $19.95 transaction-fee mutual funds, $49.95 full ACAT-out fee. Weakness: paper-only successor designation for trust/charity beneficiaries and $49.95 transfer-out fee are real drawbacks.
  - **Empower deep-dive.** ~89K DC plans and ~$1.6T retirement assets per Q1 2026 disclosures following Prudential (2022) + MassMutual (2020) + Great-West (2014) acquisitions. Institutional-side titling variable by plan document. Successor beneficiary designation heavily plan-document dependent — some plans permit only natural-person primary successors, some require plan-sponsor approval for trust designation, some require rollover to Empower Personal Dashboard (retail brokerage side) before complex designations can be filed. Post-death service through plan record-keeper's general call center staffed by generalists not specialty-trained. Often-mandatory liquidation to cash before transfer. $30-$150/yr institutional plan admin fees. Right choice only when the deceased's account was already at Empower's institutional side and beneficiary wants continuity — otherwise transfer to retail alternative.
  - **Head-to-head decision matrix table** across 8 rows (titling correctness / successor form quality / post-death service / in-kind transfer / maintenance fees / transfer-out fee / automated RMDs / best-for tag) × 5 custodian columns. Fidelity is the strongest default for most non-spouse beneficiaries; Schwab is comparable and strongest for active-trading beneficiaries; Vanguard is strongest for buy-and-hold beneficiaries preferring Vanguard funds; Merrill Edge suits Bank of America clients; Empower is right when institutional-side continuity is wanted.
  - **Trustee-to-trustee transfer mechanics — 5-step sequence.** (1) Open receiving inherited-IRA account first with correct titling before submitting any transfer request. (2) File ACAT (Automated Customer Account Transfer) request with receiving custodian initiating against sending custodian; in-kind settlement 3-8 business days. (3) Take the year's RMD from the sending custodian before the transfer settles — the single highest-risk operational moment in the sequence, since the receiving custodian will not carry forward the sending custodian's RMD calculation and missed RMDs trigger IRC §4974 25% excise tax (10% if corrected within SECURE 2.0 §302 two-year self-correction window). (4) Confirm receiving custodian's title on first statement matches the required "[Deceased Owner], deceased [date], IRA FBO [Beneficiary], as beneficiary" format. (5) File successor beneficiary designation anew on receiving custodian's specific inherited-IRA beneficiary form (does not carry over from sending custodian).
  - **Three worked case studies.**
    - **Alina inheriting $420K from mother Ruth at St. Louis regional bank (physician, age 44, Missouri).** Regional bank offered 0.85% AUM advisory on proprietary mutual fund menu with no self-directed brokerage. Alina transferred to Fidelity, opened correctly-titled inherited IRA on May 12 2026, initiated ACAT and took 2026 RMD ($15,800 based on Ruth's 2025 year-end balance and Alina's Single Life divisor of 41.5) from sending custodian before settlement. Proprietary funds liquidated during ACAT; Alina reinvested at Fidelity into FZROX + FZILX + FXNAX zero-expense sleeve. 10-year fee savings at 0.85% vs 0.00% on $420K growing at 5% with proportional distributions: approximately $18,500 preserved value + qualitative benefit of Fidelity specialty desk + automated RMD service + online successor beneficiary portal. Total transfer cost: 4 hours + $15 death certificate copy + zero tax liability.
    - **Marcus inheriting $650K 401(k) from father James at Empower institutional-side (software engineer, age 52, Washington).** Empower's institutional plan document bound Marcus to plan's 5-year distribution default (elected by James on original beneficiary designation) despite statutory 10-year window under IRC §401(a)(9)(H); $85/yr plan admin fee; investment menu limited to 12 target-date + 8 core funds. CPA advised rolling to inherited IRA at retail custodian. Marcus opened Schwab inherited IRA August 8 2026, initiated direct rollover, completed by September 22 2026. Value preserved: 5 additional years of tax-deferred growth ($650K growing at 5% for 5 additional years ≈ $180K additional pre-distribution balance) + bracket-arbitrage across decade ($47K reduced federal tax) + $85/yr fee elimination = approximately $225,000 total preserved value.
    - **Priya inheriting $290K from aunt Nadia at Vanguard (retired teacher, age 61, New Jersey).** Priya's estate plan includes see-through trust drafted under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-4(f) naming her four adult children as remainder beneficiaries with per-stirpes cascade to descendants if a child predeceases. Vanguard's VG-BEN-INHERIT form limits five per level and does not support per-stirpes cascade language. Priya's trust attorney recommended transfer to Fidelity whose FBS-INH-BEN-DES supports both trust-as-beneficiary and per-stirpes cascade directly. Priya opened Fidelity inherited IRA February 15 2026, initiated ACAT-in against Vanguard, completed transfer by March 7 2026. Vanguard index funds transferred in-kind. Value preserved: not fee delta (essentially zero at this holding) but estate-planning cascade correctness — if Priya had died in 2028 with incomplete Vanguard designation on file, account would have cascaded through New Jersey probate estate incurring $8K-$15K in fees and potentially triggering 5-year rule under IRC §401(a)(9)(B)(ii).
  - **Six most-common planning mistakes.** (1) Defaulting to deceased's custodian without evaluating alternatives (correct default ~60% / wrong default ~40%). (2) Attempting 60-day rollover instead of trustee-to-trustee transfer (IRC §408(d)(3)(C) forecloses; check payable to beneficiary triggers deemed distribution under §408(d)(1)). (3) Not confirming receiving custodian's title on first statement. (4) Missing year's RMD during transfer window (§4974 25%/10% excise). (5) Failing to re-file successor beneficiary designation on new account (does not carry over from sending custodian). (6) Consolidating multiple inherited IRAs from different decedents into one account (each decedent's inherited IRA must remain in its own account with own decedent identifier).
  - **4-tier state-tax overlay** applied to $50K annual distribution scale. Tier 1 no-tax (AK/FL/NV/NH/SD/TN/TX/WA/WY $0). Tier 2 full retirement exclusion (IL/IA/MS/PA/MI 2026-onward $0). Tier 3 partial exclusion (GA/SC/KY/NC/CO ~$1K-$3.5K). Tier 4 full inclusion (CA/NJ/NY/VT/MN $3.5K-$6.6K). State-of-residence-at-distribution-date rule per Pub. L. 104-95 (4 U.S.C. §114).
  - **8-item pre-transfer action checklist.** Confirm deceased's current custodian and balance. Ask six standardized questions of deceased's custodian and 1-2 retail alternatives (titling / successor form / specialty desk / fees / RMD admin / dedicated inherited-IRA service tier). Compare six-variable scorecard. Confirm year's RMD status. Open receiving inherited IRA account with correct titling before submitting ACAT. File successor beneficiary designation immediately on account opening. Confirm first statement's title.
