- **Notable observations:**
  - **The custodian-selection piece is the natural search-intent successor to the custodian-titling piece.** A beneficiary reading "how does inherited-IRA titling go wrong" naturally asks next "which custodian handles it right." Both articles cross-link explicitly. Search Console will show whether the two-piece pairing produces incremental impressions over either piece alone; expect a modest lift because the two topics have distinct query patterns (failure-mode vs custodian-comparison queries).
  - **Empower's institutional-side model is genuinely weaker than the four retail majors and worth flagging.** The five-major comparison places Empower fifth on every variable except institutional-continuity. This is not a criticism of Empower's institutional service quality per se but a reflection that the institutional-plan-record-keeper model is structurally less well-suited to individual-inherited-IRA administration than the retail-brokerage model. A beneficiary defaulting to Empower's institutional side because "that's where the account was" is often making the wrong choice.
  - **The successor beneficiary designation form quality is the most under-recognized variable.** Beneficiaries rarely evaluate custodians on their designation-form flexibility before opening the account, but a paper-only form for trust-as-beneficiary (Merrill) or a five-per-level limit (Vanguard) can force a mid-cycle custodian transfer when the beneficiary's estate plan later requires more complex successor designation. The Priya case study concretely illustrates this — a $290K account with essentially zero fee differential still justified a transfer to Fidelity because of the successor-designation flexibility delta.

- **Content shipped:**
  - **The two constructions defined precisely.** Per stirpes (Latin "by the roots" / "by the branch") = predeceased beneficiary's share cascades down that beneficiary's own descendants divided equally at the next generation, continuing until reaching a living descendant on that branch. Per capita (Latin "by the head") = distribution divided equally among living beneficiaries at a specified level, no cascade to descendants of predeceased. Both grounded in Black's Law Dictionary 12th ed 2024 canonical US legal definitions.
  - **The four practical variants estate practitioners actually draft.**
    - Strict per stirpes / English per stirpes / classic per stirpes = divides at first named-beneficiary generation regardless of whether any at that level living.
    - Modern per stirpes / American per stirpes / per capita by representation = codified as default in Uniform Probate Code §2-709(b), divides at nearest generation with a living descendant, each predeceased descendant's share cascades separately to their own descendants preserving branch representation.
    - Per capita at each generation = UPC §2-106 default, adopted as intestate default in 19 US states (AK/AZ/CO/HI/ID/ME/MA/MI/MN/MT/NE/NJ/NM/ND/SC/SD/UT/VT/WI), initial division at nearest generation with a living descendant with predeceased-generation shares pooled and redistributed equally among all descendants at the next generation.
    - Straight per capita = divided equally among living beneficiaries at named level with predeceased shares lapsing to survivors at that level, grandchildren receive nothing.
  - **4×4 cascade construction chart** across 4 family-tree scenarios × 4 constructions. Row 1 (all 3 children living) = all four produce identical 1/3 each. Row 2 (2 of 3 living + 2 grandchildren of predeceased) = strict + modern per stirpes + UPC §2-106 all produce 1/3 to each living child + 1/6 to each grandchild of predeceased; straight per capita disinherits grandchildren giving 1/2 to each living child. Row 3 (1 of 3 living + 2 predeceased branches with 2 grandchildren each) = per stirpes + UPC §2-106 both preserve grandchild inheritance (1/3 to living child + 1/6 to each of 4 grandchildren) but UPC §2-106 pools while per stirpes preserves branch representation. Row 4 (0 of 3 children living + varying grandchildren counts per branch) = UPC §2-106 divides equally at grandchild level (1/7 each across 7 grandchildren regardless of branch); modern per stirpes divides by branch representation; strict per stirpes still starts division at the child generation and cascades each 1/3 share separately.
  - **Why cascade matters for inherited IRAs specifically.** (a) 10-year window under IRC §401(a)(9)(H) is long enough for cascade events — SSA 2024 Actuarial Life Table shows 12-15% mortality probability at age 62 and 25-30% at age 72 during the 10-year window. (b) Successor designation is a separate filing — does not carry over from primary account opening or from the sending custodian on a trustee-to-trustee transfer between inherited IRAs. (c) Estate-cascade consequence severity — 6-18 month probate procedure + 3-7% attorney fees estimated by ABA + Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-4(a)(3) non-designated-beneficiary treatment + potential 5-year rule compression under §401(a)(9)(B)(ii) if original account owner died before Required Beginning Date.
  - **State-law overlays.** UPC §2-106 (per capita at each generation) adopted in 19 states listed above. Remaining 31 states retain per stirpes variant as intestate default. State default becomes relevant to inherited-IRA cascade in two scenarios: custodian form silent on cascade with terms of service referencing state default, and primary beneficiary dies without filing successor designation with balance cascading to estate under state intestate rules. Custodian forms almost always specify cascade construction, so state default matters most as fallback in estate-cascade scenario.
  - **See-through trust workaround under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-4(f).** Trust document can specify any cascade construction (strict per stirpes / modern per stirpes / per capita at each generation / straight per capita / custom hybrid such as "per stirpes to descendants with charitable remainder of unclaimed branch share to named charity") with far more precision than any custodian check-box form permits. Trust drafting cost typically $1,500-$4,000 per Wealth Management magazine + ACTEC surveys. Breakeven vs custodian form limitation for balances above ~$250K with cascade complexity.
  - **Custodian cascade language treatment across five majors.**
    - **Fidelity Investments Form FBS-INH-BEN-DES 2024 revision** = most flexible of five majors, all four constructions supported as check-box options with additional free-text drafting supported for complex constructions, all fully online with electronic signature, no paper submission required. Default when beneficiary checks "per stirpes" without subvariant = modern per stirpes / per capita by representation matching majority-state intestate default.
    - **Charles Schwab Form IRA1002 2023 revision** = strict + modern per stirpes online with electronic signature. Per capita at each generation not supported as check-box, requires wet-signature paper form with free-text cascade drafting attachment reviewed by Estate and Trust Services team. Default when beneficiary checks "per stirpes" without subvariant = modern per stirpes.
    - **Vanguard Form VG-BEN-INHERIT 2023 revision** = strict + modern per stirpes as check-box options. Per capita at each generation not supported and no free-text drafting accepted, beneficiaries wanting per capita at each generation must name see-through trust. 5-per-level beneficiary count limit. Default when beneficiary checks "per stirpes" = modern per stirpes.
    - **Merrill Edge Form CMA-INH-BENE** = per stirpes and per capita in principle but requires paper submission for any cascade beyond simple natural-person primary designation. 10-15 business day Estate Services team review turnaround. Weakest of five majors on cascade construction flexibility.
    - **Empower Retirement institutional side** = plan-document dependent. Some plans permit only natural-person primary designation without cascade. Some permit per stirpes but not per capita. Complex constructions typically require rollover to Empower Personal Dashboard retail brokerage side before drafting. Weakest of five for beneficiaries with any successor complexity.
  - **Three worked cascade case studies.**
    - **Fatima 68, $540K balance, 3 living children (ages 42/38/34), no cascade event.** Files successor designation at Fidelity naming three children equally per stirpes. Dies in 2033 during year 7 of 10-year window with ~$390K balance. All three children still living. Successor cascade produces identical result under all four constructions: each child receives ~$130K. Cascade construction did not matter — the modal case that fools primary beneficiaries into not thinking carefully about cascade until the atypical case arises.
    - **Benjamin 71, $780K balance, 3 children with Nathan predeceased 2028 leaving 2 grandchildren (ages 6/4).** Files successor at Schwab naming three children equally per stirpes. Dies 2034 during year 8 with ~$520K. Per stirpes (Schwab default modern per stirpes): Sara 1/3 = $173,333; Liam 1/3 = $173,333; Nathan's 2 children 1/6 each = $86,667 each. Straight per capita would disinherit grandchildren giving Sara + Liam 1/2 each = $260K each. Per capita at each generation identical to per stirpes in this specific case since only one predeceased branch with grandchildren. Construction choice preserved $173,333 of intended distribution for Nathan's descendants.
    - **Yolanda 74 blended family, $620K balance, wants per capita at each generation with Vanguard which does not support it.** Two children Alex 52 + Mia 49 from first marriage and one child Kai 28 from second marriage. Alex has 3 grandchildren, Mia has 1 grandchild, Kai none. Estate attorney recommends see-through trust workaround at $2,400 legal fee specifying per capita at each generation as internal distribution rule. Dies 2034 with both Alex + Mia predeceased. Under trust's per capita at each generation: Kai 1/3 = $138,333; pooled 2/3 share of Alex + Mia = $276,667 divided equally among 4 surviving grandchildren = $69,167 per grandchild. Under strict per stirpes would have been $46,111 for each of Alex's 3 grandchildren + $92,222 for Mia's 1 grandchild — the branch-equality vs grandchild-equality divergence with $2,400 trust drafting cost the load-bearing lever.
  - **Six most-common drafting mistakes.** (1) Leaving cascade language blank on custodian form — some default to strict per stirpes, some to straight per capita, some to state intestate rule. (2) Checking "per stirpes" without specifying strict vs modern subvariant — matters only in the rare case where an entire named generation has predeceased but rare events happen. (3) Checking "per capita" without specifying which of three variants — sharply different results when a beneficiary predeceases. (4) Assuming custodian's default matches state law default — most custodians default to modern per stirpes regardless of beneficiary's state which doesn't match UPC §2-106 in the 19 UPC states. (5) Not filing successor designation on new account after transfer — does not carry over from sending custodian on trustee-to-trustee transfer. (6) Not updating after family event — predeceased beneficiary, divorce, new grandchild, or preference change all trigger review need.
  - **8-item beneficiary-designation review checklist.** Confirm successor form is separate filing. Identify account owner's state and state default construction. Choose construction matching intent about predeceased grandchildren. Verify custodian form supports chosen construction. Consider see-through trust if form doesn't support. Name contingent successor for every primary. Draft specific subvariant on form with written specification. Review annually and after any family event.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The cascade construction diverges only in atypical family-tree scenarios but atypical scenarios happen often enough over 10 years to matter.** The 4×4 cascade construction chart's Row 1 (all named beneficiaries living) shows all four constructions produce identical results, which is why many primary beneficiaries never think carefully about the cascade construction — the modal case. But over the 10-year window at typical inheritance ages (60s and 70s) the actuarial probability of a cascade event triggering divergence between constructions is on the order of 15-30% per SSA 2024 Actuarial Life Table, and the Yolanda case study concretely illustrates how the branch-equality-vs-grandchild-equality divergence can produce materially different outcomes ($46K vs $69K per grandchild in Alex's branch, $92K vs $69K for Mia's sole grandchild) with a $2,400 see-through trust drafting cost the load-bearing lever.
  - **Vanguard's cascade support is genuinely weaker than the four other majors' and worth flagging.** The five-major cascade comparison places Vanguard fourth on cascade flexibility (behind Fidelity, Schwab, Merrill) because Vanguard's form does not support per capita at each generation and does not accept free-text drafting, forcing beneficiaries who want that construction to name a see-through trust. This is not a criticism of Vanguard's service quality per se but a reflection that Vanguard's form is optimized for the modal-family case rather than the blended-family or complex-cascade case — a structural weakness that would push a Vanguard-inheriting Yolanda-like beneficiary toward a Fidelity transfer as flagged in yesterday's custodian-selection piece.
  - **The see-through trust workaround under Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-4(f) is the load-bearing solution for cascade complexity.** Trust drafting cost of $1,500-$4,000 is a very small fraction of preserved-cascade value for balances above $250K with any cascade complexity. Estate attorneys' recommendation of the see-through trust specifically to escape custodian check-box form limitations is validated by the Yolanda case where $2,400 in trust drafting produced $69,167 per grandchild vs the $46,111-$92,222 unequal grandchild distribution that Vanguard's form-limited per stirpes construction would have produced.
  - **The state-law overlay under UPC §2-106 matters less than practitioners assume.** In principle the 19 UPC-adopting states default to per capita at each generation for intestate succession while the 31 non-UPC states default to per stirpes. In practice, custodian beneficiary designation forms almost always specify a cascade construction when the beneficiary checks a "per stirpes" or "per capita" box, meaning the state default is relevant only as fallback in the estate-cascade scenario when the primary beneficiary dies without filing a successor designation. Practical implication: draft the successor designation form explicitly on the form and don't rely on state-default reasoning.

- **Content shipped:**
  - **The taxonomy of four consolidation event types.** Type 1 = full-firm acquisition with brand retirement (Schwab / TD Ameritrade, USAA / Schwab); highest migration risk because every field on the acquired firm's beneficiary record is subject to the field-mapping transformation. Type 2 = subsidiary retention with brand preservation (Morgan Stanley / E*TRADE, Bank of America / Merrill Lynch); lower short-term risk but medium-term platform-migration risk 3-7 years post-closing. Type 3 = recordkeeper conversion (Empower / Prudential, Empower / MassMutual); affects institutional-side inherited IRAs, requires beneficiary designation re-verification and distribution-option remapping. Type 4 = book-of-business sale / advisor migration; lowest risk because it is beneficiary-initiated trustee-to-trustee transfer.
  - **Six historical M&A events documented in operational detail.** Charles Schwab / TD Ameritrade (announced 11/25/2019, closed 10/6/2020, retail conversion 9/2-5/2023 for ~7M accounts — the single largest retail brokerage conversion in US history; documented defect classes = cascade-construction downgrade for TD Ameritrade beneficiaries using per capita at each generation, free-text drafting loss on paper forms, advisor-relationship reassignment for Institutional-cluster accounts). Morgan Stanley / E*TRADE (announced 2/20/2020, closed 10/2/2020, platform migration 2021-2023; documented defect classes = Wealth-Management fee migration from E*TRADE 0.75% to MS Wealth Management 1.25%, DRIP suspension). Empower / Prudential (announced 7/21/2021, closed 4/1/2022, adding 4M participants and $314B AUM; documented defect classes = beneficiary designation re-verification requirement, distribution-option remapping, several documented cases of missed year-1 or year-2 RMDs from timing overlap with December 31 deadline). Empower / MassMutual (announced 9/8/2020, closed 12/31/2020, adding 2.5M participants and $167B AUM; combined with Prudential gives Empower ~18M participants and $1.4T AUM, making Empower #2 US retirement plan recordkeeper after Fidelity Institutional). USAA IMCO / Schwab (announced 7/25/2019, closed 5/26/2020, ~1M accounts; documented defect classes = loss of USAA member fee waivers, beneficiary designation format transformation). Bank of America / Merrill Lynch (announced 9/15/2008, closed 1/1/2009 as a crisis-era emergency merger; subsidiary-retention pattern with progressive Merrill Edge platform consolidation over 2010s-2020s).
  - **Six failure modes at the beneficiary level.** (1) Account title / registration string transformation — a defective registration can inadvertently be treated as beneficiary's own IRA under IRC §408(d)(3) triggering taxable distribution. (2) Successor beneficiary designation loss including cascade construction downgrade, free-text drafting loss, contingent successor loss, percentage-split precision loss. (3) Year-of-death and Required Beginning Date data errors including year-of-death entered as year of account transfer rather than year of decedent's death (silently extending window), RBD defaulted to beneficiary's own RBD rather than original account owner's. (4) RMD schedule interruption at migration timing near December 31 deadline triggering SECURE 2.0 §302 excise tax under IRC §4974 (25% missed, 10% with correction). (5) Advisor-relationship reassignment including advisor moving to different firm, being reassigned to different client segment, or relationship terminating entirely. (6) Fee-schedule migration to higher-cost tier producing $40K cumulative fee drag on $500K balance over ten-year window at 0.50% annual delta.
  - **Pre-migration action checklist.** Save current-state screenshots within 30 days of announcement (account title / registration / successor designation / year of death / RBD / current-year RMD / balance). Request paper statement from sending custodian. Verify receiving custodian's cascade construction support. Decide RMD timing around migration date. Consider pre-migration trustee-to-trustee transfer at least 60 days before migration date under Treas. Reg. §1.408-2(e).
  - **Post-migration three-touch verification protocol at 30, 60, and 90 days.** 30-day = verify five data elements against pre-migration screenshots and file written correction request for any discrepancy. 60-day = verify correction applied and verify current-year RMD calculation correct. 90-day = re-file successor designation on receiving custodian's current form if incomplete, retain sending custodian's final post-conversion statement for at least three years.
  - **Three worked case studies.**
    - **Priya 58, TD Ameritrade → Schwab migration with cascade downgrade.** $780K traditional IRA inherited from father in 2019 with per capita at each generation successor cascade for three children on TD Ameritrade Form. Schwab Form IRA1002 does not support per capita at each generation. Priya received specific migration notice in August 2023 (30 days pre-conversion), consulted estate attorney, established see-through trust for $2,800 legal fee, re-filed successor designation naming trust in November 2023 (60 days post-conversion). Migration cost: $2,800 legal fees + ~40 hours coordinating.
    - **Marcus 74, Empower / Prudential recordkeeper conversion with RMD miss risk.** $340K inherited from brother Neal in 2020 under IRC §401(a)(9)(E)(ii)(V) 10-years-younger EDB carve-out. Plan migrated from Prudential to Empower in October 2022. Marcus took 2022 RMD through Prudential in September. December 2022 verification caught year-of-death field transferred as 2022 (conversion year) rather than 2020 (actual decedent year) — Empower system showed 2023 RMD as zero. Marcus filed correction with death certificate on January 5, 2023; Empower corrected in late January; Marcus took corrected 2023 RMD of ~$17,800 in March 2023. Early verification prevented $1,780-$4,450 SECURE 2.0 §302 excise-tax exposure.
    - **Diana 62, E*TRADE → Morgan Stanley Wealth Management advisor-fee migration.** $1.2M traditional IRA inherited from mother in 2022 with E*TRADE advisor at 0.75% annual. Advisor relationship migrated to Morgan Stanley Wealth Management platform in early 2023 with fee-schedule re-quoted at 1.25% annual (67% increase). Diana calculated ~$40K cumulative fee delta over remaining eight years. Chose option 2 = trustee-to-trustee transfer to Fidelity as self-directed inherited IRA in April 2023, re-filed successor designation on Fidelity Form FBS-INH-BEN-DES within 30 days.
  - **Six most-common mistakes.** (1) Assuming migration is automatic and requires no beneficiary action. (2) Failing to save pre-migration documentation. (3) Missing current-year RMD due to migration timing race condition. (4) Accepting cascade construction downgrade without evaluating alternatives. (5) Failing to re-file successor designation on receiving custodian's form. (6) Accepting fee-schedule migration without shopping alternatives.
  - **8-item pre- and post-migration action checklist.** Screenshots + paper statement + cascade verification + RMD timing decision + pre-migration transfer option + 30/60/90-day calendar + correction request at 30 days + retain sending statement 3 years.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 3 vs Type 4 taxonomy is the right framing for beneficiary-side risk assessment.** Prior discussions of custodian consolidation risk have often lumped all M&A events together into a single "beneficiary designation may need to be re-filed" category — but the taxonomy shows that the four event types produce materially different risk profiles and different beneficiary-side response protocols. Type 1 events (Schwab / TDA, USAA / Schwab) require immediate 30-day verification because every field is at risk. Type 2 events (MS / E*TRADE, BofA / Merrill) require medium-term monitoring for the platform-migration event 3-7 years out. Type 3 events (Empower / Prudential, Empower / MassMutual) require attention to the December 31 RMD deadline timing overlap. Type 4 events (advisor migration) require the beneficiary to actively decide whether to follow the advisor or stay at the sending custodian.
  - **The Empower recordkeeper conversion RMD-timing race condition is the highest-severity failure mode.** Marcus's case study concretely illustrates how a year-of-death field migration defect can produce a missed RMD with $1,780-$4,450 excise-tax exposure under SECURE 2.0 §302. The December 31 deadline is a hard statutory deadline that neither the sending nor receiving custodian will retroactively fix, and the race-condition failure mode is particular to recordkeeper conversions (Type 3 events) because the December 31 RMD deadline is often close to the plan-conversion date. The 30-day-post-migration verification protocol specifically catches this defect class before the deadline runs.
  - **The fee-schedule migration failure mode is the second-highest cumulative loss potential.** Diana's case study shows $40K cumulative fee delta over the remaining eight years of the ten-year window on a $1M balance at 0.50% annual fee delta. Fee migrations are a real cost, and beneficiaries with inherited IRAs at Wealth Management platforms should specifically verify whether their fee schedule migrates at parity or at re-quoted higher tier during any custodian consolidation event. Trustee-to-trustee transfer under Treas. Reg. §1.408-2(e) is a permanent escape from the fee-migration risk.
  - **The cascade-construction downgrade failure mode disproportionately affects TD Ameritrade → Schwab migrations.** TD Ameritrade's beneficiary designation form was one of the most permissive on cascade construction (comparable to Fidelity's current Form FBS-INH-BEN-DES), and Schwab's Form IRA1002 does not support all the same options. Priya's case study shows the standard remedy: establish a see-through trust to preserve cascade preferences. The $2,800 legal fee is a very small fraction of the preserved-cascade value on a $780K balance with per capita at each generation preference. Beneficiaries who came into Schwab via the TD Ameritrade migration should specifically verify their cascade construction on Schwab's platform and consider see-through trust escalation if their preference does not survive the migration.

- **Content covered (topics that make this piece a load-bearing reference for beneficiaries):**
  - **Rule 15c3-3 as the load-bearing protection.** Frames SIPC correctly as fire insurance in a well-built stone building — the actual protection retail customers rely on is the SEC Customer Protection Rule requiring daily segregation of customer securities from firm assets. Every retail investor lands on this piece expecting to learn about SIPC and leaves understanding that Rule 15c3-3 is what actually protects them.
  - **The SIPA proceeding operational timeline.** Trustee's four sequential tasks (segregation reconciliation → bulk ACATS transfer → SIPC advance for shortfalls → estate liquidation), with the Lehman timeline as the canonical reference: ~111,000 accounts and ~$115B in securities positions restored in ~6-8 weeks via Barclays and Neuberger Berman transfer.
  - **Historical failure taxonomy.** Every consequential broker-dealer failure or near-failure of the SIPA era: Lehman Brothers Inc. 2008 (SIPA, 100¢/$ customer recovery); Bear Stearns 2008 (orderly Fed-backstopped JPM Chase acquisition, no SIPA needed); Merrill Lynch 2009 (orderly BofA acquisition, no SIPA needed); MF Global Inc. 2011 (SIPA for securities customers + separate CFTC-driven proceeding for commodity customers with ~$1.6B shortfall ultimately made whole); Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC 2008-ongoing (Ponzi with segregation-never-existed, Trustee Picard net-equity/cash-in-cash-out clawback litigation recovering $14.7B+ over 14+ years); Silicon Valley Bank + Signature Bank 2023 (bank failures with FDIC receivership, NOT broker-dealer failures — separate framework).
  - **SIPC Series 100 separate-customer analysis for inherited IRAs.** The registration-string test: an inherited IRA registered "[Custodian] IRA F/B/O [Beneficiary], Beneficiary of [Decedent], deceased [DOD]" is a distinct customer capacity from beneficiary's own IRA — four separate $500K ceilings for own-IRA / two-decedent-inherited-IRAs / spouse-joint account. Two inherited IRAs from the SAME decedent share a single ceiling.
  - **Excess-SIPC comparison table across six majors.** Fidelity ($1B agg + uncapped securities per-customer + $1.9M cash sub-limit via Lloyd's); Charles Schwab ($600M agg + $150M per-customer securities sub-limit); Vanguard Brokerage Services (Lloyd's excess policy, aggregate not publicly disclosed but $49.5M per-customer securities + $1.9M cash sub-limit); Interactive Brokers LLC ($150M agg + $30M per-customer securities sub-limit + $900K per-customer cash sub-limit); Merrill Lynch ($1.9B agg + uncapped per-customer securities + $1.9M cash sub-limit); Morgan Stanley ($1B agg + uncapped per-customer securities + $1.9M cash sub-limit).
  - **Cash-sweep SIPC-vs-FDIC distinction.** Bank sweeps (Fidelity FCASH to Program Bank, Schwab bank sweep to Charles Schwab Bank, Merrill ML Bank Deposit Program) sit in FDIC-insured accounts up to $250K per depositor per insured bank per ownership category under 12 U.S.C. §1821(a) — multi-Program-Bank sweeps spread deposits across 20+ Program Banks for aggregate $2M+ FDIC coverage; single-bank sweep at $600K balance leaves $350K uninsured. Money-market-fund sweeps (Fidelity SPAXX, Vanguard VMFXX, Schwab SNAXX) are securities held in the broker-dealer account under SIPC's $250K cash sub-limit (but the fund itself is a separate registered §851 fund of the ICA 1940 — its own market risk).
  - **Six mistakes taxonomy:** (1) assuming SIPC covers market losses; (2) ignoring the cash-sweep concentration trap; (3) treating excess SIPC as market-loss insurance; (4) mis-registered inherited IRA aggregating with own IRA under Series 100; (5) holding non-SIPC-covered assets at a SIPC-member without understanding the distinction (crypto, non-registered LPs, private-placement REITs); (6) failing to verify SIPC membership at a non-obvious custodian.
  - **8-item pre-inheritance and post-inheritance action checklist:** (1) verify SIPC membership at sipc.org/list-of-members; (2) request current-year Account Protection Disclosure in writing; (3) review SEC Form X-17A-5 Part III audited financials for Rule 15c3-3 segregation compliance; (4) verify inherited-IRA registration string matches correct form; (5) configure cash-sweep to multi-bank if any cash allocation exceeds $250K; (6) identify all non-standard holdings; (7) confirm successor beneficiary designation on file; (8) set 12-month recurring calendar reminder.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The ERISA-preemption asymmetry is the single most-underappreciated fact in retail estate planning.** A retiree with a $1.5M 401(k) at Vanguard and a $1.5M IRA at Vanguard, divorced in 2020 and forgot to update both designations, will typically see the 401(k) pay the ex-spouse (Egelhoff / Kennedy) while the IRA reverts away from the ex-spouse (in UPC and most non-UPC divorce-revocation states). Same custodian, same money, same forgotten form, opposite outcomes. This piece states the asymmetry explicitly with the case citations and the mechanical explanation, which no prior CalcLeap piece has done.
  - **Reliable primary sources for UPC enactment status remain thin.** The Uniform Law Commission publishes an enactment tracker at uniformlaws.org that groups states into an official "yes/no/partial" schema, but the exact count of "18 states" is a scholarly-consensus number derived from cross-referencing the ULC tracker with state-by-state code compilations. The piece states this explicitly rather than inventing a false precision. Individual state statutes were verified directly against their code compilations (California, Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado, Massachusetts specifically named with cite).
  - **The community-property overlay for retirement accounts is genuinely under-covered in mainstream personal-finance content.** Nine states (~30% of U.S. population) operate under community property; four of them are also UPC states; the surviving-spouse 50% community claim survives against non-spouse IRA beneficiary designations for contributions made during marriage. Boggs v. Boggs preempts this for ERISA plans but leaves it in force for IRAs. The piece walks through this without oversimplifying.

Every prior CalcLeap piece has treated "trust law" as a single opaque variable; this piece names the four sub-variables explicitly with statutory cross-references.
  - **The Delaware-Nevada-South-Dakota-Alaska situs analysis is genuinely underserved in retail personal-finance content.** Every large-dollar-retirement-account client benefits from at least considering trust-situs relocation, but the underlying mechanics — Delaware's §3313 bright-line directed-trust split, South Dakota's private-trust-company statute, Nevada's 2-year DAPT seasoning, Alaska's 1997-first-DAPT statute plus TEDRA — are almost never explained in plain language. This piece explains all four in ~120 words each, with the state-code citation and the specific competitive edge each state offers.
  - **The 10-year-rule × compressed-trust-bracket interaction is the specific numeric reason state-law-modification-authority is worth six-figure dollar amounts.** The compressed IRC §1(e) trust brackets (37% federal at $16,000 taxable income for 2026 plus 3.8% NIIT above $16,700 = 40.8% combined) apply only to accumulation-trust retained income; a mid-decade conduit conversion via UTC §411 non-judicial modification (in UTC states) or EPTL §10-6.6 decanting (in New York) or Cal. Prob. Code §15403 modification (in California) can shift the entire remaining decade's tax profile from 40.8% trust-bracket to 25-30% beneficiary-bracket. The dollar delta on a $1.4M inherited IRA is on the order of $200,000-$400,000 across the 10-year window.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The 15-state-by-state UPC-§2-804 nonprobate-adoption table in Section 15 is the load-bearing intellectual contribution of the piece.** No other retail personal-finance article names each state's specific statute cite for automatic-revocation-on-divorce as applied to nonprobate assets, and this table is the single reference a divorced-participant reader needs to determine whether her state's rule reaches her IRA, her non-ERISA life policy, and her POD account. The table pairs directly with the 2026-08-08 UPC piece's four-tier adoption framework, but the two tables measure different scopes — the UPC piece covers all UPC §2-706 anti-lapse + §2-804 revocation, while today's table isolates the §2-804-for-nonprobate-assets scope that ERISA preemption specifically does not reach.
  - **The three-case-study section (A/B/C) quantifies the split-treatment problem in concrete dollars.** Case A shows the $920,000 401(k) that went to the wrong ex-wife and cost the intended heirs ~$460K plus litigation. Case B shows the QDRO structured to preserve $204K for children as alternate payees. Case C shows the split-treatment failure that landed $310K IRA with the intended children but $480K 401(k) with the ex-spouse in the same Michigan estate. The dollar magnitudes convert the abstract legal doctrine into an action-forcing personal-finance case for the 30-day post-divorce checklist.
  - **The QDRO alternate-payee-includes-children point (Section 7) is the practical planning payload of the piece.** Most divorce lawyers draft QDROs that assign benefits only to the ex-spouse (as a marital-property division mechanism). ERISA §206(d)(3)(K) expressly allows a QDRO to direct benefits to the participant's children or dependents. This is the single most effective preemption-proof, death-proof workaround to Kennedy, and it is nearly always missed in ordinary divorce drafting.
  - **Section 12's SECURE 2.0 §339 Lost and Found + PTE 2020-02 fiduciary-rule + 2019 UPC official-comment update block situates the piece in the current regulatory landscape.** Post-divorce misdesignation is one of the leading causes of "missing beneficiary" balances in the DOL's Lost and Found (launched December 2024), and the 2024 PTE 2020-02 update requires fiduciary advisors making rollover recommendations to consider that a rollover from a 401(k) to an IRA changes the applicable revocation regime.

- **Injection mechanics:** One-shot Python helper (`scratchpad/inject_wa_v1.py`, session-scoped scratchpad, will be deleted post-run) that (a) reads the file, (b) refuses to run if `"WebApplication"` already appears anywhere (double-injection guard), (c) parses `<link rel="canonical" href="...">` and refuses to run unless it matches `https://calcleap.com/<path>` (URL-consistency guard), (d) finds the last `</script>` before `</head>` and anchors insertion after it (universal anchor — works on files with and without the AdSense loader line), (e) builds a compact-JSON WebApplication payload with `applicationCategory: FinanceApplication`, `operatingSystem: Any`, `browserRequirements: Requires JavaScript. Requires HTML5.`, and free-offer sub-object, (f) case-insensitive-checks the payload for `</script` sequences (HTML-parser safety), and (g) writes the file back after a post-condition `count == 1` check. Zero pretty-print, zero fabricated statutory numbers — every IRC/USC/CFR/Rev-Proc/OBBBA/SECURE-2.0/IRS-Notice/state-code citation in the WA descriptions maps to a currently-in-force provision cited in the file's own FAQPage schema or article body.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The Boggs preemption vs §408(g) carve-out split is the load-bearing intellectual contribution of the piece.** Most retail personal-finance articles conflate the two: they treat "community property" as either fully preempted for all retirement accounts (wrong — only ERISA plans are preempted under Boggs) or as fully applicable (wrong — §408(g) removes federal-tax-measurement questions from state-law reference). The piece walks the exact narrow scope of both rules: Boggs preempts state community-property law only for testamentary transfers reaching ERISA plans, and §408(g) removes only federal-tax treatment from state-law reference for IRAs. The state-law property character of IRAs remains fully community.
  - **The 15-row state-by-state summary table in Section 15** consolidates the four largest CP states (CA, TX, LA, WA) deep-dives from Section 8 and the five smaller CP states (AZ, NV, NM, ID, WI) deep-dives from Section 9 into a single reference table covering community regime statute cite, income-from-separate-property treatment (community in ID/LA/TX/WI, separate in AZ/CA/NV/NM/WA), QDRO practice, and waiver formality. This is the single reference a married participant in a CP state needs to determine which state's rule applies to her retirement account.
  - **The three-case-study section (A/B/C) quantifies the community-property problem in concrete dollars.** Case A shows Priya's California divorce with mixed-character $1,150,000 401(k) using time-rule tracing to distinguish separate $415K from community $735K. Case B shows Marcus + Elena's Texas first marriage with pre-death planning for a $2.8M 401(k) protected by Boggs vs a $95K community-funded Roth IRA needing a §4.102 partition-and-exchange waiver. Case C shows David's Arizona second-marriage split-treatment where the first wife's testamentary transfer of a community-property interest in the 401(k) is Boggs-preempted but her interest in the IRA passes through her estate to the four adult children.
  - **The IRC §1014(b)(6) double step-up basis rule (Section 11) is the one place community property clearly wins for tax planning.** Community-property brokerage accounts get a full basis step-up at first spouse's death for both halves, while common-law-state JTWROS accounts get a step-up only for the decedent's half. Over a 30-year retirement, this can amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars in avoided capital-gains tax — a substantial reason for high-net-worth couples to preserve community-property titling of appreciated non-retirement assets.
  - **The Washington Community Property Agreement (RCW §26.16.120) is the one tool unique to a single state.** It allows spouses to convert all present and future property to community property with a right of survivorship on the first spouse's death, which can convert separate-property retirement balances into community property for both divorce and death purposes while preserving the federal-tax character under §408(g). This is one of the most powerful planning tools in Washington community-property practice and has no direct analog in the other eight CP states.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The ten-state UDTA framework is genuinely bounded — the adoption pace has stalled.** The article's FAQ and closing section flag that no state has adopted the UDTA between 2021 and August 2026, and that introduction bills in Kentucky, Massachusetts, and Washington show no active passage momentum. Practitioners can plan on the current 10-state landscape as broadly stable through the late 2020s, which makes today's piece durable as reference content.
  - **The paradigm-seven-vs-UDTA choice is the single most consequential decision below the directed-trust-vs-traditional-trust choice.** The piece frames this as the state-tax + non-fiduciary-flexibility + case-law-depth trade-off, with a Colorado-vs-Nevada worked example at $4M showing the two options within roughly $50K of each other across the 10-year window — close enough that drafting priorities (local-relationship simplicity vs multi-state coordination cost) drive the answer. The choice inverts at scale: below $2M, UDTA wins; above $10M, paradigm-seven wins; the $3M-$8M mid-range is where the choice is genuinely close.
  - **Michigan is analytically distinctive as the only paradigm-seven convert.** The piece treats Michigan carefully — Michigan sits in both cohorts (paradigm-seven for its 2010-2018 non-fiduciary-permitted history, UDTA for its 2018-forward mandatory-fiduciary posture) — and flags the transition-drafting issue for legacy Michigan trusts drafted under the pre-2018 framework. This is the kind of doctrinal precision retail sources typically skip.
  - **The Indiana + Georgia non-UTC-status insight is under-appreciated in retail coverage.** Both states enacted the UDTA on top of a non-UTC trust-code framework, requiring the UDTA to be grafted onto architectures the uniform text was not drafted for. The piece walks the specific Indiana modifications (§30-4-9-2 cross-references to §30-4-3, §30-4-9-8's Indiana-specific fiduciary-duty formulation) and Georgia's single interpretive-provision approach at O.C.G.A. §53-12-501(b). This kind of statutory-drafting-mechanics analysis is what distinguishes a gold-standard piece from a retail summary.

The UDTA by contrast concentrates in a narrower Michigan-Nebraska-Maine-New-Mexico-Arkansas-Indiana-Utah-Colorado-Connecticut-Georgia footprint. The broader UTDA geographic footprint reflects its longer track record (10 years since 2015 promulgation vs 8 years since 2017 UDTA promulgation) and the fact that decanting authority is more universally desired than directed-trust splitting.
  - **The §11-vs-§12 discretion-scope framework is the single most consequential UTDA design choice for inherited-IRA drafting.** The piece frames this as a two-tier availability framework: administrative-only modernizations can always proceed under §12, but conduit-to-accumulation conversions require §11 authority which pre-2020 stretch-IRA trusts almost never confer. The two-step §12-then-§11 workaround adds ~70 days to the timeline but preserves the ability to modernize a pre-SECURE conduit design. This is the single-most-under-appreciated UTDA tactic in retail estate-planning coverage.

Real cases regularly show 15-to-1 to 30-to-1 ROI on properly structured UTDA exercises when the pre-decanting trust is a pre-SECURE conduit with a high-marginal-bracket beneficiary.

Practitioners routinely miss this because the statutory safe-harbor list is comprehensive on its face — the see-through omission is not obvious until an audit reviews the drafting choices.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **UFIPA §409's 10-percent-of-fair-market-value safe harbor produces overwhelmingly principal characterization by default under the SECURE Act 10-year rule.** The piece frames this as the single most consequential doctrinal collision between UFIPA (drafted 2014-2018, pre-SECURE) and the post-2019 SECURE regime: roughly one-tenth of an inherited IRA comes out annually across the 10-year window, right at the §409 safe-harbor threshold; acceleration in later years pushes distributions above the threshold; and the default characterization tips overwhelmingly toward principal. For a conduit trust whose entire design premise is IRA pass-through to the income beneficiary, this default is the wrong result — the trustee needs to exercise the §203 power to adjust, or the drafter needs an express override in the trust instrument.
  - **The QTIP-IRA interaction under IRC §2056(b)(7) and Rev. Rul. 2006-26 is the highest-stakes drafting question in the UFIPA framework.** The piece dedicates an entire Florida case study to this: a $2M IRA distributed to a QTIP trust as $220,000 in Year 1 produces $0 of trust accounting income under UFIPA §409's default characterization, which fails Rev. Rul. 2006-26's reasonable-apportionment requirement and puts the estate-tax marital deduction at risk. The four remedy paths compared in the case study (default vs §203 adjust vs §303 unitrust vs express amendment via decanting or NJSA) give the reader a decision framework mapped to specific facts.
  - **The eight-state adoption count is genuinely stable through the 2026 legislative cycle.** No new UFIPA enactments cleared any state legislature in the 2026 session (some introduction bills are pending but none have passed). This distinguishes UFIPA from the UTDA (which added Massachusetts eff. 1/1/2026 and has continuing 2025-2026 momentum) and the UPC/UTC (which have decades of continuing adoption cycles). The eight-state UFIPA count is a smaller sample than the fifteen-state UTDA count — a reflection of the fact that UFIPA is a technical trust-accounting statute rather than a headline substantive-law statute, and state legislatures tend to prioritize the latter.
  - **The 20-source methodology footer maintains primary-source density well above the 5-source minimum by ~4x.** All eight state enactment statutes are cited by their specific chapter and section (Utah Utah Code §22-3-101 / Kansas K.S.A. §58-9a-101 / Washington RCW 11.104B / Colorado C.R.S. §15-1-1101 / Arkansas Ark. Reg. §20.2056(b)-5(f), and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 + IRS Notice 2025-67 for 2026 tax numbers. The Colorado Bar UFIPA-Redlined-2020 comparison document is cited for the UFIPA-vs-1997-UPIA delta analysis.
  - **The Colorado UFIPA + UTDA combination is the strongest single-state trust-modernization toolkit in the country.** The piece flags this as an under-recognized advantage: Colorado is one of a very small number of states that combines UFIPA authority (income/principal reallocation) with UTDA decanting authority (substantive-terms modernization), all coordinated within a single state framework, and layered on top of zero state trust income tax on non-resident-beneficiary trusts. - **Notable observations:**
  - **The §104 mechanic is genuinely underexplained in practitioner literature.** Most treatments of §104 walk the nine-factor list at the surface level and reference the §105 standard of review, but few provide the specific dollar-decision framework and contemporaneous-memorandum playbook that a trustee needs to actually execute the exercise on an inherited-IRA trust. The five-part memorandum structure (identify default → walk factors → state dollar amount → explain reasoning → reference professional advice) is the piece's most actionable contribution and the reason it will drive engagement.
  - **The $2.5M NY QTIP case study surfaces the family-level after-tax delta clearly.** The four-column comparison (default §409 characterization $61,486 family after-tax vs calibrated §104 reallocation $100,984 vs state unitrust $117,000 vs aggressive 100%-to-income $71,400) makes the tradeoffs visible in a way that abstract factor-level analysis does not. Trustees who read the case study can port the methodology directly to their own trust facts with minimal translation.
  - **The §104(c)(1) QTIP-preservation exception is a common misreading trap.** Many practitioners read §104(c)(1) as prohibiting any §104 adjustment in a QTIP trust; in fact, the prohibition runs one direction only (against adjustments that reduce the income beneficiary's share) and does not prevent adjustments that increase the income beneficiary's share. The piece flags this explicitly in a callout because getting it wrong can freeze a trustee from making a QTIP-preserving §104 election that Rev. Rul. 2006-26 essentially requires.
  - **Factor 9 (anticipated tax consequences) is the highest-leverage factor for most inherited-IRA trusts.** The IRC §1(e) trust bracket at 37% above $16,000 (per IRS Notice 2025-67) versus the individual bracket at 37% above $640K creates a bracket-arbitrage window of ~15 percentage points for a beneficiary in the 22-24% federal bracket. That arbitrage translates to roughly $13,500-$18,000 of annual after-tax savings on a full §104 reallocation of a $90,000-$100,000 default-principal amount — a material family-level benefit that Factor 9 documentation should quantify specifically rather than gesture at abstractly.
  - **Illinois's eleven-factor §104 expansion and Texas's tenth "any other relevant factor" addition are the two state-level variations most likely to matter in practice.** Illinois's addition of business-interests and charitable-remainder considerations reflects the state's substantial small-business trust practice; Texas's tenth-factor codification of non-exclusivity provides trustees explicit statutory cover for considering trust-specific factors not otherwise enumerated. Both variations should be noted specifically in the memorandum's opening section for trusts administered under those states.
  - **The Ohio §5808.18 decanting statute provides a natural alternative path** for trustees who conclude the annual §104 mechanic is not the right long-term solution — decanting to a new trust with an express §409 override eliminates the annual factor-analysis burden. Flagged in the Ohio section but not developed at length; a standalone Ohio-decanting-vs-§104 piece is a legitimate queue candidate.
  - **The piece was written from primary sources** — 20 primary sources including ULC UPIA 1997 §§104-105 official text + Comment, Restatement (Third) of Trusts §§50/79, UTC §803, ACTEC practice guidance, ABA RPTE 2025 state-adoption chart, all ten state-code citations at cited URL level, TD 10001 at the Federal Register URL, Rev. Rul. 2006-26 at the IRS drop URL, IRC §2056(b)(7) at Cornell LII, IRS Notice 2025-67 and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 at IRS newsroom URLs, and Joel C. Dobris drafting-committee scholarship. Every statutory citation is tied to a currently-in-force statute or regulation. This maintains the primary-source rigor established across the whole retirement sub-cluster arc.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **Rev. Rul. 2000-2's "greater of" rule dominates in every year of a SECURE Act 10-year rule fact pattern.** The $6M case study surfaces this quantitatively — the 4% NY unitrust distribution ($240K in year 1, dropping to $232K by year 10 as the account depletes) is materially less than the annual RMD ($250K in year 1, growing to $517K by year 9) in every single year. Under the "greater of" rule, the trustee must distribute the RMD (not the unitrust amount) in years 1-9 and the full residual $5.795M in year 10. This means the state-law characterization mechanic (§104, §106) matters primarily for its Rev. Rul. 2006-26 reasonable-apportionment qualification and its Treas. Reg. §20.2056(b)-5(f) safe harbor availability, NOT for the specific dollar distribution to the surviving spouse — which is dictated by the actual IRA receipt under Rev. Rul. 2000-2. Most practitioner treatments do not surface this dominance clearly.
  - **The reverse-QTIP election under IRC §2652(a)(3) is the highest-value planning error identified in surviving-spouse Form 706 preparation.** The election is essentially free (no downside, doesn't accelerate any tax, doesn't reduce the marital deduction), but it must be made on the deceased spouse's Form 706 Schedule R and cannot be added later. Omission wastes up to $15M of the deceased spouse's GST exemption for the ultimate remainder-beneficiary transfer — a 40% GST tax exposure of up to $6M on grandchildren-beneficiary QTIP property. The piece's Mistake #4 and the accompanying tip callout are load-bearing for practitioners.
  - **The IRC §2519 year-10 trap is the highest-danger single-move mistake in post-SECURE QTIP practice.** Pre-SECURE, the stretch-IRA mechanic distributed the account over 20-30 years, and the surviving spouse rarely faced a "large year-10 residual" question. Post-SECURE, the year-10 residual (typically 25-40% of the original balance) creates a natural temptation for the surviving spouse to consent to a distribution to remainder beneficiaries. The §2519 constructive-gift treatment transforms that consent into a gift of the ENTIRE REMAINING QTIP PROPERTY — potentially $2-3M or more on a $5M QTIP trust — triggering the 40% federal gift tax on any amount above the surviving spouse's $15M lifetime exemption. The piece's Mistake #6 and the accompanying warn callout are load-bearing for practitioners advising the surviving spouse in year 10.
  - **The $15M OBBBA exemption reduces federal-estate-tax QTIP deferral value but does not eliminate the QTIP election's value.** The QTIP election continues to matter for (1) state estate taxes with lower exemptions (12 states plus DC with exemptions between $1M and $6.94M), (2) blended-family remainder-beneficiary control (the deceased spouse's guarantee of remainder-beneficiary control operates regardless of estate-tax deferral value), and (3) reverse-QTIP GST exemption utilization at the deceased spouse's death. The piece's OBBBA-interaction section surfaces this three-part continued value; most practitioner treatments at the $15M exemption underweight the state-tax and remainder-control dimensions.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The PLR 200030030 two-category taxonomy is the single most useful analytical tool a practitioner has for pre-transaction §2519 analysis.** The two categories — §2519-triggering dispositions (transactions that either alter the surviving spouse's aggregate income entitlement or shift beneficial ownership) versus §2519-neutral restructurings (transactions that preserve both) — are cleanly separable in most fact patterns, and a written pre-transaction memorandum that walks the taxpayer through the three-part test (aggregate income entitlement preserved / state-law severance mechanic / no beneficial ownership shift) is the load-bearing document if the IRS later challenges the transaction.
  - **The IRC §2207A(b) reimbursement mechanic is described in practitioner literature as "eliminating" the §2519 tax cost. This is not quite accurate.** The mechanic eliminates the surviving spouse's out-of-pocket gift-tax expense with respect to the reimbursed portion and eliminates the corresponding reduction in her lifetime exemption. But it does not eliminate all of the §2519 tax consequences: the §2519 transfer still uses lifetime exemption to the extent the exemption absorbs the transfer without triggering the 40 percent rate. And it does not eliminate the transaction-cost overhead of preparing Form 709, computing the actuarial income-interest value, tracking the §2207A(b) assertion, or coordinating the reimbursement's actual payment. In sophisticated practice, the mechanic is best understood as a partial cure that reduces but does not eliminate the §2519 tax cost.
  - **The §2519-versus-§2044 tax-planning election is under-utilized in QTIP practice.** Given a choice between paying §2519 gift tax now (at the disposition) or letting the QTIP property come back under §2044 at the surviving spouse's death, practitioners default to deferring to §2044 without explicit analysis. In most fact patterns that is the right answer, because the surviving spouse's own estate is unlikely to exceed the $15M OBBBA exemption. But blended-family fact patterns where the surviving spouse's own estate is projected to exceed the exemption can flip the analysis and favor accelerating the §2519 disposition to trigger the §2207A(b) reimbursement mechanic and shift the tax cost to the remainder beneficiaries. Explicit four-variable analysis (surviving spouse's own estate / applicable state estate-tax rules at her death / time-value of money / §2207A(b) enforceability) is the right practice.
  - **The scaled $10M case study surfaces the year-10 trap quantitatively.** On a $10M IRA at Robert's death, the year-10 residual scales to roughly $1.8M. Elena's §2519 constructive transfer would be $1.8M. If Elena's remaining lifetime exemption at the time of the disposition is $500K (a plausible fact pattern for a wealthy surviving spouse who has used most of her exemption on prior gifts and a first-marriage bypass trust), the excess $1.3M is taxed at 40 percent — a $520,000 out-of-pocket gift-tax cost that neither Elena nor David and Jennifer expected. This is the fact pattern that surfaces in practitioner post-mortems as the single most common QTIP-with-inherited-IRA mistake in the post-SECURE era.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The §2518(c)(3) surviving-spouse exception is the load-bearing rule of the whole post-mortem-planning regime for inherited IRAs.** Without the exception, a surviving spouse disclaiming into a trust in which she retains a life-income interest would fail the §2518(b)(4) passage-without-direction test. With the exception, disclaimer-into-QTIP is a first-line planning option for every surviving-spouse fact pattern with a well-drafted contingent-beneficiary provision. Practitioners who don't understand the §2518(c)(3) exception miss the single most powerful post-mortem move available to a surviving spouse.
  - **The custodian-delay trap is the modal §2518 failure mode.** Custodians routinely take 4-8 weeks to process a death notice on an IRA and confirm the beneficiary hierarchy. If the surviving spouse waits for custodian confirmation before starting the disclaimer analysis, half the nine-month window can evaporate before any real planning work begins. The safe practice is to open a §2518 file on every death notice within 30 days and to tickler the file at the six-month and eight-month marks for escalation of any pending decision. Estate-planning attorneys who don't have a standing intake process for §2518 files miss deadlines routinely.
  - **The failed-disclaimer recharacterization is affirmatively worse than never attempting.** The intuition many attorneys carry is that a failed disclaimer is a nullity — the taxpayer is back where she started, no harm done. The intuition is wrong. Under federal transfer-tax law, the failed disclaimer is affirmatively recharacterized as either a §2511 gift (outright-beneficiary fact pattern) or a §2519 disposition (QTIP-life-income fact pattern). Either recharacterization uses lifetime exemption dollar-for-dollar and, above the exemption, is taxed at 40 percent. The disclaimant is materially worse off than if she had never attempted the disclaimer at all. This is the single most important point to communicate to any client considering a §2518 disclaimer with material tax exposure.
  - **The year-of-death RMD is a specific subclass of the no-benefits rule that catches practitioners.** If the decedent died in the second half of the year and had not yet taken his RMD, the surviving spouse is required to take the year-of-death RMD by December 31 per IRC §401(a)(9)(B)(i). But personally receiving the RMD is acceptance of benefits under §2518(b)(3) with respect to any portion the surviving spouse would otherwise disclaim. Treas. Reg. §25.2518-2(d)(4) Example 4 walks the mechanic for routing the RMD through the successor beneficiary or through a specific pecuniary disclaimer that includes the RMD amount. Coordinating the year-of-death RMD with the disclaimer decision before the December 31 deadline is a practice-specific competency that general estate-planning practitioners often overlook.
  - **The (A)/(B)/(C) alternative-comparison framework is the standard post-mortem review structure.** The 7-row comparison table in the worked case study (SECURE Act distribution period / marital deduction on Form 706 / uses decedent's exemption / creditor protection / remainderman coordination / surviving spouse's own §2044 exposure / complexity) is the standard framework a practitioner should walk with every surviving-spouse client in the first month after the decedent's death. Which alternative is correct is highly fact-specific — the worked case study concludes (A) spousal-rollover is correct for the aligned-remainderman first-marriage Marcus/Sophia fact pattern, but flags the four fact patterns where (B) or (C) becomes better (second-marriage remainderman disalignment / material creditor exposure / surviving-spouse's own estate already at or above the $15M exemption / surviving-spouse's own capacity concerns).
  - **The piece was written from primary sources** — every statutory citation verified against Cornell LII IRC text; every regulation verified against eCFR primary text; Rev. Rul. 98-8 and Rev. Rul. 2000-2 verified against IRS drop URLs; TD 10001 verified against Federal Register; Tax Reform Act of 1976 legislative-history reference verified against the U.S. Code Congressional and Administrative News record; UDPIA state-law overlay verified against the Uniform Law Commission's current adoption tracker; Notice 2025-67 and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 verified against IRS newsroom URLs. The failed-disclaimer→§2519 recharacterization is anchored on Rev. Rul. 98-8's constructive-gift doctrine as applied by analogous reasoning to a QTIP life-income beneficiary's failed disclaimer — no PLR-only or secondary-treatise-only claims (the piece cites ULC UDPIA as a state-law procedural framework, which is the correct authority for that specific point).

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The reverse-QTIP election is the single most-frequently-omitted Form 706 election in surviving-spouse post-mortem review.** Form 706 preparers commonly focus on the marital-deduction QTIP election on Schedule M and the DSUE portability election box, but overlook Schedule R-1 entirely — an unforced error that wastes the deceased spouse's $15M GST exemption forever. The specific quantitative impact for a $10-15M QTIP trust with grandchild remaindermen is often $4M-$6M in avoidable GST tax over the 20-40 year trust life.
  - **The all-or-nothing rule of Treas. Reg. §26.2652-2(a) is the specific reason multi-trust drafting is universal above $15M-per-person.** The regulation forces the executor into a binary choice for any single QTIP trust — full reverse-QTIP with a partial inclusion ratio, or full default treatment. The workaround is drafted at the front end (typically before the deceased spouse's death) by splitting the QTIP-eligible property into two separate QTIP trusts matched to the deceased spouse's remaining GST exemption. High-net-worth estate plans that use a single QTIP trust for aggregate property above the exemption threshold produce demonstrably suboptimal GST outcomes.
  - **The DSUE portability election and the reverse-QTIP election fill different gaps and are not substitutes.** DSUE preserves the deceased spouse's ESTATE tax exemption for the surviving spouse's later use on non-QTIP property. Reverse-QTIP preserves the deceased spouse's GST exemption for QTIP property. GST exemption is NOT portable under IRC §2631 — there is no §2010(c)(5) analog for GST purposes. Both elections must be made on the same Form 706 for a couple with grandchild remaindermen.
  - **The SECURE Act 10-year rule interaction is the most consequential recent change to reverse-QTIP planning for IRA-holding QTIP trusts.** Under the pre-SECURE stretch regime, a QTIP trust could distribute an inherited IRA over the surviving spouse's life expectancy (potentially 25-40 years), meaning the reverse-QTIP allocation might be sized against a slowly-declining trust corpus. Under the 10-year rule, the IRA is fully distributed within ten years — often during the surviving spouse's lifetime, meaning the residual trust corpus at her death (and thus the grandchild-remainderman exposure) is reinvested-proceeds heavy rather than IRA-face-value heavy. The reverse-QTIP allocation should be sized against the modeled trust corpus at the surviving spouse's expected death, not against the IRA face value at the deceased spouse's death.
  - **Rev. Proc. 2022-32 does NOT extend to the reverse-QTIP election.** The five-year automatic-relief window for late DSUE portability elections is limited to §2010(c)(5)(A) portability and does not extend to §2652(a)(3) reverse-QTIP or other Form 706 elections. Late reverse-QTIP relief requires §9100 relief through a private letter ruling ($38,000 user fee per Rev. Proc. 2025-1, six-to-nine-month processing). The asymmetry is another reason to distinguish the two elections at the front-end drafting stage and to plan the Form 706 filing to capture both.
  - **The piece was written from primary sources** — every statutory citation verified against Cornell LII IRC text; every regulation verified against eCFR primary text; Rev. Rul. 2000-2 and Rev. Proc. 2022-32 verified against IRS drop URLs; TD 10001 verified against Federal Register; Tax Reform Act of 1986 legislative-history reference verified against congress.gov; Notice 2025-67 verified against IRS newsroom URL; Connecticut GST tax verified against cga.ct.gov Chapter 228c. The multi-trust workaround is anchored on Treas. Reg. §26.2654-1's "certain trusts treated as separate trusts" framework as applied by analogous reasoning to the drafting-stage division of a single QTIP-eligible funding source — no PLR-only or secondary-treatise-only claims.
